But the thing that she gets at in that essay is that, you know, there is a passion for the subject that a student might exhibit or have an interest in an intellectual journey, and women, when they are expressing that interest, have that interest, can have that interest diverted by their professor into like, “now we’re having a romantic relationship.” Whereas men will often have that introverted into like, “We’re having these long stimulating conversations about these issues.” And so you are actually taking advantage of your role to not push your student towards this intellectual apotheosis, but towards your own sexual gratification.

And I think, to me, what this essay and what many things like this get at is like, what you want is for people to think of women differently, as like not just as — as being people who are, you might interact with in non-sexual ways, even if you find them attractive, in the same way that you might, you know, interact with men in that role. And that is the goal.

And I just — it’s a really, really hard thing to do to get people to behave this way. And I — while I have my criticisms of these leadershipless movements, my criticism of that is largely downstream of the fact that social media has made it really, really easy for someone to be an author, for someone to be like, start up a protest, and it doesn’t require the institutional force of like an NAACP or whatever it is in order to generate that public visibility. And as a result, people who are upset can just sort of be a movement without it actually indicating anything about an organizational structure that has the ability to affect change in policy.

Matthew Yglesias: So, OK, but I think — I mean, this is nobody’s fault because it’s the nature of a leaderless movement.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But I think this Srinivasan essay, which came out quite a bit after peak Me Too, is interesting precisely because it is outlining a much more specific idea, and an idea that’s quite different from the power dynamic idea that is more commonly invoked.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: There was just a case where there was a story in the New York Post, and it said that Sen. Ruben Gallego, when he was a young House member, had dated staffers in other House offices. I think it was Anna Paulina Luna — a Republican, but who doesn’t like Gallego — she did a tweet, and she was like, “this is wrong because of the extreme power differential that exists.” And it was funny because she’s a conservative Republican, and she’s invoking this lib power dynamic kind of thing.

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: And then most people just kind of shrugged it off because there’s no formal authority that a House member has against staffers in other members’ offices. And there isn’t a rule against it or anything like it. And so it’s like the world moves on, right?

I think if you could re-rephrase the complaint in Srinivasian terms, it becomes a little bit clearer what you are trying to say there, which is essentially that members of Congress and congressional staffers in other offices are bound to interact in contexts that are not like boss-reportee, but that are professional in nature.

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? Like, you’re talking to the legislative director in somebody else’s office. Even if you’re at a happy hour, right, it’s like a Democratic House happy hour. It’s a work event, right?

And so, there’s this idea that Srinivasan is putting on the table, that we want to completely kind of silo off our professional interactions with people from sexual interactions with people, because it is going to disproportionately hamper the work of women, whether it’s in a scholarly context, but anything where it’s like you have a passion for politics, that’s why you’re there. You’re interested in talking to members because they are senior figures in the pantheon.

Jerusalem Demsas: And it’s exciting. If you’re a young person, you’re like, “Oh cool.”

Matthew Yglesias: Exactly. And that is actually a different idea from the idea that has been mainly put forward here. And I think her book — she did the podcast tour, and the book was respectfully reviewed, and if you’re a thinky person, you should be familiar with these ideas. But it’s also at a level of if people want to scandal monger about a House member, that it’s not expressed in those terms.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Because it’s not the actual common social understanding of what the complaint is here.

Jerusalem Demsas: This is what I’m saying. Me Too didn’t go far enough. We need Srinivasian Me Too.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, maybe, right? But it’s a whole different process, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: It’s a whole different — because that’s actually talking — because part of Me Too was putting these power dynamics on a continuum with really coercive physical assault and rape, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And part of what you’re saying, and this Srinivasian concept is, is like to say “No, that’s actually not the issue here,” right? Like, it’s not fundamentally a question of coercion.

And then you open like a whole set of other conversations that people are having about dating apps, right? And the shift of, for the longest time — I shouldn’t say for the longest time. For a good span of time, it was very common for people to meet their wives and husbands through the workplace or workplace-related socializing.

And now everything has moved to apps and dating websites and things like that. And the technology has at least made it feasible to say, “OK, it’s like if you want to find a date with somebody, you go here, right? You go to the dating website.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: And if you want to just shoot the shit with people at a work-adjacent happy hour, you go to the happy hour. And these are completely distinct spheres of human life.

I have aged out of this. I met my wife on Match.com, etc. It’s all fine by me. Let’s have a separation. But a lot of people seem actually very unhappy with the kind of apps-based dating universe. And it would be good, I think, to explicitly have that conversation rather than the conversation about power.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. I mean, I think there are a couple things here. One is like this question of solidarity, right? Which is like, I think this is a difficult thing in all social movements, which is that the thing you want to do, especially if you are in a minority, which women technically are not in a minority, but if you’re in a disadvantaged situation, is you want to create as much — as many people as possible who feel like they are invested in your movement personally, right?

And this is like the invention of Asian American as an identity, right? That brings together someone who’s Hmong with someone who’s, you know, Chinese. I mean, just it’s like a bunch of different people with a bunch of different technically cleaving differences. But we’re gonna have this big umbrella understanding like we are Asian American. There are harms that happen to our community that we have in common with one another. We’re gonna identify with those harms.

Like, this is — this is politics, right? Like, you need to do this in order to have the interests of sometimes a very small minority of people actually respected.

And so, I remember during Me Too, right, there were these articles that were really focused on the harassment that restaurant servers faced, and that, you know, in order to get tips, you had to be really OK and friendly and often welcoming of interactions that were sexually inappropriate or that were really uncomfortable, and you couldn’t really express that because your actual financial needs were on the line.

I remember there was one article, I forget where it was, we can put it in the show notes, that talked about how, you know, servers had to be OK with sexual harassment from their colleagues in order to make sure that, you know, if the cook is mad at you for being shitty about how he commented on your body, then maybe he will burn your food and you won’t get tips, or he won’t treat your lunch order as being as important to rush out the door, and then people will be mad about how long it took to get their food.

And, you know, I think that every person understands that there’s like really bad cases of sexual abuse and, and rape, and there’s also like really bad cases of sexual harassment when someone’s in an extremely vulnerable economic position that exceeds that of high-powered professional working-class, white-collar women in media or in, you know, in, in Hollywood or whatever.

But tying together the fates of all these people in like a solidaristic movement is like how you get change. Like you need the power of the women in Hollywood to be with the women who are servers at, you know, Wendy’s or whatever it is.

And that is a difficult process because often — we see this time and again, right — when these kinds of processes happen, that solidarity is often used to attack sometimes the low-hanging fruit. Which is stuff that doesn’t actually benefit clearly the women who are the most harmed.

But to me, I mean obviously this is very hard to do, but you know we — you would want — you would want to find out like is life better for young girls who are doing serving jobs? Like, it seems unclear to me. Like, in some ways it seems like tip culture has shifted significantly. It seems like somewhat in relation to this, but not largely in relation to this, mostly in relation to COVID and you know tipping your — your waitstaff appropriately. And has that been the big shift there?

So, I think that a big part of the critique here is like, how do you manage a solidaristic movement where the interests are like so actually divergent in some cases because the class position of the people in question is quite different?

And I don’t know, I mean, it’s just a hard problem. And it’s very, very difficult right now to imagine a feminist organization or any kind of like, you know, social movement organization being able to maintain a level of discipline over all the people who are interested in this movement and consider themselves a part of it in order to say, “Yeah, like, this is what we’re fighting for. These are the rules. No, that doesn’t count.”

Because anyone can get 10,000 views — or sorry, like 10 million views on Twitter by saying, like, someone’s a sexual harasser, and then they’re viewed as part of this other thing that like, you know…

Matthew Yglesias: Well, that’s why I just, like, I want to know. Because, I mean, I agree, right? It’s like, everybody’s working with the world that exists, and they can’t do certain things.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And, I mean, I’m just curious, and I think it’s been underexplored, like, what has changed actually? Like, are things different? Are they better? Like, in what way? Like, what happened here?

Because it seems to me like certain kinds of stories that would have run in 2018 just wouldn’t run today. That the Harvey Weinstein investigation happened originally because this is a super prominent person engaged in really egregious misconduct.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And then that came out, there was a lot of discussion about it, there was a lot of follow-on stuff, there was Matt Lauer. And so then the bar starts getting lowered for how noteworthy does something have to be to get published. And then other things happened, you know, and the world moves on.

Jerusalem Demsas: It’s obviously very difficult to quantify this, not in a way that I would — I would love. I think that it is really clear to me that a lot of — I mean, if you want to look just specifically in Hollywood, I mean, the rise of intimacy coordinators is literally a function of people worrying that these sexual scenes are not being treated in a professional context. They’re making people uncomfortable.

Like that’s like — that was like not a thing pre-Me Too. And now it’s like very much a thing like everywhere and mandated in many studios.

Matthew Yglesias: But is a waitress less likely to be sexually harassed?

Jerusalem Demsas: I don’t know.

Matthew Yglesias: By the cook?

Jerusalem Demsas: I have no idea.

Matthew Yglesias: No, me neither. It just, it seems like a thing that has been so discussed has been very little measured.

Jerusalem Demsas: But I actually think this is like a measurement problem rather than an interest problem. Like, I just think it’s like how — you would measure this through reporting, but reporting is obviously variable, particularly in these categories where there’s a lot of gray area.

And so, are people reporting different things now than they were before? And so, actually there’s increased reporting as a result of people being willing to understand that they’re, you know, reporting something that was already happening earlier. Like, I think it’s actually like almost unknowable to know when was peak sexual harassment happening. Like, I just — it’s just like not something you can understand.

But I just like, as, like, an observer of culture, when I watch like rom-coms or things like that now, the shifting script I think is incredibly evident in culture. Like, it was a really normal trope in many, many kind of romantic comedies to imagine like, you know, you, you get drunk and you go home with, you know, with someone and then you guys end up having sex in the morning. You’re like, “Oh shit, what did I do, right?”

Like the most popular, I think — I mean, I don’t have the stats in front of me, but an extremely popular romantic TV show that has just come out on Amazon Prime, which is called Off Campus. It’s like the straight Heated Rivalry, the straight hockey TV show, for anyone who hasn’t listened to this.

I mean, there’s like a literal scene where the main love interest is drunk and the guy who is like the heartthrob of the movie doesn’t have sex with her. And it’s not like a cringe, like whatever. It’s just like, oh, of course, like he’s not gonna have sex with her right now. And it just — everyone just kind of moves on.

I’m just like, these are things that are very difficult to quantify, but I just do think social scripts have shifted in a way that have made people, like, more aware of what types of behavior are like good or what it means to be like a good person.

Like, that movie, that TV show does not say “never have sex if you’ve had a drink.” But it indicates to you that you should be thoughtful about when you are choosing to engage in the first-time sexual encounter with someone and whether it’s appropriate to do that when they seem impaired.

Matthew Yglesias: Time for some peer review?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, now you guys all have to go watch this show.

Matthew Yglesias: That’s right. Yeah, we got to stop — Well…

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, for the actually…

Matthew Yglesias: No, listen to the peer review segment and then go watch this show.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, no, they haven’t sponsored us yet, so maybe don’t go watch the show.

Matthew Yglesias: OK, don’t.

Jerusalem Demsas: Amazon Prime, we’re waiting.

Matthew Yglesias: All right, we’ll take a break and then come to something that we can quantify.

Jerusalem Demsas: All right, welcome back. So this is our peer review section where we talk about a recent working paper or white paper. Today’s is “Dynamic Individuals, Static Neighborhoods: Migration and Earnings Changes in Poor Neighborhoods.” Not a very fun title, but it is a very descriptive title. These are by some economists: Andrew Garin, Evan Mast, Ethan Jenkins, and Bryan Stuart. They’re at various different universities.

So there’s like this problem that this paper is trying to engage in, which is sort of this why is it that some poor neighborhoods stay poor? Like there are some places in town, like anywhere you live, where you’re like this place has been poor forever. Like what’s going on here, right?

And there’s like this — often this view where it’s just like, oh well, it’s almost like it’s like endemic to this population of people. And what this paper does is finds that actually the migration rates, like people leaving these neighborhoods, is actually incredibly high. Like, people leave poorer neighborhoods all the time at higher rates than other people are moving out of other neighborhoods. And it is when they’re able to make more money that people immediately leave, which creates this really difficult cycle, right?

Where if the people who are now making money don’t stay and continue to pay rent and go to the local shops or whatever, that place is actually suffering from constant drain of its most productive individuals that make it difficult for those neighborhoods to ever kind of rise up out of it.

But this should shift people’s, I think, conventional understandings of that’s like the poor part of town where poor people live to like, yeah, anyone who’s lived there for some small period of time just kind of gets the hell out of Dodge the second they’re able to get a job, they’re able to afford housing opportunities in better neighborhoods. And I really — there’s so much talk about in this paper, but I don’t know, Matt, if you have kind of your reactions.

Matthew Yglesias: Right. So, I mean, I just think — to kind of like set the groundwork here, right? Because America has a political system in which elected officials represent specific geographies.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: So if the geography that you represent contains a lot of troubled people, or just people who are poor, right, there’s this natural impulse to say, “I want a place-based solution. I want this universe of low-income South Bronx neighborhoods that I represent to not be like that anymore.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But there’s only two ways that that can happen: The individual people who live there can get more money, or different people who don’t live there and have money can move there.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? Like, just logically, those are the two possibilities. And the problem that we see is that when a place becomes less poor due to more affluent newcomers arriving there, that’s usually not considered like a success story, right? That’s gentrification, and it’s bad, or it’s “bad,” quote unquote. Certainly, it’s not necessarily helping the poor people who were living there originally.

Jerusalem Demsas: Allegedly.

Matthew Yglesias: When the people who were living there get more money, that definitely helps them. But the first thing that poor people do when they become less poor is they’re like, “You know what? Like, I don’t need to keep living here in this shitty neighborhood.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And they leave. So there’s this kind of like impossible dream of the rising tide lifting all boats in which the community stays stable and intact, but the individuals who live in the community become more prosperous. And then some of the dysfunctions associated with the neighborhood being full of poor people go away. There’s like nicer stores and, you know, all the lawns are kept up better, etc. And it just, it doesn’t seem like you can actually do that. That you can, in a minority of cases, you can gentrify.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And in a larger number of cases, you can have exit. But you can, in a society of individuals, you can’t make there be a rule that’s like, you get a better job, but you’re not allowed to take your higher paycheck for your better job to go personally move to a better neighborhood. You need to stay.

Jerusalem Demsas: You actually tend to do this, Matt. This is what happened during — I mean, I wrote this piece at The Atlantic a few years back about the declining number of Black — or the Black share of the population in many cities kind of going down. And people often lament this, right? And they talk about this.

And, similarly to this paper, what you see is that often what’s occurring is that for a long time, racial discrimination meant that the fate of middle-class Black people was, like, tied to the fate of lower-class Black people because they were, like, literally racially segregated into a specific area of town.

Matthew Yglesias: Sure.

Jerusalem Demsas: And then as racial discrimination started to decline and formal levers of segregation were removed — like D.C.’s a great example of this. Like, a lot of middle-class Black people moved from neighborhoods in D.C. across the river towards the suburbs. And you see suburbanization of the middle-class Black community across the United States happening all the time.

And in this paper, they find that 78% of people who are exiting high-poverty neighborhoods are relocating to areas below the high-poverty threshold, including many tracts that have much lower poverty rates, right? So these are not people who are just like going and transient and moving to like similarly shitty neighborhoods. They’re moving to like better areas.

And this actually raises — I mean, they reference William Julius Wilson’s The Truly Disadvantaged in this paper, and it’s just like it raises like a really difficult problem here, which is that yes, it is literally better for the very, very poor, for the truly disadvantaged, when middle-class people are forced to live next to them and remain part of their community. But that’s obviously like in contest with our views around individuals having rights to make their lives better.

I mean, to me, you know, you can solve this very easily by eliminating most zoning regulations and providing vouchers to poor people to be able to live wherever, and so that affordable housing gets mixed in with all other neighborhoods and there’s not this kind of segregation happening anywhere else.

But I do think that, in this current society, if you’re gonna have this kind of segregation and then you’re going to say, “Why is it that this area of town is persistently high poverty?” Yeah, you constructed it this way when you’ve done this.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. Well, right, but I mean, to give even, I think, just more credit to people, just people coping with these kinds of things, if you are a House member who represents a low-income district someplace, it’s hard.

Jerusalem Demsas: You should be pro-gentrification.

Matthew Yglesias: Sure, yes. So there’s the gentrification solution, but I mean, the Jerusalem solution, that’s like, “People are just going to leave my district and go elsewhere,” that’s probably — it would be morally wrong to try to prevent that from happening. But the nature of representative government in a democracy is that you have to fight for your district.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, I don’t know. Many, many people obviously don’t want to leave. I think there are lots of people who would prefer their neighborhood to get better such that they didn’t have to move. Some people had bad experiences, they want to leave, whatever. That’s fine. That happens all the time.

But lots of people make more money and remain in their communities because they like their communities. Like, it is possible to, again, through gentrification often, or through whatever we can call something else, through public and private investment, increasing the amenities of a community and therefore attracting higher-income individuals and college-educated individuals. By doing that, you can make it possible that everyone wants to both stay and new people want to move there. Like, that’s actually like the solution to this problem.

The issue is that, as you know, I’m preaching to the choir here or whatever, but the issue is that people don’t just want, Oh, I want to help the people in my community make more money and have more material well-being.” It’s they like — they literally don’t want anything to change.

They’re, like, mad when the corner store is no longer the same corner store. They’re mad when the, you know, the park nearby now is being used for soccer as well as basketball. It’s just like you’re, like, both want everything to change about the material circumstances of the community and also nothing to change visibly, culturally, institutionally.

And that to me is what’s like, why I don’t have very much sympathy for people here. Because there is a solution if you are in — to be clear, when we’re talking about the — I mean, I think often what we’re talking about here are, like, high poverty neighborhoods in urban areas. I think it’s a very different problem for high poverty areas in rural areas — in rural places.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, so, I mean, yes. I mean, I definitely think, one takeaway from this is that you should be — have a more positive view of gentrification as a process, right? That in terms of possible things that can happen to a neighborhood that’s full of poor people, having non-poor people move into it is better for almost everyone involved than a scenario where the least poor people in the poor neighborhood all just exit.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? Which is not to say that we should stop people from leaving. It’s just that that’s a problematic dynamic. Whereas more affluent people come in, it’s fine. But then, yeah, as you say, it’s like so much of our politics, I feel like, is dominated right now by, on the one hand, people say they want big changes to the economic structure of American society, but on the other hand, they’re like very resistant to anything being different.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And you just, you can’t do that. Like if things were different…

Jerusalem Demsas: Things would be different.

Matthew Yglesias: I mean, not just things would be different, but things would look different.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? That if you go — I mean, this is very dramatic — but if you go, you look at Shenzhen going from an obscure fishing village to a center of global tech production, it looks completely different.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: It’s not like, “Oh, it’s secretly different.” It’s quite obviously different.

And the same thing is true — I mean, if you look at a high-poverty neighborhood in the United States, if that were to become a thriving middle-class neighborhood, it would look different. There would be a different ethnic balance of people who are there. There would be different stores there. There would be different physical structures there. And if you want it to be the same, fine, but then nothing’s going to change if everything is the same.

Jerusalem Demsas: I will say, too, we have a homeownership episode that we’ve taped, and this paper yet again is another check in the anti-homeownership take bucket for Jerusalem.

They find in this paper that renters have — it’s much easier for them to take advantage of increased amounts of money that they’re making to leave poor neighborhoods. So if you’re a homeowner, you’re kind of like, it’s harder for you to leave.

So, one strategy, if you want to keep people really locked in place is to help them buy homes in shitty neighborhoods, which is, I think, actually the policy of the U.S. federal government right now. So they are doing that.

Matthew Yglesias: There you go.

Jerusalem Demsas: Great. OK. Anything else in this paper you want to chat about? I don’t know. I thought it was a great paper. I really enjoyed it. I mean, obviously it’s kind of our jam.

I did think you need to do a Jane — I forgot about this. Matt needs to do a Jane Jacobs apology, mea culpa here. So, in the paper, they talk about The Death and Life of Great American Cities, which Matt and I recently read for a podcast. This is Jane Jacobs’ great book. And Matt had, you know, a real scorching hot disagreement with Jacobs about her failure to think about economics.

And in this paper, they validate the Jacobian thesis about how slum formation happens. She writes, “Once a slum has formed, the pattern of immigration that made it is apt to continue ... Successful people, including those who achieve very modest gains indeed, keep moving out ... They are quickly replaced by others who currently have little economic choice.”

She did econ. Are you happy?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, maybe. I mean, whatever. I don’t want to get back into Jane Jacobs.

You know, I think part of the relevance of this, though, is to ethnic enclave neighborhoods as well, which is the kind of thing where a lot of people — this came up like Mamdani put — his administration put out some map of New York’s immigrant neighborhoods. And because of Mamdani Derangement Syndrome, he got, like, a lot of shit from people for not having Little Italy be on the map.

And of course, anybody who knows New York knows that it’s been a long time since Little Italy was an Italian ethnic neighborhood. But when I was a kid, it was, like, quite common to lament the fact that Little Italy wasn’t really there anymore.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Because Little Italy was, like, a fun place to visit, and it was semi-existent in the early ’90s, but clearly on its way out.

And it’s like the same thing. It’s like in D.C., we have, like, a Chinatown, but it’s completely fake. And it would be way more entertaining for non-Chinese residents of Washington, D.C., to have a proper Chinatown to go to. But, again, the only way to preserve a neighborhood like that is with some kind of, like, hard exclusion.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, as people make more money, or develop language skills or whatever it is that’s keeping them stuck, they’re going to go.

Jerusalem Demsas: We could have targeted immigration programs to bring Italians and Chinese people to specific areas in town. They have to remain in those communities. I think that could be a nice win-win situation.

Matthew Yglesias: We could have a Hukou system for it. No, but I mean, it also becomes like a development thing.

Jerusalem Demsas: No, we do place-based visas for Chinese immigrants.

Matthew Yglesias: Probably because there’s so many people in China, you could do this, but it’s like Italy’s not poor enough, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: I think you would get enough Italians to make Little Italy happen again. I believe, I believe in Mamdani.

Matthew Yglesias: OK, that would be fun.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, we’ve come out in favor of a Hukou system, so I think it’s time to close out the pod.

Join us again next week, guys, for, for our next podcast. We are reading Robert Putnam’s Bowling Alone for our next book episode, so.

Matthew Yglesias: A book by a man.

Jerusalem Demsas: A book by —

Matthew Yglesias: Shameful.

Jerusalem Demsas: Finally. They’ve been underrepresented for so long. But thanks everyone. See you next week.

Matthew Yglesias: Bye.

title: The Good News Trump Won’t Mention

The Good News Trump Won’t Mention

Crime is plunging, but he can’t handle that truth

Paul Krugman
Aug 6
 
READ IN APP
 

Monday was a day ending in the letter “y,” so Donald Trump spent much of the day boasting about how great he is and whining about not getting credit. At this point most observers tune his rants out. However, the screed at the top of this post has received some attention, possibly because it was marked by a kind of purity: every one of Trump’s bombastic claims was completely, verifiably false.

I was struck, however, by the fact that Trump didn’t mention one important thing that has been going right: crime has been plunging. Jeff Asher reports that the number of murders, which rose in the aftermath of Covid but has been declining ever since, is now approaching lows not seen since the 1960s in a number of big cities, with New York probably the safest it has ever been (the numbers in parentheses are the most recent year murders were this low):

One might have expected that Trump, whose inaugural address in 2017 was devoted to “American carnage,” the wave of violence supposedly sweeping U.S. cities, would be celebrating low crime and taking credit. Indeed, every once in a while the Trumpified Justice department puts out a press release attributing falling homicides to Dear Leader’s guidance. But nothing from Trump himself.

Just to be clear, Trump does not in fact deserve credit for falling crime. The bump in murders 6 years ago took place mostly on Trump’s watch, and the big decline began on Joe Biden’s:

Murders, rolling 12-month total. Source

Indeed, while there is no consensus about what caused the big decline in crime, many observers give partial credit to social support programs made possible by Biden’s American Rescue Plan Act. If they’re right, by the way, the drastic spending cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill, the attack on any kind of social spending — having failed to gut funding for Head Start, the administration is trying to sabotage the program, seemingly out of sheer spite — could well show up as an uptick in crime a few years from now.

Yet while Trump isn’t responsible for falling murder rates, claiming credit for anything good that happens on his watch (while blaming others for everything bad) is his normal behavior. Why, then, is he silent about the good news on crime?

The answer is threefold. First, Trump (along with much of his party) hates American cities, and isn’t open to hearing anything good about them. Second, he (again along with much of his party) has an image of what life is like in our cities that is 40 years out of date. Finally — and again in accord with his party — he wants to punish people, and acknowledging good behavior would get in the way.

About city-hatred: During a Monday White House event Trump went off on a tangent about “blue cities” in which he declared

What do they have in common? They’re all dirty. They’re filthy, dirty. Their streets are dirty. Their streets smell. Their storefronts are broken. Their trees are all gross. Everything about the place is dirty.

This wasn’t really a comment about “blue cities,” it was an attack on American cities in general, since almost all major cities — 9 of the top 10, with 95 percent of their combined population — have Democratic mayors. And as usual, try to imagine any public figure saying something similar about rural America.

Also, what would Trump know about what American cities are like? When was the last time he walked around a major city? For what it’s worth, here’s a picture I recently took of New York’s gross trees:

About living in the past: When Trump gave his “American carnage” speech, it was obvious that he was still stuck in a vision of urban life as it was in 1989, when he demanded the death penalty for the Central Park Five, wrongly convicted of an assault on a jogger. (Trump refuses to this day to acknowledge that he was wrong.) The epic decline in crime that took place in the years that followed clearly escaped his attention. To put his anachronistic vision in context, here’s an enlarged and annotated panel from Jeff Asher’s post about plunging crime:

Murders through June of each year

Obviously urban crime hasn’t disappeared. But obsessing about it at this point is wildly out of date. Next thing you know Trump is going to start ranting about the Communist menace. Oh, wait.

Fundamentally, however, the reason Trump can’t claim credit for, or even acknowledge, falling crime isn’t ignorance. It is, instead, as Adam Serwer memorably put it, that the cruelty is the point. Punishment isn’t a means to an end, a way to fight crime; it’s an end in itself, with crime only a rationale.

And if one wants to inflict pain — deporting, imprisoning, and, yes, shooting people — it’s necessary to claim that those people are doing terrible things. They’re dirty, they’re disgusting, they’re criminals. Acknowledging that crime is plunging, even while falsely claiming credit, would undermine the case for cruelty.

So Trump can’t talk about the fact that crime is down, not even falsely to claim credit, even though falling crime is one of the few ways in which America really is doing much better than it was a few years ago. Instead he must claim that “Radical Left” pollsters — like, for example, Fox News — are hiding his immense popularity, and that his Iran debacle was a great victory.

The message behind Christopher Nolan’s most important change to “The Odyssey”

Are we the Sea Peoples?

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 6
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

When I finally went to see Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” (it’s harder to get to the movies in rural Maine), I was surprised that relatively little of the gargantuan discourse around the film focused on what I thought was the largest departure from Homer’s text: Nolan inserts multiple references to a historical phenomenon known as the Sea Peoples and a historical episode known as the Bronze Age Collapse.

Some of this falls under the general heading of historical inaccuracy — a person living in the Bronze Age would not refer to himself as living in the Bronze Age, because the idea of a Bronze Age is a modern characterization of the past. It’s based on knowledge that in the future, people would learn how to work with iron on a large scale and bronze weapons would become obsolete. The Sea Peoples, similarly, is a phrase coined in the 19th century by a French Egyptologist putting forward a hypothesis about something he thought happened in the ancient Eastern Mediterranean. It’s not a phrase that we have any evidence was in use at the time.

But anachronisms aside, these references are a bold adaptive choice by Nolan.

We know that the Mycenaean Greek civilization depicted in Homer’s epic would eventually collapse, that there would be a Greek Dark Age with no written material, and that later the rise of Classical Greek civilization would bring about a return to writing with a new script. One strain of thought holds that this collapse was linked to the near-simultaneous collapse of several other civilizations in the region and that this may have had something to do with the Sea Peoples.

But none of this is in the text of “The Odyssey.”

This is all information that I (and many others) learned about from Eric Cline’s well-regarded 2014 book “1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed.” And Cline himself wrote a 2013 book on the Trojan War as part of the Oxford University Press Very Short Introductions series that suggests some of the linkages Nolan makes in the movie.

Nolan is incorporating it to reinterpret, recontextualize, and to a substantial extent subvert the source text, suggesting that the Greek attack on Troy sowed the seeds of Mycenaean Greece’s downfall.

Given the incredible commercial success of the film, you clearly can enjoy it without knowing much about these historical debates. I think the point Nolan is trying to make about the present is clear enough: The contemporary West risks collapse not because of external adversaries but because we are abandoning our own values.

But I enjoy a good ancient history debate, so let’s get into it anyway.

The two ancient Greeces

Ancient Greece is foundational to Western culture. It’s not true that all of philosophy is just footnotes to Plato, but Plato’s inquiries set the stage for the whole discipline of Western philosophy, just as Herodotus gave us the template for what it means to be a historian.

Math, medicine, drama, and so much more have their origins in Greek culture.

This is why the old Greek epic poems “The Odyssey” and “The Iliad” have such enduring importance in the West. Both those specific texts and the more general set of topics they deal with were important to people in Classical Greece and the works of the Classical Greeks are the building blocks of so much of our society.

A diverse “Odyssey” is the triumph of Western civilization

Matthew Yglesias
·
May 19

My ninth-grade history teacher was a bit old-fashioned. She’d taught the class for many years and always referred to it as Western Civilization I rather than its official title World History I, presumably because that was the name when she began teaching it.

Read full story

But importantly, even though the Homeric epics were important to people in Classical Greece, they are not epics about the people of Classical Greece.

They were instead “period pieces” about events that occurred hundreds of years earlier. The Greeks and the Romans who followed them understood that these epics were not works of history, but they did regard the Trojan War as a historical event and took the main figures described in the epics — Menelaus, Agamemnon, Odysseus, Priam, Paris, etc. — to be historical personalities.

People in Christian Europe were skeptical, though. They appreciated the stories and their significance, but they didn’t believe in Zeus or Poseidon or Athena and saw no reason to believe in Odysseus or Agamemnon either, especially since the epics contain obviously fantastical elements.

But a rich German businessman and Homer enthusiast named Heinrich Schliemann set out in the 1870s to demonstrate the historicity of the epics, and while there’s a lot about his work that doesn’t stand up to scrutiny, he did find an ancient city (or rather a series of cities at the same location) that is now broadly accepted to be Troy. He also did pioneering excavations at Mycenae. These Mycenaean excavations did not find a historical Agamemnon, but they did uncover an outpost of the civilization we now call Mycenaean Greece.

The Mycenaeans wrote in a script known as Linear B, which wasn’t deciphered until the 1950s. They used bronze weapons (as described in Homer) and had lots of small palaces, suggesting something like the numerous petty kingdoms that Homer depicts.

But written language disappears entirely from the Greek archaeological record for hundreds of years, and all the Linear B texts that we do have are banal record-keeping and bureaucratic minutia — there’s no epic poetry or literature of any kind to be found. Knowledge of writing is lost. The palaces and petty kingdoms of this once-flourishing civilization are destroyed. And the oral tradition that gave us the Homeric epics begins some time in this Dark Age.

Nolan has incorporated these facts gleaned from archaeological investigations into the Homeric epics and read them back into the story itself, having characters openly worry that all of Mycenaean civilization will collapse soon and that literacy will vanish. That’s in line with our contemporary understanding of the history, but it’s not in the original stories.

Becoming the Sea Peoples

A lot of historical investigation of the Trojan War has focused on the Hittites, another civilization entirely, who had an empire that was adjacent to Troy in modern-day Turkey.

Homer sometimes refers to Troy as Ilios (hence “The Iliad”), and linguists believe that the Greeks used to pronounce that word like Wilios. The Hittite records refer to a city of Wilusa. They also mention a people further to the west called the Ahhiyawa, which is similar to Homer’s term, Achaeans, for the Greeks. And the Hittites do indeed record the Ahhiyawa as being involved in several different wars for control of Wilusa and the surrounding territory.

Interestingly, the Hittite Empire collapsed at around the same time as Mycenaean civilization. The Assyrian Empire also dramatically shrank during this period, and the New Kingdom of Egypt came under considerable stress and nearly also fell apart.

These events are known to us as the Late Bronze Age Collapse, and are not perfectly understood since the records from this time are so fragmentary.

What is clear is that before the collapse, the Eastern Mediterranean had a thriving multi-state system with complicated economies, long-distance trade, and diplomacy, so I think this naturally raises questions about what happened.

The Egyptian archaeological record recounts battles with people from the sea or from the north who were said to have laid waste to other territory. Emmanuel de Rougé, a curator of the Louvre, moved from this fragmentary textual evidence to a bold hypothesis that a multinational coalition of Sea Peoples attacked Egypt. Other scholars working in this tradition came up with the idea that roaming Sea Peoples had maybe destroyed all the Late Bronze Age civilizations. After all, someone was responsible for the destruction of Mycenaean palaces — why not the Sea Peoples?

Subscribed

Nolan inserts this idea into the film, depicting a number of characters (notably Menelaus and the unseen elders of Ithaca) as worried that people from the sea are coming to attack Greece.

But modern scholars doubt there was anything like a coherent Sea Peoples confederacy and think this whole narrative probably confuses cause and effect.

Pre-modern economies were delicate. Long-distance trade allowed for more efficient production of basic goods, facilitating the existence of complicated urban settlements with specialized craftsmen and scribes. But the trade itself also depended on the existence of urban complexity. Negative shocks from changing weather, which seem to have happened, could start unraveling the whole thing. When living standards can’t be sustained, people turn to raiding and war. That disrupts trade, which in turn reduces living standards. “Sea Peoples” are a mix of raiders and migration flows that exacerbate these problems, but are also consequences of the problems themselves.

And that’s the idea that Nolan concludes with — the revelation that rumors of dangerous Sea Peoples are largely rumors about Odysseus and his men and other Mycenaean crews making their way back home.

In the film, Helen is real, but she’s also a pretext. Agamemnon goes to war because he wants to halt Trojan control over trade routes. He wins but is murdered after arriving home. Odysseus knows that he can’t just return home, proclaim himself, and expect the suitors to fall into line — the political underpinnings of Mycenaean society are falling apart.

In this recontextualization, the story of “The Odyssey” is the story of the Bronze Age Collapse.

Homer’s heroes are not the apogee of Mycenaean civilization but its undoers. They are people who, facing political instability at home, defected from the terms of the global trading system, laid waste to cities, and became disorganized raiders, only to find they could not help but turn on each other.

The big archaeological problem with identifying the Trojan War turns out to be that the city of Troy was destroyed several different times, and the Ahhiyawa are recorded as participating in several different wars.

One hypothesis from Manfred Korfmann is that the destruction of the city recorded in the excavations as Troy VIIa was “the” Trojan War, though Cline in his book notes that the actual archaeological evidence Korfmann unearths is ambiguous.

“Such bronze arrowheads could have been used by the Mycenaeans, but they could also have been used by the Sea Peoples or someone else entirely,” Cline writes. “If the event that caused the destruction of the city were to be dated as late as 1180 BCE, as Korfmann indicated, then the destruction could as readily be linked with the second invasion of the Sea Peoples during the time of Ramses III as it could with the Mycenaeans.”

Or you could, as Nolan has it, say that the Mycenaean destruction of Troy was simply part of the same Sea Peoples phenomenon that the Egyptians recorded.

The West and the enemy within

Marco Rubio, in a speech at the Munich Security Conference in February, said that he and his colleagues in the Trump administration “have no interest in being polite and orderly caretakers of the West’s managed decline.”

And looking at their work, they have certainly not been polite or orderly.

Subscribed

The question, though, is whether the impolite and disorderly approach to world affairs taken by the American conservative movement is bold action to save the West or, in fact, simply sowing the seeds of its own destruction.

It seems to me that going back to George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq, there is a consistent story of Republican administrations tearing down the pillars of the international order in the name of defending it. By the time of the second Trump administration’s Iran war, we have completely dispensed with ideas like seeking congressional authorization for the use of force, to say nothing of United Nations resolutions.

The Obama administration did a fair amount of trying to put Humpty Dumpty together again from a legal standpoint, but still found itself stretching the Afghanistan use-of-force authorization in comical ways.

Trump also proved that you can’t make international agreements on a partisan basis. All the work that went into the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action with Iran was erased in an instant, and by the time Joe Biden took office the Iranians, reasonably, were not willing to just go back to the terms of a deal that a Republican administration would cancel.

Twenty-five years of preemptive behavior since 9/11 has provided questionable hard security benefits for the United States but has unquestionably driven wedges between America and broadly like-minded countries. Trump’s predatory approach to foreign policy in his second term has kicked this into overdrive, and America is now less liked than China and flailing in a military competition with the objectively weaker Iran.

The self-proclaimed defenders of Western civilization are also undermining the core pillars of the rule of law at home with election denial, bogus prosecutions, threats to central bank independence, and the corruption of routine governance decisions.

None of this is what Homer’s “Odyssey” is about.

But Nolan’s spin on it does resonate, and much of today’s politics has a kind of Greek tragedy structure, with the right ushering in the very collapse they think they’re staving off.

Lying Liars Lie to Each Other Too

A bad-faith government is also an incompetent government

Paul Krugman
Aug 7
 
READ IN APP
 

There is no longer a presumption of regularity

Lately Donald Trump has been raging against several of his own appointees. He has publicly raged against his attorney general Jeannine Pirro, for admitting that the failure of the Reflecting Pool was due to shoddy work by Trump’s chosen contractors, and for dropping charges against David Hearn and supposed saboteurs. He has raged at RFK Jr. for not making a stronger case for the false link between vaccines and autism. And according to the Washington Post, Trump has privately raged at Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, for misleading him about the state of U.S. munitions, which have been critically depleted by his failed war on Iran.

These may sound like unrelated stories, linked only by the fact they all involve presidential tantrums. In a larger sense, however, they are part of the same story — what happens when a government operates entirely in bad faith, never telling the truth about what it is doing or why. Inevitably, officials in such a government don’t merely lie to the public: they lie to each other too. As a result, they can’t govern effectively, even in the pursuit of evil.

Legal scholars have a term of art, the “presumption of regularity,” which means that one assumes that the government is generally honest when undertaking legal proceedings.

Thus, if the Department of Justice brings charges against an individual, the historical presumption has been that there must be a good basis for those charges. In other words, that they aren’t simply a vindictive prosecution of one of Trump’s perceived enemies. When DOJ succeeds in securing an indictment from a grand jury, the historical presumption has been that government lawyers secured that indictment honestly, presenting the grand jury with complete and accurate information.

Under Trump II, this presumption is no longer reasonable — and the courts have begun to acknowledge this reality. In a number of recent cases judges have demanded information about what the government told a grand jury or dismissed charges because the government was clearly engaged in vindictive prosecution. At this point the Trump administration’s word is worth nothing, or less than nothing.

The same is true on broader policy issues. After most of its initial tariffs were ruled illegal, the administration reimposed them by claiming that more than 60 nations are engaged in “unfair trade practices” because they aren’t doing enough to block “the importation of goods produced with forced labor.” It’s safe to say that literally nobody believes this rationale, or for that matter believes that the Trump administration has any objection to slave labor. It’s all being done in sneeringly bad faith.

Domestically, the administration is denying food stamps to millions of poor Americans, many of them children. The alleged rationale is that this is a crackdown on fraud. Yet the real rationale is that this administration doesn’t want to help anyone afford to put food on the table, whether or not they’re legally entitled to aid. Similarly, the administration has denied FEMA aid to blue states, not because the claims are fraudulent, but to punish blue states for being blue.

So this is an administration of lying liars. But we knew that. The new information is how much this administration lies to itself, and the disasters this creates.

Trump’s war on Iran has been an epic disaster on many fronts. One of the most damning is the fact that the U.S. military has squandered a huge share of its precision munitions, drastically undermining national security in a matter of months. One obvious question is why Trump didn’t move much sooner to conserve interceptor missiles etc., either by calling off the whole war or at least by calling off actions that used up already depleted stockpiles of weapons like ATACMs.

Most attempts to answer that question focus on deranged Trump syndrome — his pathological inability to admit failure, which has led him to double down even as he runs out of ammunition. But it now appears that a contributing factor may be that he didn’t know how bad things were, because Hegseth lied to him, telling him that the munitions problem had been “fixed.” Hegseth, you won’t be surprised to learn, blames his own deputy, Stephen Feinberg. And to be fair, it’s quite possible that Hegseth’s staff were misleading him even as he misled Trump. Last week, in a post about the Putinization of the U.S. military, I cited a Telegraph article about a “culture of silence” at the Pentagon, in which nobody wants to tell Hegseth things he doesn’t want to hear.

It’s liars all the way down. The fact is that it isn’t possible for an administration to be completely dishonest with the courts and the general public while being honest with itself. Do you believe that when Trump boasts about $18 trillion in foreign investment, Kevin Hassett, the administration’s top economist, quietly tells him, “Just between you and me, Mr. President, that number comes out of nowhere, and even the investment promises we have received are vaporware”?

Of course not. This is an administration in which to serve is to abase yourself constantly, rendering fealty to Dear Leader, lying to your colleagues and lying to the American people. And if this administration doesn’t like the official government reports that are detailing the many disasters it has caused, it just quashes them .

So the Iran War is just the most visible of many ongoing, self-inflicted disasters perpetrated by this administration. Furthermore, Americans should be prepared for more chaos and mendacity, because we are governed by people who, just like Trump, are unwilling to acknowledge the truth. Unfortunately, things can get worse – and they probably will.

In praise of commercial culture

Plus when I’d vote for a Republican, the case for generalists, and why live theater is weird now

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 7
 
READ IN APP
 

Someone told me the other day that I should become safety-pilled about artificial intelligence.

I will admit that I don’t write about this topic all that frequently because I don’t think it necessarily lends itself to a ton of interesting articles, but I want to assure everyone that I am quite concerned that A.I. will kill everyone. In particular, I think that just as depicted in the “Terminator” films, the U.S.-China geopolitical rivalry creates bad incentives for both countries to facilitate excessively aggressive and excessively reckless deployment of technologies whose real workings and capabilities they don’t understand very well. There is a view on the left that everything about A.I. is terrible except for the existential risk, which is dismissed as just hype designed to inflate a financial bubble, and I think that’s crazy. There is also a libertarian techno-optimist’s fallacy of inferring “every technological advancement is good” from the observation that “technological progress has been very good on average.”

So let’s not have any doubt, I think, that this is a big problem. It’s why Alex Bores was on the November donation recommendations list and Manny Rutinel is on the updated one and housing is not the only reason I’m looking forward to Scott Wiener making it to Congress this fall.

On to our regularly scheduled Mailbag!

This Mailbag is free for everyone to read, but paid subscribers ask the questions you see below. Upgrade to send in your own!

Subscribed

BBDC: What is the most realistic scenario for you supporting a Republican presidential candidate in 2028 or 2032? Or a Republican Governor of a large, important state?

I think it’s pretty easy to imagine a scenario where I’d prefer a YIMBY-pilled Republican gubernatorial candidate to a left-wing Democratic candidate in a blue state where the policy status quo is already pretty progressive. That’s basically how Phil Scott keeps winning in Vermont.

The trick with pulling it off in a “large, important state” is that the surge of gerrymandering activity that Donald Trump has orchestrated combined with January 6 and election denial means that I now come to state races with a lot of federal concerns. It’s very notable to me that Republicans have a trifecta in New Hampshire and are not using it to redraw the state’s House maps to try and create a G.O.P. seat. That’s savvy of them and reduces the pressure on moderates in the state to vote them out. But looking ahead to the 2028 cycle, I think it’s actually quite important that blue states like Virginia, Maryland, New York, and Colorado engage in retaliatory gerrymandering. Right now the median House seat is way to the right of the national average because the intra-census gerrymandering has been so asymmetrical. It’s very hard to imagine recommending a Republican candidate in those situations because it’s hard for me to imagine a Republican promising to do a pro-Dem gerrymander.

That being said, the real moral of this story is that gerrymandering isn’t just bad on its own terms — it’s that gerrymandering has negative downstream consequences. It is very bad for the state of Wisconsin to have lots of people who don’t live in Wisconsin be invested in the outcome of its state races based entirely on their impact on the House map. If we had a national ban on gerrymandering, that would make Congress work a little bit better. But I think that ban would potentially make state politics work a lot better by simply creating a situation where only people who live in Maryland actually care what happens in Maryland politics, allowing the debates to focus more on the actual specific issues facing the state.

Joe Saia: You’ve talked about the how foreign policy and energy/climate policy were on different tracks in the Biden white house, even though there were clear win-win opportunities to increase domestic energy production and reduce climate emissions by focusing on reducing Russian oil exports. Seems like there is a similar dichotomy around animal welfare and traditional environmental review where we tolerate horrible factory farming practices but entirely block development to avoid disturbing a couple turtles. I realize a lot of environmental review is not really about protecting the environment but should there be some pressure on various groups to focus more on improving animal welfare by limiting factory farming practices and less on blocking development to avoid inconveniencing turtles?

For those who missed the post that Saia is talking about, the point I was making is that the Biden administration treated sanctions enforcement as a balancing act between the economic benefits of cheap oil and the foreign-policy benefits of cracking down on Russian and Iranian production.

At the same time, the administration treated domestic drilling as a balancing act between the economic benefits of cheap oil and the environmental negatives of fossil fuel production. If you had integrated across these two policy silos, you could have gotten an outcome that was better for the environment, better for the American economy, and better for American foreign-policy objectives. But that would have required an integrated look at the whole board rather than a narrow set of responses to interest group and activist pressure.

I think this is, in general, the virtue of being a generalist.

And the point about animal welfare speaks to the same issue. People have a lot of different reasons for being interested in animal habitat loss. Some of that is just enjoying a litigation hook. Some of it is good-faith concern with the idea that there is special sacred value in preserving rare species as such. But clearly some of it is a generalized concern about animal welfare. Habitat loss causes suffering, and people are reasonably bothered by that suffering. But to the extent that animal welfare is the hook that matters for you, it’s clearly the case that it’s possible to achieve more suffering-alleviation at dramatically lower economic cost by focusing on very small changes to how farm animals are treated. The simple fact that there are so many farm animals means that very incremental low-cost improvements in their well-being have huge benefits.

But to see that, you have to think across policy domains.

Share

Nik Gupta: I remember you called the Iran war “A precision strike to take out pro-Israel democrats” on twitter. I do notice that the more recent Democratic primaries since the war has started have taken a very different turn that the earlier part of the year. There are a multitude of factors, including the states involved, but has the Iran war been boosting anti-Israel democrats?

I think this is a very underrated factor. AIPAC, going back to Obama’s second term and the nuclear deal with Iran, has tried to set the bar for being pro-Israel extremely high.

To them, it’s not good enough to be anti-anti-Zionist and respect Israel’s right to exist or to oppose the B.D.S. movement or an arms embargo on Israel. It’s not even good enough to support generous financial assistance to Israel. AIPAC has wanted politicians to support orienting American foreign policy in the broader region around Israel’s views of Iran. That’s a ridiculous thing to ask of people. It’s a bar that very few Democrats meet, and once they ended up getting the war they wanted, it instantly became super-unpopular due to the negative impact on Americans’ economic well-being. The fact that this is all bad and terrible does not logically mean that the right course of action is to flip all the way around to totalizing investment in Palestinian nationalism. But most people’s level of engagement with specific issues is a lot fuzzier than that, and the war has just totally torched the brand image of “pro-Israel” in part because the custodians of that brand spent the past 15 years pitching this insane Iran policy.

Brian from Beaverton: You mentioned in your most recent mailbag that you find live theatre weird. As someone who does it professionally, I found that intriguing! What do you find weird about it?

I’ve had a theory for a while that a big reason behind the struggles of theatre as a whole right now (at least in the U.S.) is that we as theatre artists have gotten too far away from the tastes of the people who regularly attend theatre. We’re artists, and it takes a particular brand of crazy to choose this particular art, so we constantly want to push the boundaries. That’s all well and good in small doses, but when 75% of the shows are like that, as are 75% of the choices within those shows (even the 25% of “normal” shows), it can become alienating to a lot of people. I’m not arguing that every show be a revival of Oklahoma, but I think we need more balance than we’ve had, especially post-2020.

This is definitely part of it.

Different art forms go through different phases and trajectories. In the 19th century, literary fiction was a commercially vibrant form of mass entertainment. That’s not to say that every successful novel had high literary value or that every great work of literature was a commercial success. But publishing novels was a mainstream business endeavor and the writers who are today considered to be the great masters of their time were operating in a commercial framework. This ends up being something that you need to incorporate into critical assessment of them. The major works of Charles Dickens and Fyodor Dostoevsky were published in serialized form, so some of the literary choices being made about pace and structure were really commercial dictates.

This isn’t really what fiction is like today. There are certainly mass-market authors, but they exist in a niche that is siloed off from seriously literary fiction. Literary fiction, in turn, is a small niche that’s not expected to generate big sales and that participates in a somewhat incestuous circle of favor-granting. It’s important to be in the right writers’ workshops and have the right connections and be in the right circles because it’s not really a mainstream business.

Live theater, obviously, was a totally commercial business for hundreds of years.

Works of incredible literary merit were generated by the commercial mass-market theater. Shakespeare’s plays were staged to make money by selling tickets to a mainstream audience. But the rise of movie theaters and especially television largely killed that off. Of course you can see “The Lion King” on Broadway and people stage crowd-pleasing things like the “Oklahoma!” revival. But I was talking about living right near the Studio Theatre in D.C. and basically never going. What they put on there is more serious than adaptations of Disney cartoons and more original than revivals of the greatest hits of the American theatrical tradition. But there’s no expectation that an original play is going to be a hit success with mainstream audiences. As a result, they’re not really trying. You end up doing stuff that’s supposed to be interesting to a fairly insular world of theater enthusiasts.

In other fields this can sometimes be addressed differently. The normal structure of a show at the National Symphony is that before the big famous piece that everyone is really there to see, you get the performance of some contemporary composition that 90 percent of people don’t care about. That’s more elegant than the theater situation, but it’s still quite different from a commercial medium. If you go to a rock show at the 9:30 Club or The Anthem, the opening act will be less famous and less interesting than the headliner. But there is a good-faith belief that the audience will genuinely enjoy the opener. I’ll always remember going to see The Walkmen play at the 9:30 Club in 2004 and being blown away by the opening act, a Canadian band called Metric that I’d never heard of. Over the years they’ve become one of my absolute favorites and more successful and longer-lasting than The Walkmen. That’s not going to happen at the Kennedy Center.

To me, part of what’s interesting and vital about movies is that while you certainly have arthouse fare that almost nobody sees (“Train Dreams”) and pure cynical cash grabs (live-action “Moana,” “Super Mario Galaxy”), there are real artistic aspirations behind “Project Hail Mary,” “Obsession,” or “The Odyssey” but also real commercial aspirations. Part of the deal with the career of a successful director or a big movie star is that a track record of securing profits for a movie studio earns them some running room to pursue ideas that they believe in. They’re not begging for grant money or trying to appeal to a narrow in-group. Sometimes, of course, commercial imperatives incentivize people to make dreck. Oftentimes, commercial imperatives limit artists’ creativity in ways that they find annoying. But the ability to achieve commercial success is also freeing — over and above the fact that it means artists have the opportunity to connect with mass audiences.

Goose: Would love some thoughts on the first mover penalty for breaking from/against the groups. If Dem politicians en masse move against them, it’d work, but the first few to do so will likely just end up with bad reputations I would think.

This is why I said in my “how the center-left can come back” piece that it’s really all about the 2028 primary.

The Republican Party didn’t execute its MAGA pivot toward the right on immigration but toward the middle on Social Security and retirement programs via dozens of separate downballot primaries. Trump won a presidential primary and redefined the party. Bernie Sanders lost in 2016, but he did well enough on the basis of a clear enough message to lay the groundwork for what became a durable factional enterprise. In 2028, there will be a chance for people to run high-impact primary campaigns and we’ll have to see what happens.

Mathew: With playstation customers losing digital movies that they had purchased after playstation lost licensing agreements.

Do you support legislation preventing that from happening? Basically, if you purchased a digital copy, it doesn’t matter if they lose a licensing agreement, you get the movie forever.

We should always remember that all aspects of intellectual property law are pure legislative and judicial contrivances that are supposed to advance the general interest. And I would say the current situation in which a purchase isn’t really a purchase does not serve the public interest well. I hear people saying that if you really want to own a film and be sure you’ll have access to it, you have to buy it on physical media. That sounds insane, but it’s also true.

But it shouldn’t be true! Digital clearly has a lot of beneficial properties compared with physical discs. There should be a legal status whereby a digital purchase can entail the kind of irrevocable rights that we associate with ownership. I don’t know exactly what the details should look like, but this should be a solvable problem.

Max Haas: I’m wondering if you think there’s any way we can get someone like Marie Glusenkamp Perez to run to run for president. An actual Blue Dog Democrat but who sort of presents in a way that millennial progressives don’t find alienating. And if you think her (or someone like her) would have any hope at all.

This is what I’m praying for, at least.

I respect and cherish all of my Blue Dog caucus overperformers. As presidential candidates, I don’t think it works because one thing the primary electorate definitely demands is feisty and aggressive partisanship, and if you’re representing a district Trump won repeatedly, it’s not smart politics to deliver feisty and aggressive partisanship. The advantage a first-term senator like Elissa Slotkin or Ruben Gallego has is that they can do feisty partisanship through 2028 and then if necessary shift into dealmaking mode in time for 2030.

News of the Weak (Labor Market)

A note on this morning’s report

Paul Krugman
Aug 7
 
READ IN APP
 

Not so hot

This morning’s employment report was a downside surprise, so I thought I would post a quick note about what the data are telling us.

The surprise fall in employment — 23,000 jobs lost, when the consensus forecast was for around 80,000 gained — made headlines. As always, it’s important to realize that monthly jobs numbers are noisy, so you shouldn’t overreact to one report. However, this report also revised data for several earlier months down, so the broader picture of job growth in Trump’s “golden age” is significantly worse than it seemed.

Now, very low job growth — around 26,000 a month over the past year — doesn’t mean the same thing it would have a few years ago. Why? Because anti-immigrant policies have drastically slowed the growth of the pool of potential workers. We used to need more than 100,000 jobs a month to keep up with the growing work force and keep unemployment level. At this point we can have low job creation without a major rise in unemployment.

On the other hand, the fact that job growth has slowed so sharply puts the lie to claims that anti-immigration policies would free up jobs for the native-born. To a first approximation, U.S. losses of immigrant workers have been matched 1 for 1 by a fall in total employment relative to trend, with no improvement at all in native-born opportunities.

And several indicators suggest that the labor market has in fact weakened, although not as drastically as the employment number might suggest. Wage growth keeps falling, suggesting weak worker bargaining power:

And there’s a private-sector measure I find informative, the Conference Board’s “labor market differential” — the difference between the percentage of workers saying that jobs are “plentiful” and those saying that they are “hard to get.” This number is normally positive — we are a nation of optimists — but has fallen a lot, indicating that people actually out there in the labor market feel that it’s weak:

Source: Haver Analytics

Trump keeps insisting that the U.S. economy is “the hottest it has ever been.” But American workers aren’t feeling it — and neither are the hard data.
