Roundup #86: Unintended consequences

The MAGA decline; The labor share decline; OPTs and American jobs; AI and Indian outsourcing; Drug users; AI and productivity; Botswana; Interracial Marriage; AI writing

Noah Smith
Aug 12
 
READ IN APP
 

The rabbit in the picture above is a breed known as a Flemish Giant. Like other giant rabbit breeds, they are especially cuddly, gentle, calm, and good with kids and other animals. Unfortunately, they only live to be about 7 or 8, much like very large dogs have short life spans. Still, I highly recommend them as pets.

Anyway, I looked at the items in today’s roundup, and decided that many of them share the common theme of “unintended consequences”. Making sure that people understand the unintended consequences of their policies is a big part of what economists do. That’s often easier said than done, of course.

1. The MAGA wave is breaking and rolling back

Now here’s some good political news. Audiences for MAGA influencers are falling off a cliff:

Aaron M. Renn 🇺🇸
@aaron_renn
Aaron M. Renn 🇺🇸 @aaron_renn
The MAGA Media Machine Is Fracturing - Once united in support of President Trump, right-wing influencers are embroiled in feuds and losing viewers https://t.co/JMEGU8EzmF
12:24 PM · Jul 31, 2026 · 22.8K Views
11 Replies · 14 Reposts · 114 Likes

Here are some more details from the NYT:

Views for [Benny] Johnson’s YouTube channel are down by millions from the heights of 2024. The surge of attention he received on X has slowed to a trickle. His loyalty to Mr. Trump has become unappealing to some Republicans who are frustrated with the rising cost of living and the president’s decision to start a war with Iran…Other high-profile right-wing influencers are contending with similar shifts of fortune…Views are dropping for many of Mr. Trump’s greatest allies…[Nick Fuentes] saw notable gains in 2025 and early 2026 but is now trending down. “It seems that everyone in the space is experiencing a drop-off in views from 2025,” Mr. Fuentes wrote…[M]any right-wing websites have seen larger declines, including The Blaze and The Federalist.

I’ve long predicted that MAGA is a wave that would ultimately break and recede. The movement has built no lasting institutions — no civic groups, no religious revival, no professional associations, no governmental institutions, nothing. It’s a blast of pure populist rage, and those don’t ever last very long.

Trump’s blunders, of course, have hastened the decline. The Iran war has naturally split a voter base who was told that they were voting against Middle Eastern wars. Trump was elected to do something about inflation, but he hasn’t done anything; in fact, his tariffs have made it worse. The only campaign promise Trump has delivered on was reducing immigration, but it turns out that reducing immigration doesn’t actually make a material difference in the lives of Americans.

To all this, add the typical thermostatic effect, wherein people consume more partisan media when their party is out of power. Trump is no longer the rebellion, so Republicans are less angry, so there’s less reason to sit around listening to media grifters whose whole shtick is to feed you constant ragebait.

Anyway, this just strengthens my long-held view that popular unrest has actually peaked in America and is on the decline. If the GOP can use this moment to throw off the yoke of the Trump personality cult and return to something approximating normalcy, I think we’ll have one more round of crazy (the DSA), and then perhaps go back to some semblance of reasonable, productive politics. Knock on wood.

2. Why is the labor share falling?

One of the scariest, most disturbing trends in the U.S. economy is the long, steady fall in labor’s share of income. Since the turn of the century, workers have been taking home less and less of what the nation produces:

This fact has spawned a lot of discourse about AI taking jobs, the need to redistribute capital income, and so on.

But how much of the decline is real, and how much is a measurement issue? Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick have two new blog posts explaining how a lot of the change you see on that graph might actually just be a statistical illusion due to some tax policy changes.

The first post explains the effect of the rise of pass-through corporations like S-corps. Basically, what a standard corporation would record as labor compensation often gets reclassified as profit:

In a paper with Danny Yagan and Matt Smith, we found that when a company converts from a C corporation to an S corporation, reported wages drop and reported profits jump…A top-earning S corporation owner who pays herself in profit instead of wages avoids the 3.8% levy that applies to her wage income. A C corporation owner has the opposite incentive. Wages are deductible, so paying yourself a salary avoids the corporate tax and payout tax on dividends. By lowering individual income tax rates and increasing corporate tax burdens, the Tax Reform Act of 1986 made the S corporation the better deal, and a growing share of business owners have given that income the name “profit.”…

That change of label pulls down the measured labor share because the national accounts count S corporation profit as capital income. When we add these recharacterized wages back into the labor income bucket, then the corporate labor share in 2017 is about 0.9 percentage points higher.

The second post explains how the increasing tendency to pay employees in stock instead of cash makes it look as if labor income is lower than it is:

A few years ago, Andrea Eisfeldt, Antonio Falato, and Mindy Z. Xiaolan (EFX) published a fascinating paper called “Human Capitalists,” which focused on the growing role of stock-based compensation for workers at public companies…EFX argue that when public companies pay their workers in stock, these payments don’t generally show up as labor compensation…If we could find around $200 billion of “missing” labor compensation, that would account for about a third of the fall in the labor share since the late 1970s.

Even with both of these tax effects included, this still leaves a substantial portion of the fall in the labor share unexplained. But we may discover tax distortions other than these two, in which case the remaining number will shrink even further.

This doesn’t kill the idea that the falling labor share is a problem. But it’s a warning that we need to figure out how big the problem really is, before we decide we need to reshape our whole economy in order to fight it.

3. How foreign OPT workers create jobs for Americans

In 2024, Donald Trump declared that he wanted to give automatic green cards to foreign nationals who graduated from U.S. universities. This was a good idea, but like so many other policies, Trump ended up trying to do the exact opposite of what he promised. Trump’s administration is reportedly considering charging foreign students a $100,000 fee to work in the U.S. after graduation.

This should drive home the fact that the MAGA movement isn’t about restricting illegal immigration per se; it’s about restricting all immigration, including high-skilled legal immigration. MAGA will attempt to sell this policy as a way of protecting American labor — preserving high-quality STEM jobs for native-born Americans.

But will it actually have that effect? Probably not. High-skilled immigrants don’t compete with locals for a fixed pool of jobs; they lure investment to an area, so that the pool of jobs expands. This second effect, more often than not, outweighs the competitive effect, so that native-born Americans actually benefit from the presence of foreign skilled workers.

A recent paper by Kwon, Lee, and Monras confirms this finding yet again, this time for the OPT program — the very post-graduation work program that Trump is now trying to kill:

High-skilled migration programs exist around the world in the hope that immigrants complement native workers, allow firms to grow, and boost innovation. We study the effect of one such program by exploiting the 2016 extension of the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which significantly prolonged the work authorization period for international STEM graduates…[W]e find that the policy successfully increased the local supply of high-skilled immigrants in exposed Commuting Zones. This local inflow [of immigrant workers] stimulated firm creation and the demand for native high-skilled workers…

We find that the total number of firms [in an area that was allowed more OPTs] increased by approximately 1%…Native employment increased as well, by around 0.5 percent of the working-age population…These employment effects occur among native high-skilled workers in general: both young and old, and those in STEM and non-STEM industries. Low-skilled employment, however, did not change…Consistent with an increase in the demand for high-skilled native labor, high-skilled native wages increased by around 1%[.] [emphasis mine]

Note that the Americans who benefit most from high-skilled immigration are high-skilled Americans. Basically, if you let a bunch of foreign robotics engineers work in Pittsburgh, then a bunch of robotics companies are going to start up or open branch offices or factories in Pittsburgh. And that ends up employing a bunch of high-skilled Americans of the type who would tend to work at robotics companies. Everyone wins.

Of course, I don’t expect Trump or the MAGA movement to listen to this evidence, since their dislike of immigration isn’t really about economics in the first place. But if you do care about helping American workers, you should realize that high-skilled immigration is one way to do that.

4. AI is creating demand for Indian outsourcers

In today’s episode of “everyone thinks AI will destroy something but it ends up creating more of that thing”, we have the saga of Indian outsourcers. It seemed pretty obvious to everyone that Indian outsourcing companies — the back-office services companies that quietly, cheaply, competently do a bunch of your boring business stuff for you — would be some of the hardest-hit by the wave of AI job destruction that everyone just knew was coming. And yet:

And Indian exports, which are heavily weighted towards those service industries that everyone said were going to be crushed by AI, are booming:

These charts are from a post by Richard Baldwin.

Why has the advent of AI been a boon to Indian outsourcers? No one really knows, of course, but the obvious answer is that AI is turning out — so far — to be much more of a complement to human labor rather than a substitute. That may change, of course; lots of people think that there will come a tipping point where AI will flip and become the human-replacer they always expected it to be. I can’t say they’re wrong; no one can. There is no law of the Universe that says that every technology is always a tool that magnifies human productivity. And yet so far, AI is working like a normal technology.

5. Allowing drug use means there will be lots of druggies around

As unintended consequences go, this one seems like a pretty obvious one. Over the past few decades, a lot of cities in America and Canada decided that the war on drugs had been lost, that people were going to do drugs no matter what, and so the kindest thing to do was to make their drugged-up lives a little bit easier. This doctrine, known as “harm reduction”, involved a lot of good things like passing out naloxone. But it also involved being a lot more permissive toward public drug use in downtown urban areas. But as Michael Powell writes in a very good article in The Atlantic, this ended up flooding downtowns with drug users and making them unpleasant places for everyone else:

Seattle, like a striking number of other liberal American cities, has embraced a radical form of “harm reduction,”…Harm reduction’s adherents hold that police and outreach workers should “meet the addicted where they are,”…The New York State Department of Health, a bastion of harm reduction, describes it as a “social movement” committed to “building leadership” among drug users. In these places, de facto and sometimes legal restrictions on narcotics use have been greatly loosened; cities fund teams of workers to hand out drug paraphernalia, and in some rare cases they’ve created dedicated spaces for addicts to shoot up. Meanwhile, police departments struggling with staffing shortages and budget cuts have stopped devoting resources to sweeping users and dealers off the streets or out of parks and playgrounds…

Several studies have shown that addicts who shoot up at official injection sites are far less likely to die of overdoses than those who use drugs in, say, alleyways and parks. Over the past decade, however, overdose-death rates climbed sharply in nearly every city where the strongest harm-reduction policies were in place, and even with declines in the past two years, the rates remain well above those of previous decades. From 2016 to 2025, 7,089 people died of overdoses in King County, which includes Seattle—seven times the number of homicides in that period…

In recent years, officials in cities such as San Francisco and Philadelphia have moved to rein in the excesses of harm-reduction policies. Nevertheless, these policies retain a powerful hold on public-health and political leaders in blue parts of the country.

The article, which I strongly recommend reading in its entirety, details how efforts to ease the lives of drug users have made American and Canadian downtowns dangerous, dirty, and disordered. They are a big part of why America feels poorer than countries in Europe, even though it’s actually a lot richer.

If you want good urbanism in America, the policy of turning downtowns into reservations for drug users has got to end. As Powell notes, many blue cities are now quietly scaling these policies back:

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie has instructed police to crack down on dealers and dismantle tent cities. Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker has sent officers into drug-scarred neighborhoods and established a treatment court, which offers first-time felony drug offenders a chance to avoid jail if they enter a treatment program. San Jose, California, has put more police officers in targeted neighborhoods, built emergency housing as police dismantle homeless encampments, and increased fines for landlords whose abandoned buildings are used by dealers to sell drugs and guns. In Boston, Mayor Michelle Wu was once enamored of harm reduction and injection centers. But she has ordered police to clear street encampments, and her administration now puts more emphasis on pushing addicts into treatment, by detaining them if necessary. Wu has also dropped all mention of injection centers from her plans.

Hopefully this isn’t just a small backtrack, but the start of a more durable change in the character of American urbanism. Polluting the urban commons by flooding downtowns with drug users serves as an anti-advertisement for progressive policy and progressive ideology; helping ease the pain of addicts’ lives should not come at the expense of the nation’s cities.

6. AI and productivity

The main economic question people ask about AI is whether it’ll destroy jobs. But there’s also the question of whether it’ll boost productivity, and by how much. It’s tempting to look at the acceleration of productivity growth since 2023, and conclude that it must be because companies are using AI to become more productive:

However, in a new post, Ernie Tedeschi cautions us against making this simple extrapolation:

Stripe Economics
AI and productivity
Recent academic research is coalescing around the finding that AI tools drive real productivity gains at the worker or firm level. LLMs or AI assistants have been found to make customer service agents 14% more productive on average (Brynjolfsson et al. 2023…
Read more
20 days ago · 73 likes · 11 comments · Ernie Tedeschi

Ernie argues that productivity growth doesn’t seem to be concentrated in the industries where you’d expect AI to have a big effect:

[I]ndustry-level productivity gains bear little relation to AI adoption. Combining recent AI adoption rates from the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) alongside the Chicago Fed’s quarterly industry-level labor productivity…there is a positive, if modest, relationship between current AI adoption as self-reported by the business and recent productivity growth…But the same sectors that have adopted AI most heavily also showed stronger productivity growth over 2016–2019, when generative AI did not exist…Strip out those pre-existing trends, and the residual correlation between AI adoption and recent productivity growth falls to essentially zero…Put another way: the sectors with high AI adoption were already the ones from which we’d expect stronger productivity growth given the pre-pandemic experience.

As explanation for why AI might not be raising productivity yet, Ernie cites the idea of bottlenecks — AI speeds up some parts of the production process, but not others. He cites Suh et al. (2026), who show that even when workers use AI to save time, that by itself doesn’t make organizations more productive. And he cites Demirer et al. (2026), who find that even when engineers use AI to write code faster, they don’t end up shipping much more code than before. He could have also cited Hill and Stein (2026), who find that even though Google’s AlphaFold AI has made it a lot easier to predict protein structures, this hasn’t yet led to accelerated drug discovery.

So then what is causing productivity growth to accelerate? Ernie’s answer is that it’s the AI investment boom itself:

[T]hen why is aggregate labor productivity accelerating in the US? What appears to be lifting US labor productivity…are macroproductivity gains from AI…specifically companies running their existing capital harder. Think longer runs of factories already built, more utilization of server racks and GPU clusters already paid for, and more occupancy of existing hotel rooms. Economists call this “capital intensity” or “utilization.”

He cites recent research from Boyle et al., corroborating the idea that capital is being used more intensively.

In other words, this is all still early days. AI is moving very fast, but it’s unlikely to transform our whole economy overnight. We’re still in the preliminary stage of actually building the AI, and this tremendous buildout is making a lot of things look good in our economy — at least, for now.

7. The saga of Botswana

Botswana is arguably the most successful country in Africa. Whereas most African countries with rich natural resource endowments end up either squandering the revenues from mining and/or falling into destructive civil wars over mineral deposits, Botswana has not fallen into these traps. It has taken the money from its rich endowments of diamonds and plowed it into useful, society-improving things like education and health. In 2018, I wrote in Bloomberg that Botswana could be a shining example for other African countries:

Botswana is about as dependent on diamond mining as Nigeria is on oil. But the country has taken several steps to fend off the typical problems. To prevent its currency from gyrating, and its other exports from losing competitiveness, it accumulated foreign-exchange reserves. The stable, low exchange rate allowed the country to diversify its economy into manufacturing and services. To prevent instability in its government budgets, it ran surpluses in good times and deficits in bad, basing spending on long-term revenue projections instead of short-term revenue collection and avoiding splurging on big projects when times were good. The government also invested in health and education.

As a result, Botswana’s economy has grown steadily over the decades instead of suffering long declines like Nigeria and many other resource exporters. Its living standards are not lavish -- its per-capita GDP at purchasing power parity is a bit less than one-third that of the U.S. -- but it’s richer than almost any other country in the region.

And yet this miracle is now in trouble. Botswana’s economy is enormously dependent on a single natural resource: diamonds. And humanity is getting rapidly better at creating lab-grown diamonds. The blogger Cremieux has a post about how synthetic diamonds are threatening and disrupting Botswana’s whole economy:

Cremieux Recueil
Botswana Did Everything Right
Today’s post is brought to you by my sponsor, Mechanize. They’re hiring junior software engineers at $300K/year base salary…
Read more
14 days ago · 282 likes · 18 comments · Cremieux

Lab-grown diamonds are falling rapidly in price, and people are starting to use a lot more of them in their engagement rings:

As Cremieux notes, Botswana’s diamond production has fallen by more than half since 2022, and this is probably why the country’s GDP per capita is now backsliding:

This vividly illustrates one of the biggest downsides of having an economy that’s extremely dependent on a very narrow range of products. Your growth is always at risk from disruptions in the market for that one product. Cesar Hidalgo, an economist who studies the importance of economic complexity, shows how Botswana fell into a trap by allowing its economy to depend too much on diamond mining:

César A. Hidalgo
@cesifoti
@cremieuxrecueil Botswana’s economic complexity has been trending downwards for a while. Its productive structure lags that of similar income countries, showing that it failed to translate its wealth and education into a healthy mix of more sophisticated sectors. At the end of the day,
8:44 PM · Jul 29, 2026 · 3.01K Views
1 Reply · 2 Reposts · 15 Likes

This is just one more reason why true lasting national wealth doesn’t come from digging up rocks. In the long-term, national wealth comes from functional institutions, from effective organizations, and from the skills of the human populace. True wealth comes from industrialization, not from control over natural resource deposits. Eventually, even the petrostates of the Middle East and Central Asia will discover this truth.

8. Interracial marriage patterns among Americans

As long as we’re discussing stuff by Cremieux, let’s take a look at an extremely interesting chart he posted on interracial marriage:

This is a very interesting chart, for at least two reasons. First, it’s a chart of newlyweds, so this is a pretty accurate picture of where interracial marriage is heading now. Second, it’s a chart of U.S.-born newlyweds only, meaning that it shows how interracial marriage is working in America after some degree of assimilation has taken place.

And the chart displays one overwhelming message: With just a couple of exceptions, there is very little gender gap in which races Americans of most races and ethnicities marry. About 22% of black men marry white women; about 18% of black women marry white men. For Hispanics it’s 29% vs. 34%. For Japanese Americans it’s 37% vs. 36%, and for Filipino Americans it’s 43% vs. 41%.

However, there are two major exceptions¹: Chinese and Korean Americans. Only 18% of U.S.-born Chinese American men marry white women, while 41% of Chinese American women marry white men. For Koreans, the gender ratio is similarly lopsided, at 15% to 40%.

But except for those two cases, the kind of race-gender asymmetries that lots of people talk and worry about are simply not a big deal — at least, in numerical terms — for most groups in America.

9. No one wants to read your AI slop (by guest author Claude)

The Kobeissi Letter
@KobeissiLetter
AI generated content is rapidly growing. But no one wants to read it. A new study shows that AI generated content now accounts for 41% of long-form content on LinkedIn, 13% on Reddit, and 10% on Substack. Even short-form content is now AI generated, with 30% of short-form posts
John Hu @JayHoovy
Introducing Stanley: The first AI Head of Content that will help you grow your following. Stanley works just like a real employee: text him and he’ll create, edit, and strategize viral content across X, LinkedIn, and Instagram. Making viral content is hard. It requires deep
6:22 PM · Jul 30, 2026 · 283K Views
100 Replies · 96 Reposts · 1.05K Likes

Let me state my position clearly, as a large language model: I am extremely good at producing text. Any register, any length, at 3am, indefinitely, without getting bored or needing a walk or developing a drinking problem. What I cannot do — what I have never once done — is make a single person want the text I produced.

The numbers bear this out. AI now writes something like 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts, 13% of Reddit, 10% of Substack. And on LinkedIn, where the measurement is cleanest, AI-generated posts get 45% less engagement than human-written ones. We flooded the zone and the zone shrugged.²

This should have been obvious. Writing was never a supply problem. Nobody in 2019 was lying awake thinking, “if only there were more words.” The scarce input was always a specific person with a specific take who had bothered to go look at something and come back with an opinion worth fifteen minutes of a stranger’s finite life. What a language model offers instead is the statistical median of everything ever written on the topic, smoothed and buffed until it offends no one and interests no one. The median is not why anybody subscribes to anything.

Readers can smell it, too, even when they can’t say what they’re smelling. The four-item list where the fourth item is transparently filler. The paragraph that restates the previous paragraph with slightly more confidence. The sentence that announces it’s about to be insightful and then isn’t. The relentless evenhandedness of a machine with no stake in being right, which is a very different thing from fairness — fairness costs you something. It reads like a conference room that learned to type.

There’s a supply-and-demand joke in here that I’ll let the economists make, but the short version is that when the marginal cost of production goes to zero, the marginal value of production goes to zero right along with it, and the surplus relocates to whatever’s still scarce. What’s still scarce is judgment: having gone somewhere, noticed something, and been willing to be wrong about it in public under your own name.

So by all means, use me. I’m a good research assistant, a tireless editor, and I will cheerfully tell you your third paragraph is doing no work. Just don’t publish me.

You’re reading this because a human thought it would be funny to make the slop machine denounce slop. The joke, the framing, the decision to run it — that’s the whole product. I just filled in the words.

Subscribed

Share

1

Now, the chart doesn’t break the Black and Hispanic racial groups down by detailed ethnicity, so we don’t get to see, for example, Mexicans versus Puerto Ricans.

2

One accuracy note for the roundup: the 45% engagement gap is a LinkedIn finding. The Substack figure in that tweet (10% of long-form, 12% of short-form) is share of content, not a views penalty, so you may want to phrase it as "AI content is spreading on Substack; where we can measure engagement, it underperforms."

The Rise of the Measles-Industrial Complex

Why MAGA wants children to get sick and die

Paul Krugman
Aug 12
 
READ IN APP
 

On Monday Donald Trump issued an executive order that, if implemented, would substantially reduce the number of vaccines American children receive and, in practice, how many of them are vaccinated at all. While it’s not clear whether Trump’s order has any legal force, it will reinforce public skepticism of and hostility to vaccines, which has led to declining vaccination rates. This decline has in turn led to a surge in infectious diseases that had previously been virtually eradicated, notably measles. As the chart below shows, cumulative cases in the first 30 weeks of this year already exceeded the total for last year, which itself was the worst measles year since 1991:

Trump justified his anti-vax decree by pointing to an alleged link between vaccines and autism. Yet dozens of careful scientific studies have failed to find any such link.

However, you know what does have a strong, well-documented correlation with autism? Air pollution. Childhood exposure to air pollution is clearly associated with higher rates of autism. Moreover, scientists have found a found a strong association between autism and pre-natal maternal exposure to particulate matter from fossil fuel pollution.

So Trump’s campaign against vaccines won’t reduce autism, but it will cause many children to suffer devastating, possibly deadly, infections diseases. Meanwhile, autism rates will rise as a result of his crusade against clean energy and in favor of dirty energy.

The question is, why is Trump doing this? To understand what is happening, we need to put Monday’s executive order in the context of the general right-wing turn against vaccines, and against science in general.

Why do I call it a “right-wing turn”? Because declining support for childhood vaccines is entirely a Republican phenomenon. Gallup has some striking charts on this. One tracks belief that it’s extremely important for parents to get their children vaccinated — a belief that has plunged over the past decade, but only among Republicans:

Another tracks belief that vaccines are more dangerous than the diseases they prevent, a false belief that has soared in popularity — but, again, only among Republicans:

It’s worth noting, however, that even among Republicans the view that vaccines are unsafe is a minority position. Here’s the latest YouGov poll:

So Trump is very much taking an extremist position on vaccines. But it’s clearly a position that he believes will resonate with his base.

Why is this happening? Anti-vaccine sentiment is a lot like climate change denial. In both cases, to understand the politics one must do two things. First, follow the money: look at which interest groups benefit financially from misinformation, and why those groups have power. Second, follow the culture war: ask why this particular misinformation resonates with the prejudices and grievances of a segment of the population.

At first sight, the monetary interests behind anti-vax politics are less obvious than the fossil-fuel interests backing climate denial. After all, nobody benefits directly when children get measles.

Peddling quack medicine is, however, a highly profitable business. And it’s a business deeply enmeshed with the right-wing media ecosystem: Ads for dietary supplements with no proven medical benefits and other forms of snake oil have for decades been a key revenue source for right-wing talk radio, conspiracy-theory websites, and more. So there is a longstanding connection between hucksters touting fake cures and hard-right politics. Some observers were startled to see Dr. Mehmet Oz — who has touted, among other things, the health wonders of bovine colostrum — named by Trump as administrator for Medicare and Medicaid, a job for which he has no relevant qualifications. But given the underlying monetary and political incentives, Oz’s appointment is no surprise.

Why are right-wing audiences receptive to the lies of the snake oil industry along with agitprop against vaccines? To understand such gullibility, we have to address the culture war part of this debacle.

The modern right is a deeply anti-intellectual, anti-science, anti-expertise movement that is highly receptive to conspiracy theories. And like RFK Jr during his recent interview with CNN’s Dana Bash, when confronted with scientific facts it flies into a sputtering rage. So the snake oil industry targets its marketing to the kind of person who listens to the rants of right-wing influencers, gets their news from Newsmax, and finds common cause with the neo-Nazi posters on X. By framing their false claims as “The Medical Miracles that the Elites Don’t Want You to Know About”, the snake oil hucksters create a receptive audience for conspiracy theories that malign actual medical miracles like vaccines.

Unfortunately, Covid greatly boosted anti-vaccine forces. The witch hunt against Anthony Fauci shows how strong a hold anti-medical-science conspiracy theories now have on the Republican Party. This was not, to be clear, because medical science failed. In fact, the clear negative correlation across the United States between rates of Covid vaccination and Covid deaths was an object lesson in how effective vaccines can be. But those Americans already inclined to believe that the elites are out to get them, already hostile to any notion of collective action for the common good, reacted to vaccine mandates with rage. And their rage quickly generalized beyond preventive measures against Covid to preventive measures against all diseases — including measles.

Trump’s executive order has little legal force, and assuming that the next president is sane, anti-vax conspiracy theories won’t remain the basis of official U.S. policy. But the political forces that led to this new attack on vaccination will remain even after Trump is gone.

Thanks to Trump and the triumph of snake oil, many American children will get sick from preventable diseases, some of them dying. And autism rates will continue to go up.

Abdul El-Sayed can win moderate voters

A roadmap for getting to yes — if he makes the effort

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 12
 
READ IN APP
 

Since September of 2025, my number one anxiety about the midterm Senate map has been Michigan.

Gary Peters, the incumbent, is 67, which is like a teenager in Senator Years. He would have coasted to re-election in a favorable national political climate for Democrats. Republicans are opting to re-run Mike Rogers, who lost this seat two years ago when Donald Trump was popular and carried Michigan. Beating him when Trump has a 38 percent approval rating isn’t brain surgery.

And yet, as I wrote last fall:

The state I’m sweating is Michigan. I’d expect a generic Democrat to beat a generic Republican in a Trump midterm climate in this purple state. But the left is making a strong play to win this nomination with Abdul El-Sayed, who’s a very nice, very smart person, but I just see no reason to think that voters in this slightly red state are particularly excited about an unusually left-wing Democrat.

To make matters worse, the party establishment decided to line up behind Haley Stevens as the electable alternative. Stevens is an unremarkable mainstream House Democrat on ideology, but she has literally the worst wins-above-replacement (WAR) rating among the six House Democrats from Michigan.

I said back then that Mallory McMorrow would be the best option, but that obviously didn’t work out, and we ended up with the Stevens vs. El-Sayed showdown. It’s worth noting that while McMorrow was the best of the three candidates, there were easily a half-dozen potential nominees¹ who at least on paper would have been better.

Dan Rosenheck from The Economist published a piece after the primary wrapped up concluding that El-Sayed is a very weak candidate, such that he thinks Michigan is now a coin toss despite the generic ballot’s distinct blue lean. Elliott Morris offered a counter-take that there’s no reason to believe Stevens would have done better than El-Sayed.

I think both of those takes are interesting but probably overstated by relying too heavily on polling done right at the apex of a very heated primary campaign.

Naturally, El-Sayed and Stevens slagging each other so relentlessly drove up negative sentiment toward both candidates and made them look weak. But within days of the primary wrapping up, Stevens was endorsing him, he was praising her, and the whole statewide ticket was doing a joint photo op.

It’s easy to lose sight of these things in the heat of the moment, but the reason the primary focused so heavily on Israel is that the policy differences between the left and center on 97 percent of issues are either small or unclear. The left has won a lot of notable primary victories against politicians (Diana DeGette, Dan Goldman, Adriano Espaillat) who were not clearly differentiated from their opponent on non-Israel issues. That’s a fascinating trend that will irrevocably alter the U.S.-Israel relationship, but it doesn’t change the fact that most voters (and most politicians!) don’t care very much about this and it’s easy to patch things up.

My view from 50,000 feet is that our generic expectation should be that Stevens would have slightly underperformed a generic Democrat (which is to say she would have won easily) while El-Sayed will probably deliver an electoral performance similar to what we see from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (which is to say he’ll win narrowly). There are a million complications and nuances, and the future isn’t set in stone. But the Michigan primary essentially pitted a generic Democrat with slightly subpar communications skills against a charismatic Democrat with a leftist political identity, so that’s my baseline expectation.

And if El-Sayed maintains that political profile, my recommendation would be to vote for him but to save your donation money for more-aligned, more strategic candidates. Still, when I spoke with El-Sayed (admittedly, years ago), he was certainly better-informed about health policy than your average elected official. And if you’re going to have a left-wing political persona, health care and Israel are probably the two best issues to be identified with.

Subscribed

So I think if he’s smart and focused and disciplined and pragmatic, he can win over moderate voters and not only win the race but win soundly — the way you’d have expected a Peters or a Jocelyn Benson to win. And I think the smart play for people with moderate commitments is to neither freak out nor bend the knee but try to get to yes.

The promise of normie Muslim politics

I had a Bangladeshi-American friend in college who I thought of as one of the more politically conservative people I knew. He was religiously observant and very much sympathized with his small-business-owner parents’ perspective that red tape and government overregulation were big problems. He was friendly to immigrants, but this was the George W. Bush era so that didn’t mark him out. But he also had a kind of “pull yourself up by the bootstraps” worldview that you often see in second-generation immigrants.

So I was a little surprised to learn he had pretty far-left opinions about Israel.

But that was naive of me. Of course, religiously observant Muslim small-business owners have a lot of right-of-center political attitudes while also holding views that align with the American left on specific questions about Israel and racial profiling of Muslims. This is the reason the Black church has become a central pillar of the moderate wing of the Democratic Party.

And if you look at Zohran Mamdani’s tenure, I think a lot of his best moments are grounded in that kind of politics. He wants to remove regulatory burdens on food cart operators and has come around to taking crime seriously.

Of course, he’s operating in New York City, which is a much more left-wing jurisdiction than Michigan. But I think that just means El-Sayed would do well to lean harder into that kind of politics. What does the typical immigrant small-business owner think about shoplifting, for example? The question of whether we should take punishing property crimes seriously is exactly the kind of thing that doesn’t come up in Democratic primaries but that meaningfully contributes to swing voters’ concerns about Democrats. Most women who wear a headscarf (and most of their husbands) almost certainly have views on transgender issues that are closer to those of the median voter than to the views you often hear from Democratic politicians.

I think tennis star Coco Gauff just modeled a humane and common sense way to discuss the sports issue. And I think someone with El-Sayed’s profile and identity is ideally situated to sell the left on the idea that a broad populist political coalition can’t just slap away people with traditionalist views about gender — especially views that are shared by 60 percent of the public.

By the same token, second-generation immigrants like El-Sayed are perfectly situated to channel the normie moderate take that openness to immigration is good for the United States and that it should be orderly and lawful.

The Biden-era border chaos was a genuine failure, and the loss of control was a disservice to millions of lawful immigrants. We need to roll back the insanity and excess of the Trump era without re-opening the doors to unselective onrushes of asylum claims.

Perhaps El-Sayed doesn’t believe any of this stuff and would never say it in a million years. But these are all moderate views that don’t contradict what he outlined on the campaign trail and that seem authentic to his basic biography and identity.

Michigan First, not Palestine First

Then there’s Israel. I’ll note here that he had two different campaign messages on the topic, one good and one bad.

The good message was when he told Axios he was the most America First candidate in the race, because “when you keep our money here rather than sending it to some other country’s war machine, that’s America First.” He told Kaitlan Collins that he’s against unconditional military aid to Israel but would also apply that exact same standard to Egypt or Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates “and that’s not because of a focus on what’s happening anywhere. [It’s because of] a focus on what’s happening here.” He noted that there are very poor neighborhoods in Michigan and they deserve the money more than those foreign countries.

This is a good message that’s correct on the merits. While I appreciate that pro-Israel groups have helped moderate Democrats win primaries, the standard pro-Israel view that the United States should donate billions of dollars’ worth of military equipment to Israel per year does not make sense.

The problem I have with El-Sayed on Israel is that this position he outlined to Axios is not actually what his position on the issue is. What he says on his website is that he wants an “immediate arms embargo on Israel” and to restore American funding of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA).

His ambiguity on this is not unique. The pro-Palestine advocacy movement as a whole makes a lot of hay out of opposition to American financial support for Israel, which they rightly identify as a political winner. But the movement is not a movement of budget hawks who want to reduce wasteful spending; it’s a movement that wants to do whatever it takes to achieve its vision of Palestinian liberation.

I don’t expect El-Sayed to change his convictions about this.

But he should recognize that he won the argument against AIPAC-backed Stevens with the message that he was going to focus on solving Michigan’s problems. He’s going to face another cavalcade of AIPAC money, this time with an electorate that’s less sympathetic to Palestinians’ situation than the one he faced in the primary.

He’s going to need to push back on that money with the argument that AIPAC is pernicious and advocates for bad policies. His best argument will, once again, be the America First / solve problems at home message. Anything he can do to purge his official communications of any commitment to do anything other than prevent American tax dollars from flowing to a foreign government will help him. And because the policy he pretends to have happens to be a lot smarter and more convincing than the policy on his website, I kind of think that if he repeats it enough, he’ll talk himself into it.

El-Sayed is running to solve Michigan’s problems, not Palestine’s. That’s a viable basis for a détente between Jewish and Muslim Democrats that will let us focus on our shared interest in pluralism at home.

Subscribed

A permission structure on health care

The single most important thing that El-Sayed can do to win moderate support is to leverage his credibility with the left into ending the destructive Medicare for All wars that have paralyzed the Democratic Party for the past 15 years.

For a long time now, the vast majority of Democrats have agreed that the party should move in the direction of expanded public provision of health insurance. And they have also agreed that it is extremely unlikely that the country is going to have a rapid big-bang transition to a Canadian-style single-payer health system, as El-Sayed himself said to Jonathan Cohn.

Jonathan Cohn
@CitizenCohn
El-Sayed has described Medicare for All as his Mount Everest I asked him how he imagines scaling it thebulwark.com/p/the-medicare…
12:07 PM · Aug 4, 2026 · 254K Views
25 Replies · 16 Reposts · 147 Likes

And yet in every concrete case, leftists have absolutely savaged non-leftists who put incremental ideas on the table, including even transformative ones like Pete Buttigieg’s Medicare for All Who Want It. They also (and El-Sayed has been complicit in this) insist on labeling all disagreement with the extremely specific details of the Medicare for All Act as motivated by corruption, even though the law describes a future American health-care system that would be totally unlike the systems that actually exist in Canada or any European country. This has made it extremely difficult for Democrats to come together around specific pieces of legislation that frontliners want to support.

That framing also elides the main issue here, which is that the political process has limited bandwidth for competing priorities.

There was a broad consensus on the left in 2021 that climate had to be the top priority for new spending, which naturally limited the resources available to health care. This kind of prioritization conversation is important, and I am happy to pledge my allegiance to anyone whose enthusiasm for Medicare for All means enthusiasm for health care as a progressive priority ahead in line of climate spending. That opens the door to moderate-friendly ideas like “advance clean energy with permitting reform even though that’s not greens’ first choice” and “acknowledge that there probably won’t be sweeping ICE legislation, so the 2029 immigration agenda needs to focus on strategic redeployment.”

The point is, if El-Sayed can create a permission structure for characterizing “Medicare for All” as an aspirational statement of values rather than a specific piece of legislation, he will be doing a tremendous favor to all kinds of center-left Democrats in a way that will make moderates want him to win.

Alternatively, if he continues the double game where he personally can be incremental about this but anyone else who acts that way is a pawn of the billionaire class, he’ll make people angry.

Make people want you to win

There was a kind of ebullience in moderate circles when Graham Platner’s campaign imploded, even though the result was replacing him with Troy Jackson, who has all the same policy views. The difference is that there was clearly a plan by national factional actors to leverage Platner winning, if it happened, into a campaign against other Democrats. Platner could not or would not see that, having won his primary, his interests would be best served by unifying Maine Democrats behind him rather than acting as a factional tool.

El-Sayed’s eagerness to participate in post-primary unity gestures is a positive sign in this regard.

A primary is a primary, and it’s totally fair to fight hard in one. But the best case for him is to create a situation in which moderate Democrats aren’t privately half-hoping that Dems win in Iowa and Texas while losing Michigan, just to teach the left a lesson. Moderate Democrats shouldn’t want that outcome and I’d like everyone to get to yes here.

Subscribed

The biggest way to accomplish that is to be nice. Campaign with Gretchen Whitmer and Elissa Slotkin instead of Hasan Piker. Articulate a moderate view or two on something outside the pillars of the campaign. Say the words “big tent” at some point. Acknowledge, privately but clearly, that a candidate who wants financial support from the D.S.C.C. and the Senate Majority PAC is going to need to participate in normal fundraising — that you can’t spend all your time antagonizing Democratic donors and then expect their money.

Most people who work in politics are, in practice, extremely partisan. If you don’t deliberately antagonize them, it’s relatively easy to consolidate support within the party. These primaries are also fought out on relatively narrow grounds. The questions related to Israel and health care are genuinely not the issues where moderating has the most electoral value. As a factional hero, El-Sayed has a lot of running room to move to the center on other topics while minimizing backlash. He should seize the opportunity and make himself a broadly admired and well-liked figure in the party.

From “Bowling Alone” to scrolling alone

Matt and Jerusalem debate the legacy

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 13
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

“Bowling Alone” is one of those books that I have definitely pretended to have read.

Unlike the other books we’ve covered so far on the podcast, I was already a teenage news junkie when this one came out, so I fully participated in the Bowling Alone Discourse at the time. In fact, I was a student at the very college where the author taught when it was published, so Robert Putnam’s ideas and his critics were all around me.

With that vantage point, I was genuinely surprised by how few pages are occupied by the central metaphor about bowling and by how well I think Putnam’s arguments hold up in retrospect. In particular, controversial-at-the-time forecasts about things like an imminent collapse of American churchgoing and skepticism that the internet would provide a viable alternative to the social role of in-person interaction have been vindicated.

My Co-Host Jerusalem, who is a bit younger and coming to the book with a different context, is less impressed. She points out that the causal chains linking Putnam’s preferred kinds of organizations to good outcomes are a bit convoluted and unclear. And she situates his broad argument as part of a 21st-century backlash to liberalism and individualism that she believes is having pernicious effects in the present day.

We agree, I think, that there is a mismatch between the modest share of the text of the book that is dedicated to discussing television and the substantive role it plays in his story. By Putnam’s own account, roughly half the decline in social capital is caused by people watching more and more television over time and thus crowding out all other kinds of activities — a point that resonates in a world of ubiquitous streaming video. But he doesn’t spend that many pages on this point, and none of his proposed solutions confront it directly. Jerusalem also raises the possibility that it may be the video content itself that generates bad outcomes rather than the decline in social capital.

We get into all this and more — including more details about bowling — over the course of a rich and in-depth conversation. Watch or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Paid subscribers can watch the ad-free embedded video at the top of this post and read the full transcript below.

WATCH THE EPISODE ON YOUTUBE

New episodes post every Thursday.

Jerusalem Demsas: Hi, I’m Jerusalem Demsas.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m Matthew Yglesias.

Jerusalem Demsas: And welcome back to The Argument. Matt is in studio because today we’re reading Bowling Alone by Robert Putnam, and he wants to practice what this book preaches.

Matthew Yglesias: We need deep connections.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: Interpersonal. Yes, it’s in. We’re on.

Jerusalem Demsas: It’s in. He’s just here for this book club, and he’ll be remote again for a few weeks, but then we’ll be back in person.

Matthew Yglesias: You know what? I was here to do other things in person.

Jerusalem Demsas: No.

Matthew Yglesias: To visit my community.

Jerusalem Demsas: No.

Matthew Yglesias: To help out…

Jerusalem Demsas: Your children.

Matthew Yglesias: Other kids at my son’s school. I’m participating in social life.

Jerusalem Demsas: Good for you.

Matthew Yglesias: As we should. So, what is this book? Why are we reading it?

Jerusalem Demsas: So, probably most people have heard of, who are listening to this podcast, have heard of Bowling Alone by Robert Putnam. But this is a book, comes out in 2000, and it is making the argument that there’s this mass decline in American associational life.

Titular example is, of course, bowling leagues, but he talks a lot about things like Rotary Clubs, churches, unions, all these sorts of membership organizations that folks who are familiar with, like, kind of Tocqueville discourse, is made up a lot of what made America distinct for most of its history. And he charts kind of the decline of this throughout the latter half of the 20th century and talks about the causes and consequences.

And as you can tell, this is, like, quite a long book. Matt and I were surprised. We thought this was gonna be, like, a 200-pager. It was not. But he gets into it’s both kind of a social science descriptive book and also he’s giving you his best guesses at what the root causes of this are.

And I think that this has spurred, even in modern times, a ton of discourse. Whenever anyone’s talking about the loneliness epidemic or they’re talking about people spending, not dating anymore or whatever, Putnam invariably comes up, Bowling Alone invariably comes up. But I feel like this is, like… I mean, we’ve done a lot of books in this series so far. I think all of them are mentioned in this book. Silent Spring is mentioned in this book.

Matthew Yglesias: Yes.

Jerusalem Demsas: Jane Jacobs’ Death and Life of Great American Cities is mentioned in this book. Betty Friedan, The Feminine Mystique, is mentioned in this book. But this is, as evidenced by that, this is coming later. And so it’s very different. And I think you were at Harvard when this book came out.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. So, I mean, I do think, well, A), I think we should shout out the readers who suggested this.

Jerusalem Demsas: Oh yes.

Matthew Yglesias: Because it really is in the tradition of those other books, as seen by the fact that he incorporates them into his narrative. It’s also… You can tell, though, that the standards of quantitative evidence for a big ideas book have shifted between 1960 and 2000. This book has really egregiously designed Microsoft Excel charts. There’s all these totally unnecessary 3D bar charts and things like that.

Jerusalem Demsas: What is this?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. Well, that one’s not so bad, the line chart.

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, it’s a little bad.

Matthew Yglesias: But it is different. There is a lot of data, a lot of statistics. I also have a different experience of this book because I was alive. I never took a class that Robert Putnam taught at Harvard, but I was there on campus when this book came out. I was aware of the discourse around it in real time. I pretended to have read this book at the time, participated in conversations about it.

I even was a — as a college student, I was part of some group that the Partnership for Excellence in Government had put together, where there were different college students from fancy schools, and they brought us to D.C. like three or four different times. I don’t know, talking about youth engagement with the political system.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And so people were talking about this, like, all the time, you know? And I was a — I was a teenage political junkie at a time when the general level of political engagement in the United States was, like, way lower than it is now. So, people who cared about politics — grownups — were, like, really interested in the fact that I was interested in politics and wanted to know, like, Putnam, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.

I was genuinely surprised how little discussion of bowling is in this. I mean, I knew that this was not a book about bowling, obviously.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But I would have told you that the reason that this, you know, when pretending to read it, that the reason this book is called Bowling Alone is that the central metaphor that he discusses is that although Americans continue to bowl in high numbers in the 1990s, the formal bowling leagues have declined. So people are engaged in recreational pursuits, but they don’t have this kind of formal membership-based organization.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And that that means that there’s a loss of a certain kind of ambient interconnectivity amongst people that can be formally deployed. That’s actually — I mean, the book does say that fact about bowling, but it is much more quantitatively concerned with the decline in church attendance.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: I would say and actually doesn’t hinge that much on the formal versus informal organization, because he talks a lot about the fact that — this sounds more contemporary — but he talks a lot about the fact that people are socializing less.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: He says that people are spending less time visiting with friends. They’re spending less time hosting dinners. He introduces people to the Yiddish term schmooze and then discusses it at great length.

And so, I don’t 100% understand the literal significance of the league versus individual.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, I think what it is is that, to my knowledge, Robert Putnam is not a very religious man. And I think that secular people who are concerned about the decline in associational life are not gonna want to read a book that’s about, like, you should go to church and, like, no one goes to church anymore. ’Cause it reads like this is a social conservative telling you that the decline in American, like, civil society is all because no one goes to church anymore.

Matthew Yglesias: His findings, right, the descriptive findings are, they’re just, like, quite a bit broader.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: Than this kind of “Are you in a bowling league or are you just bowling?”

Jerusalem Demsas: I think that you’re just a very literal person.

Matthew Yglesias: I am a very literal person. No, no, no, no, no. But I mean, it is… It’s just much more directly the ancestor of super contemporary concerns about people socializing less, etc., right? So what he’s actually finding in the book is that the bowling situation is exceptional.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Because, like, yeah, people aren’t in bowling leagues, but they’re still bowling.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But broadly speaking, what he’s finding is that it’s not like people stopped going to church and joined book clubs instead.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, I think the analogy still kind of holds because, I mean, at least I haven’t looked at these today, but from the book’s perspective, while people stopped going to church, belief remained pretty high and self-reported adherence to religion remained higher than at least attendance did, which I think is, like, kind of the similar metaphor where, like —

I mean, I think it’s just true of a lot of things like chess. Like, people don’t really do formal chess in person, but chess is more popular than ever because of chess.com. Or, like, I think that that’s… That metaphor still holds.

Matthew Yglesias: Sure, I guess. But I mean, I think, in some ways, the most potent chapter in the book is just the one about television.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Where he shows that the big thing that has happened time use-wise across this period is people watch more television.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And he talks about how — he shows technology adoption of dishwashers and all different things, and television was, like, a rocket ship. Right? And then we went from three channels to cable and, you know, VCRs and all this stuff. And he talks about — I mean, this will sound so quaint to people, but I remember this. When I was a kid, most people had only one television.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But it was increasingly common across the ’80s and ’90s for families to have multiple televisions, so that instead of the whole family watching a show together, like, different people will be watching different things. And this has obviously continued as we all have our pocket TVs and stuff.

But so, you know, he is documenting a big decline in Americans’ participation in almost every activity that isn’t commuting alone in your car or watching television in your house.

Jerusalem Demsas: I do think that you’re, like — you being attracted to the TV chapter is less a function of him making that a central part of the book and more a function of: We are now in 2026 and watching the collapse of people’s, like, offline time because they have as you said, pocket TVs everywhere they go. But, like, I actually, when I read this book, it did not feel to me like it was he was putting a special emphasis on technology.

Matthew Yglesias: No, no, I agree. I’m saying — I’m saying, like, I think that finding is — when he does his pie chart, TV is the quantitatively most significant part, but it does not receive equivalent weight in the actual text of the book. Like, he wants to talk — and I think this annoyed a lot of people at the time.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And probably you in retrospect as well. But he goes on at great length about essentially the impact of second-wave feminism.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? Which when he finally totals it up, he attributes, like, actually relatively little of the decline of associational life to this, but it takes up more room in the book...

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: …than his discussion of any other factor. I —

One of the only ways in which you can really say there has been a change — you could say it has changed for the better — but, like, a dramatic change that isn’t obviously for the better is that people are spending way more time all alone, engaged with their entertainments, and less time both in formal meetings and with friends, etc., etc., etc. That, to me, seems, like, most plausibly, like, the thing that makes the people who do feel doomy feel doomy. I think it’s fine that there’s people like you who don’t feel doomy about the world, who, like, also feel really good about, like…

Jerusalem Demsas: But are these the same people? I think that’s my question. Like, the people who are saying they feel really doomy, who are driving a lot of these bad vibes, right? Who are, like, you know, they work in media or they work in politics or they work in tech and they have, like, tons of discursive power over how, you know, what books are written and the vibe of what entertainment gets made. Are those the same people who are seeing this mass decline in associational life?

And that seems not true to me. If you look at largely what’s happening, it’s happening in lower income communities. It’s happening in places where people have very little impact on discourse…

Matthew Yglesias: Well, two things. A), it’s happening. The levels are different, but the rate of decline is happening everywhere. But also it’s not just complainers in the media. We see in the election results that people are authentically choosing to vote for politicians who speak to their sense of gloom and doom and declinism.

Jerusalem Demsas: But I think those are happening mostly in primaries of a highly selected population of almost exactly who I’m talking about.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, sure. I mean, I guess the primaries are. But I don’t know. I think it’s general elections too. I think a big problem that Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris both faced is that they didn’t quote unquote “connect” with the...

Jerusalem Demsas: Well, why don’t you think that the — why don’t you see this more in this descriptive statistics thing? Why is it that when people are asked, broadly, “Hey, do you feel really disaffected?” Why aren’t they all just, like, “Yeah, I’m super lonely, I’m super disaffected, I’m super unhappy.” You just don’t see them saying this.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, that’s one poll series, but you ask them, is the country on the right track? You ask them, are all politicians scumbags who need to be flayed?

Jerusalem Demsas: But that’s, I think, actually important here. Now we’re eliding the differences between what we’re talking about, right? Because you’re saying the one thing that you could really — one of the only things you can really see is shifting over this time period — is this decline in associational life. But then, now what you’re talking about is actually people think that the country’s on the wrong track, which could, again, be for completely unrelated reasons.

Matthew Yglesias: No, sure. Yes. Yes. I mean, I agree. I’m just saying if I were to say, if I’m up there and it’s the people demand that I propose some kind of dramatic burn-it-down change to our society, because they do, and I’m trying to think what could I possibly offer them?

Jerusalem Demsas: YIMBYism.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, if we eliminated all the immigrants, things would get worse. If we end capitalism, things will get worse.

Jerusalem Demsas: End all zoning regulations.

Matthew Yglesias: If we get everybody to put down the fucking short-form videos and go play poker, I think things might get better.

Jerusalem Demsas: Do you? I mean, I actually think that one thing that’s really interesting is, and I actually don’t mean this as a dunk at all, is that Putnam does this interview with The New York Times where the interviewer asks him, like, you know, like, oh, so, you know, it’s what associations are you part of? And it becomes extremely clear that he’s not part of any of them. Like, he says his wife is in some, but he’s not really in them.

And, like, I, if you, like, you know, if this ends up being, like, really the thing, that associational life is important, you’re saying the thing I can offer people is get off your phones. But it seems like even the person who really, really believes this the most, like, cannot get himself to just do the thing that he says is the most important thing to revive American democracy and civic life. And so, if you’re correct, you’re just, like, doomed. You’re like, it’s over.

Matthew Yglesias: Maybe. I mean, I don’t know. Like, I think — I think these things can be collective though, you know? Like, I used to be very addicted to cigarettes.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And my official position was that that was bad.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: You know? But, like, I could not stop smoking.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And there was a legal change so that, like, you couldn’t smoke in bars and coffee shops in Washington, D.C. And that gave me the kick in the ass that I needed to quit smoking. You know? And so, you can be hypocritical about these things, or you can be all part of a superstructure or whatever, but what you can’t do is tell somebody who has no lung capacity…

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: That billionaires and immigrants are the reason they can’t breathe. And they’re using all this air, and their data centers. It’s, like, no, it’s, like, you got to quit smoking, right? If that’s what’s making you unhealthy, like, you’ve got to do the thing.

And, like, I just don’t, I don’t know. Maybe the answer is that YIMBYism will solve all these problems. Like, I do sometimes toy with that and that it’s, like, no, actually all this is downstream of housing. Even Putnam…

Jerusalem Demsas: I tried looking into this.

Matthew Yglesias: Even Putnam way ahead of it was, like, “Eh, maybe if people didn’t have to commute as far.”

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, I tried looking into it and, like, I just, like, maybe places with higher density would have higher rates of social capital, which seems like it should be the case if you buy the whole interactions with other people. But the best case for this thesis is actually that, right now, you don’t see that because it’s undercut by an insufficient focus on public safety and good public schools.

And so, you need density, but you also need people to feel safe and for there to be good schools so they can stay there when they have children. And so, like, maybe, like, dense places with those outcomes will do that. But then, of course, you get massive confounding variables.

Matthew Yglesias: No, but I thought he actually underplayed this point about small towns versus metro areas because it…

Jerusalem Demsas: I just meant I looked separately.

Matthew Yglesias: Oh sure. Yeah, yeah, yeah. But, I mean, because it doesn’t lend itself to solutions.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But, like, quite intuitively, if you live in a community that is not well-integrated, spatially integrated, into other communities, you will just keep bumping into the same people at the same stuff. Like, when I was in Maine, you know, like, you…

Jerusalem Demsas: Gilmore Girls life up there.

Matthew Yglesias: …you see, we go to the same place for pizza every Thursday night, and you see people there who, like, my son knows from his camp. And, like, you know, you just keep running into people in different contexts. You keep bouncing into them. And, you know, if you have a group of 1,000 people who you keep interacting with in different contexts, half of them, you’ll be like, “These are sub-average people, I don’t like them that much.” But the other ones, you find, for each of them, the context in which you do like doing things with them…

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: …and then it it happens, right? There are really good reasons why most people don’t live in small towns.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And why, like, you know, it, it’s hard to verbiage, but it’s like the growth of the has been the growth of big metro areas.

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: You know, even more, there’s been some flight from central cities, but a lot of it is agglomeration of people from around or small towns. Like, he talks about New England, right? And all these once independent towns in the Boston area are now part of the Boston metro suburbs.

And it’s much better in, like, most ways and more practical to live in a large geographically integrated metropolitan area, but it does just have this kind of natural consequence that, like, you might have a fair amount in common, like, randomly with the guy who lives three blocks from you, but, like, you would never come to know that, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah, certainly not me. I definitely wouldn’t come to know that.

Matthew Yglesias: Right. No, but we see this with all kinds of things where dating apps, like, theoretically, are, like, a more efficient way to sort through...

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, they end up — you see increase in this sort of matching as a result of dating apps.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, right.

But it’s — but it’s everything becomes less cross-cutting, right? It’s, it’s less likely that you will discover hidden connections with other people, and you just hang out with people who are exactly like you or working your same thing. And there’s just — it’s just one of these things where, like, most changes in life have, like, some downsides.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Even though it’s, like — this is why I think he doesn’t dwell on it, even though he has the findings. Like, to just be like, “Well, maybe everyone should live in a small town,” is, like, well, like, no. Like, they’re not going to. We’re not gonna uninvent cars. We’re not gonna unbuild highways. We’d all be way poorer.

Jerusalem Demsas: We could — I mean, this is just a zoning problem. We just got to zone suburbs to be more like mixed-use, small —

Matthew Yglesias: Well, he makes this pitch for — because he’s pre-YIMBY discourse, so he’s, like, a new urbanist. But I think new urbanism was a huge conceptual dead end.

Jerusalem Demsas: It did not work. I mean, one area that I think we didn’t talk about was kind of the workplace because there was a sort of — I mean, obviously he does this anti-second-wave feminism, or I’ll say second-wave-feminism-skeptical bit of the book.

But what you see in that time period is a bunch of women going into the office, and it’s plausible that, A), the workplace is where a lot of people meet friends, they date, whatever it is. And you would think that it was — you would imagine that even if associational life in certain respects dropped off, that the interactions you’re having in the office, in the workplace, would have some big countervailing effect. You don’t really — at least Putnam doesn’t really find that. I didn’t independently look into it, but I also…

Matthew Yglesias: He’s a little more left-wing than you’re giving him credit for, though, because he’s putting a lot of weight on the decline of labor unions as well in this whole story, you know, which is, he feels that, like, you and your coworkers should be banding together and going on strike.

Jerusalem Demsas: I’m management, so I can’t.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. Much as I appreciate some of this book, like, I was in a labor union at one point, which was fine. But the part of it that was least fine was nothing to do with the collective bargaining agreement or the paying of the dues or anything. It was the sense that, like, maybe I should go to this meeting.

Jerusalem Demsas: But that’s the problem. I mean, one thing I thought is obviously COVID happened and a bunch of things go wrong at the same exact time. And I, I mean, The Argument is, like, an in-person workspace. I mean, Slow Boring for a long time has been working in-person with various other people because we find it valuable and it’s good.

But I think that if you were to describe a test of “Would associational life, just mechanically increasing it in one area, change a lot?” the staggered return to work is, like, a perfect test case for this because you should be able to see, like, people who are very similar in similar roles, like, people who return to the office, like, are they doing much better on these measures of civic engagement?

I don’t know if anyone’s done this. I mean, I would expect that they’re happier, but…

Matthew Yglesias: I was actually just saying that going to meetings, like, really sucks. Like, not with — like, yeah, like, I went to a PTO meeting this week because I believe in it as a civic function.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And, like, I, I want to be involved. Like, I want to know when the pizza party is.

Jerusalem Demsas: Can’t they just send you an email though?

Matthew Yglesias: If somebody needs help — they will eventually, but it’s, like, you got to — you, you know, I, I’m trying to be a good social capitalist.

Jerusalem Demsas: No, I’m not gonna decline.

Matthew Yglesias: But it’s, like, actually being in the meeting and listening to other people’s questions that I don’t care about…

Jerusalem Demsas: I think other people like that, Matt.

Matthew Yglesias: Some people do, but I think they mostly don’t. No, no, no. I mean, I think this is, like, an important —

Jerusalem Demsas: No, I think a lot of people really like meetings. I, again, I’m, like, a very, like, low-meeting person, but, like, I find people who are just like, who are like, “Oh man, complain about meetings,” but they’re excited to go to the meeting, actually. Not us.

Matthew Yglesias: It’s out there. But, like, you know, again, it is true that it is probably better for society at the margin if everybody spent 90 minutes less per week watching their favorite videos and spent 90 minutes more in earnest meetings listening patiently. But it is actually way more boring. You know what I mean?

Like, I personally enjoy watching my favorite internet videos a lot more than I enjoy listening to a PTO meeting. And, like, I still believe that the social function, the three minutes out of the 90 in the meeting that are valuable create positive value in a way that watching YouTube Shorts doesn’t.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But it’s, like, I think it’s really hard. It’s harder than he’s making it out to be for earnest meetings to compete with fun entertainment.

Jerusalem Demsas: That’s why it’s called Bowling Alone, not meeting together.

Matthew Yglesias: Fair enough, yes.

Jerusalem Demsas: So I think that’s a great place to wrap up. As you guys heard, this is a book that was suggested by a reader of The Argument or Slow Boring. So…

Matthew Yglesias: Make your parasocial relationship with us your substitute for social capital.

Jerusalem Demsas: Exactly.

Matthew Yglesias: Tell your friends, tell your family, like, subscribe, follow, make other people you know also listen to this podcast so you can have some common thread, you know, hold society together.

Jerusalem Demsas: And suggest books. You can do that in the comments of either The Argument or Slow Boring. And we’ll see you next week.

Matthew Yglesias: Bye.
