Two kinds of moderate Democrats

There are many pragmatists, but few have the courage to say what they really think.

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 19
 
READ IN APP
 

Yesterday, I wrote about the distinction between the Insurgent Left and the Progressive Establishment. Today, I want to continue trying to enrich people’s understanding of the Democratic Party factional landscape by drawing a distinction on the moderate side between Tactical Moderates and True Believers.

It can be a little hard to tell the difference because if you’re moderate for tactical reasons, you’re of course going to say that you’re a True Believer. And True Believers still believe in the tactical case for moderation and will make that case in an effort to gain support.

The distinction is often revealed only in the moment.

Abigail Spanberger had a somewhat moderate-ish profile as a House member from a blue-leaning purple district, and she ran for governor of Virginia on that profile and won. Virginia only allows governors to serve one term and is a solidly blue state on the federal level, so to whatever extent Spanberger has ambitions to become a senator or serve on a national ticket or in a cabinet, her incentive is to cater to the Progressive Establishment.

The fact that she is instead operating as a force of restraint against the Democratic legislature is thus a source of real frustration to a lot of Virginia Democrats. But I think she’s correct on the merits to raise doubts about mandating collective bargaining for local government employees.

When Sarah McBride went on “The Ezra Klein Show,” it seemed to me that she was trying to create space for a tactical retreat from an electorally indefensible line on trans women’s participation in competitive women’s sports. Martina Navratilova, by contrast, is trying to persuade Democrats that the left’s line on this is genuinely wrong.

I think that within reasonable bounds, tactical moderation is smart.

I do not agree with John Bel Edwards’s positions on guns or abortion, but it’s obviously the case that no candidate espousing progressive views on those topics would have won a gubernatorial election in Louisiana. It would’ve been great if he’d been persuaded to run for Senate. In general, I’d love to see Democrats nominate more politicians like that in the Deep South because it would create a chance to make progress on Medicaid expansion. Both parties’ decision to just write off huge swaths of the country as unwinnable is bad for America, and a renewed spirit of tactical moderation would bring real substantive benefits.

But I also think moderate Democrats are running on fumes in terms of what tactical moderation can accomplish. Expanding the tent in terms of red state recruiting is a totally reasonable agenda that I think even very left-wing people should see the merits of.

At the end of the day, though, if you want to capture the heart of the party, you need to make arguments that are grounded in conviction, and that means arguing on the merits.

Subscribed

The Joe Manchin paradox

Consider former Senator Joe Manchin of West Virginia. Everyone who wasn’t completely addled understood that Democrats were wildly lucky to have a West Virginia Senate seat and that there was no way a conventional progressive could have won the 2012 and 2018 Senate races there.

But I think most progressives felt that Manchin was clearly drawing dead in terms of re-election in 2024 and what they wanted him to do in 2021–22 was YOLO it and vote for filibuster abolition and a sweeping progressive agenda.

And that really is the logic of tactical moderation.

Harry Reid had an old joke about Susan Collins, saying she’ll always be with us except when we need her vote. And there’s clearly something to this. Collins cast a totally inconsequential but highly salient “no” vote on Amy Coney Barrett right before her 2020 re-election, but she cast a consequential vote in favor of Brett Kavanaugh and many lower court judges earlier. She’s criticized or broken with Trump on a number of issues but never really collaborated with Democrats to meaningfully restrain him and clearly maintains a sufficiently cordial relationship with the White House that unlike John Cornyn, she never faced a serious MAGA challenger.

But it’s also true that Collins provided decisive votes in favor of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act in 2009, the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010, and against Affordable Care Act repeal in 2017.

There’s probably just no such thing as a politician who at heart agrees with the base about everything but is also good enough at faking moderation to repeatedly win races in tough states like West Virginia and Maine.

So while it’s certainly coherent to appreciate a Manchin-style figure on a purely tactical level without agreeing with him on anything, I think it’s unrealistic to expect that actual politicians are just totally faking it.

Among other things, once you start playing the role of “guy who champions the interests of coal communities against the demands of green groups,” you’ll come to realize that the green groups are genuinely wrong about some things. At the end of the day, I think environmentalists are basically right about coal. But no advocacy community is right about everything, and there’s plenty the climate movement gets wrong. Most elected officials are not incentivized to delve too deeply into the merits of policy or to really scrutinize their coalition partners’ demands. But a Democrat from West Virginia is incentivized to find things the Progressive Establishment is wrong about, so over and above anything tactical, he’s likely to find genuine points of disagreement.

Personally, I think Manchin was wrong on the merits about some important stuff (notably the filibuster) but also substantially correct that the Build Back Better legislation that congressional leadership was pushing for was inflationary. His push to make Democratic climate efforts more focused on innovation and clean energy deployment and less focused on blocking pipelines was right on the merits. The country would be better off today if Democrats had embraced his permitting legislation more fulsomely.

The True Believers

All the way at the other end of the spectrum, you have Representative Ed Case of Hawaii.

Case is a formidable electoral over-performer. In the Split Ticket database, he overperformed by 17 points in 2018, 14 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022, and 17 points in 2024. He’s been in and out of the Blue Dog caucus over some internecine disputes that I don’t really understand, but he generally has a moderate Blue Dog-ish record. He faced a primary challenge this cycle that, for example, slammed him for supporting the SAVE America Act.

The thing about this is that while Case’s vote-getting skills are impressive, there is genuinely no tactical case for having a moderate in this seat.

Kamala Harris won his district 62 to 37. Elizabeth Warren is, as Slow Boring readers know, an absolutely terrible electoral underperformer. It just doesn’t matter because she represents Massachusetts. But Harris did slightly worse in Massachusetts statewide than she did in Case’s district.

Case is moderate because it’s what he believes, not because it’s what he needs to believe to win his district. He’s also lost several statewide primaries — once for governor, twice for Senate — in part because the Democratic Party primary voters of Hawaii generally prefer someone more progressive. In that light, it’s actually pretty impressive that he fended off an insurgent challenger this cycle, and it’s notable that he had to do so based purely on arguing the merits with no real electability case to be made.

Case is truly a one of one in this regard.

But I have absolutely talked to members of Congress who’ve told me they secretly wish they had purple seats so they could mod-out a bit more and then plead electability when the groups give them shit for it. I think this is mostly a mix of lying and self-deception, but it contains a grain of truth. Most people — even people who would describe themselves as quite progressive — have an issue or two where they break from the pack. But vanishingly few safe-seat members are like this. You don’t see many guys in a D+7 seat who espouse an idiosyncratic moderate position on something unless it’s closely related to home state or district politics.

But plenty of people have a heterodoxy or two they’re quietly stifling. There are also plenty of members who like to engage in what I’ve termed “dog-whistle moderation” or maybe meta-moderation, where they’ll speak in abstract terms about the need to meet voters where they are and change the Democratic Party’s brand and not be held hostage to extremists.

Subscribed

These types tend to complain a lot about the Insurgent Left in a way that doesn’t totally make sense. Iowa didn’t flip from being an Obama-Obama state to a Trump-Trump-Trump state because of Bernie Sanders (who, after all, was in the caucus the whole time). It flipped because mainstream Democrats got more left-wing.

But if you want to change that, you need less obfuscation and more Ed Case energy.

Beyond “the establishment”

Mike Zapler wrote a piece for Axios this week titled “The Democratic Establishment’s Ideas Deficit” in which he argues that “centrists” know what they’re against but have a harder time defining what they’re for.

I think he made some good points but also repeats a fundamental conceptual confusion about this.

If by “the Democratic establishment” you mean something like “the party’s congressional leaders and its past few presidential nominees,” then the reason they have a hard time defining what centrist agenda they favor is that they do not favor a centrist agenda.

It’s actually not even slightly difficult to specify the policy priorities of the Biden-Harris administration as advanced in Congress by Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. The Biden-Harris administration wanted to increase the tax revenue share of G.D.P. while making the tax code more progressive and to use the vast majority of that new revenue to increase spending on clean energy and social services. They believed in abortion rights and affirmative action in college admissions and a fairly crude approach to elite representational politics. On their watch, domestic oil-and-gas production reached new record levels but only after efforts to halt new leases were blocked in court. They believed in the neo-Brandeisian antitrust agenda and appointed its key leaders to top regulatory jobs.

The reason this agenda appears to be just “stuff progressives want, minus some of the stuff that progressives want” is because literally that’s what it is.

The establishment’s enthusiasm for progressive policy is tempered by electoral prudence, court losses, and leadership’s need to set priorities, but their agenda is genuinely a subset of the progressive agenda.

At the same time, an alternative centrist agenda is not hard to find or hard to understand. It would emphasize deficit reduction to put downward pressure on inflation and interest rates and prioritize clean energy abundance while championing domestic fossil-fuel production as superior to foreign production as long as demand for oil and gas exists. It would center ideas, like performance pay for teachers, that aim to increase the productivity of the public sector. It would be an agenda that balances the need for an inclusive economy with a healthy respect for the virtues of free markets and that takes seriously supply-side regulatory constraints on things like housing and health care. Add in the notions that crime control and border security are genuinely important state functions, not things to be engaged in reluctantly as a rearguard effort to avoid political harm.

These are not unfamiliar or secret ideas. They represent substantive moderation, a belief that the progressive NGO blob’s analysis of the major policy problems in American life is not really correct or adequate to the scale of the challenges the country is facing.

I understand why many moderate True Believers don’t want to be more assertive about these kinds of issues. They’re afraid of losing primaries to candidates to their left, and they think that articulating some loud and proud moderate positions is risky compared with minimizing the substantive differences and making a tactical case for moderation.

That analysis makes sense, to an extent, but I think that after 10 years of factional warfare, we can see that it’s a losing strategy for the long term. Nobody wins elections based on a pure politics of from-the-heart conviction. But opportunism and practicality can’t be your whole argument. Actually picking fights about important public-policy questions — not fights with the far left but fights with the establishment and the status quo — makes you seem more authentic and interesting. Picking these fights could also help push back against the sense that moderates practice an inherently dreary politics of limits and “no, you can’t do that.” I think there’s something genuinely inspiring about an agenda that uses abundant housing, rapid economic growth in blue states, and low crime to unlock new avenues of opportunity. It’s really shameful for New York and California to be worse at teaching kids to read than Mississippi, and it would be really amazing if the results achieved by their public school systems were commensurate with the resources invested.

The collective action problem around taking on the groups is real, but a presidential campaign could provide a good context for doing so.

Since moderates are better at winning votes, they’ll always have a tactical argument at their disposal. But I think there are a lot of closeted True Believers out there who right now are so afraid of losing to leftists that they forget to actually be different from the leftists they’re afraid of. That needs to change.

Economists should be worried about birth rates

Don’t be so quick to dismiss the threat of an aging, declining population.

Noah Smith
Aug 19
 
READ IN APP
 

The Economist has an interesting article this week, in which it goes after Daron Acemoglu. Acemoglu is probably the top economist in the world at this point, having just earned a Nobel prize, and sitting right at the top of the list of most cited economists. So it’s kind of funny that when it talks about people who doubt Acemoglu’s research, the one person it mentions is…me!

Give an economist a few drinks, however, and some of them will venture their true opinions about this giant. “Much of his theoretical work is useful, but he uses his models to inform populist policies that have been tried before and failed,” blasts one well-known economist. Some commentators do not require Dutch courage. “I’ve been yelling about Acemoglu for literally a decade,” Noah Smith, an economics blogger, has said, in response to a flurry of online criticism of Mr Acemoglu’s work.

It is true that I have been pretty critical of much of Acemoglu’s work over the years. In 2012 I argued strongly against a paper he wrote in which he claimed that America is more entrepreneurial than Sweden because America’s weaker safety net forces people to work harder (in actuality, Sweden is more entrepreneurial by most measures). In 2022 I pointed out that a famous Acemoglu paper claiming that robots destroy jobs was actually an outlier, and listed a bunch of other papers that reach the opposite conclusion. I liked his book Why Nations Fail, but I also admit that its empirical foundations are fairly shaky. I didn’t like Acemoglu’s more recent book Power and Progress, and I was highly critical of a recent paper Acemoglu wrote about AI and productivity.

But this is hardly newsworthy. I go after Acemoglu’s work because I know he can take it; he’s a titan of the economics field, and I am but a lowly blogger. Nothing I say is going to affect his reputation or his prestige, even if someone at The Economist mentions my critiques in an article. Indeed, after the article came out, top figures in the profession rushed to condemn it and to defend Acemoglu. The Economist does list a bunch of — usually justified — criticisms of Acemoglu’s work, but this does not mean Acemoglu has been discredited as a researcher or exposed as overrated; indeed, it would be difficult to name a top economist whose body of work does not contain a variety of questionable theoretical assumptions, motivated reasoning, and/or shaky empirical results. This is a problem with the field itself, not the man; it’s part of a broader crisis of unreliability throughout much of academia.

But for that same reason, despite the Economist article’s lack of newsworthiness, I think it’s good that the magazine decided to come at the king. Economics is far too hierarchical and closed of a profession. Younger and less accomplished researchers routinely defer to the authority of famous and senior figures, and critics from outside the field are typically brushed off. Exactly how it got to be this way is a topic that deserves a longer post, but I believe the hierarchical, closed culture of econ has resulted in a research literature that has been too skewed toward the priorities and intuition of top authority figures. I thus think it’s generally a healthy thing to tweak the tails of those Olympian figures, as long as criticisms are grounded in substance. As they say, “science is the belief in the ignorance of experts.”

So in that spirit, let’s critique another Acemoglu paper.

First, the background. Recently, a lot of people (including myself, but also prominent economists) have begun worrying about low fertility rates. Across all countries — poor as well as rich — fertility just keeps going down and down, with no floor in sight.

This presents two distinct dangers: population aging and population shrinkage. Aging, rather mechanically, creates a burden for young people, because you have more retirees who have to be supported by each worker, either through taxes or through family support. It also might reduce productivity, for example if older managers are less innovative, but that’s more speculative. Population shrinkage, meanwhile, is a threat to total GDP, which you might care about if you want your country to be more powerful. There’s also the possibility that a smaller population might reduce growth — by reducing the opportunities for specialization, or by reducing the available pool of researchers.

But some people argue that a shrinking population is no problem — or might even be a good thing. When you make human workers scarce, it creates an incentive to invest in labor-saving technology, which boosts productivity. This mechanism has been proposed by some growth theorists, and some economic historians, like Robert Allen, even think this is what caused the Industrial Revolution! This effect might be strong enough to cancel out the aggregate effect of population aging, so that society stays just as rich — or even gets richer — due to low fertility rates.

This is actually a plausible mechanism. I have to say, I’m skeptical that it works in the general case. Human beings aren’t just labor supply; they also create labor demand. The incentive for businesses to buy new machine tools, robots, AI, etc. is that someone is going to buy the stuff they produce with those tools. If you have fewer people, you have fewer consumers. This is probably the reason why the effect of immigration on wages is typically close to zero. Babies are not that different from immigrants. A larger market size can also create an incentive for more rapid innovation — in fact, Acemoglu and Linn (2004) find that faster population growth increases pharmaceutical innovation.¹

But anyway, the idea that population scarcity stimulates innovation is the thesis of a new paper by Daron Acemoglu, David Autor, Keelan Beirne, and Andrew Scott. This is from the abstract:

Contrary to the widespread expectation that [low birth rates] hamper economic growth, we find lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings. These patterns are not explained by educational upgrading, rising female labor force participation, the declining importance of agriculture, or neoclassical-Solow mechanisms. We argue that they reflect the endogenous, labor-saving response of technology to the scarcity of younger workers. Consistent with this interpretation, countries and regions with lower birth rates exhibit more labor-saving patents and growing high-tech activity. There is also higher TFP growth across countries and industries. [emphasis mine]

It’s a plausible result. But before we go on to the details of the paper, let’s talk about what this result would imply, if it does turn out to be true.

One of the paper’s basic theses is that technological automation raises wages. That flies in the face of the empirical work that Acemoglu has done on robots.² It also more broadly seems to contradict what Acemoglu has been saying about AI, both in his research papers and in his public statements. In his 2024 paper, “The Simple Macroeconomics of AI”, Acemoglu writes that “predicted TFP gains over the next 10 years [from AI] are…predicted to be less than 0.53%.” In his 2021 paper, “Harms of AI”, Acemoglu writes:

I argue that if AI continues to be deployed along its current trajectory and remains unregulated, it may produce various social, economic and political harms. These include: damaging competition, consumer privacy and consumer choice; excessively automating work, fueling inequality, inefficiently pushing down wages, and failing to improve worker productivity. [emphasis mine]

This stands in direct contradiction to Acemoglu’s new paper with Autor, Beirne, and Scott. If modern automation technologies push down wages without raising productivity, it cannot compensate for population aging in the way that Acemoglu, Autor, Beirne, and Scott claim that it must — and therefore, population aging is dangerous in a way that it wasn’t before.

Now, it’s fine for a researcher to find two seemingly contradictory things — or even put forward two contradictory theories — in two different papers. The real world is messy and complicated, and there are plenty of “puzzles” in the literature. But if Acemoglu goes around simultaneously telling us:

  1. not to worry about population aging, because automation will compensate for it with higher productivity and higher wages, and

  2. to worry a lot about automation, because it pushes down wages without raising productivity much…

…then we have a problem.³

But anyway, on to the actual details of Acemoglu et al. (2026). First of all, I’m not convinced by their result that lower birth rates raise per capita GDP at the country level. The reason is that once they control for a bunch of stuff — education, urbanization, geographic region, etc. — the result loses statistical significance. Here’s their Table 1, with the estimates I’m talking about circled in red:

In their abstract, the authors declare that “these patterns are not explained by educational upgrading, rising female labor force participation, the declining importance of agriculture, or neoclassical-Solow mechanisms.” But at least some of these patterns can apparently be explained by other things — initial education levels, urbanization, and so on — which makes the claim in the abstract a lot less impressive than it sounds.⁴

Also, note that the more controls the authors add, the weaker the estimated effect becomes. That’s generally a red flag in empirical papers. No matter how smart and careful you are, there are always things you don’t control for, especially in a cross-country regression, since countries differ in so many ways. So if the things you do control for tend to weaken your headline result by a lot, you should be worried that the rest of your result can be explained by the controls you left out.

For example, what about institutions, which Acemoglu has spent much of his career telling us are the main determinants of development? If the legacy of colonialism can be canceled out by passing out free condoms, why did Acemoglu win a Nobel prize? The word “institutions” does not even appear once in this new paper!⁵

A more realistic possibility is that lower birth rates in 1940 were correlated with other things — maybe a lot of other things — and that it’s these other things, rather than birth rates, that give rise to the correlation in the paper.

Of course, what we ultimately care about isn’t GDP per working-age adult⁶ — it’s GDP per capita. The authors have data on GDP per capita, but they barely mention it in the analysis;⁷ I’m not sure why. They do look at total GDP, and here they find no correlation, but a big standard error:

We shouldn’t interpret absence of evidence as evidence of absence. Cross-country regressions have small samples and tons of heterogeneity, so their standard errors tend to be huge — they just have trouble explaining much about the world. But the authors sort of blur this line, saying things like “no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings”, when really they should say “we can’t find a negative impact.” There could be a positive relationship between birth rates and growth hiding in that cloud of data points. (Sadly, this is standard practice in economics, but it makes a difference in how results get sold.)

Anyway, the result for wages in U.S. commuting zones holds up somewhat better. It’s a bit more statistically significant, and it doesn’t get attenuated as much by adding controls. But here, I’m worried about different issues: sorting and clustering. Basically, the result shows that coastal cities — places like New York City, San Francisco, Boston, etc. — had both lower birth rates in 1940 and faster wage growth from 1970 to 2020. The authors’ interpretation is that businesses in NYC, SF, and Boston had fewer workers, and so were forced to embrace labor-saving automation, while businesses in places like Birmingham, Alabama or Gary, Indiana refused to automate because they were endowed with plentiful cheap labor thanks to the legacy of an extra-large Baby Boom.

I am suspicious of this result, because American cities are not independent of each other. People can pretty easily move from Gary, Indiana to Boston, and vice versa! Ideas and capital can move even more easily — it’s pretty trivial for a company that patents a robot in Boston to actually put that robot to work in Gary. In fact, things like this happen all the time in America. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017) note that the commuting zones with the greatest exposure to robots include Detroit, Lansing, Saginaw, Defiance, OH, Lorain, OH, Muncie, IN, Racine, WI, and Wilmington, DE.

Just to take one example of how different regions in America are dependent on each other, suppose that over the period from 1970 to 2020, Americans with lots of talent tended to move from Gary to Boston in order to take advantage of the increasing number of knowledge-industry jobs there. And suppose that at the same time, less talented Americans moved from Boston to Gary, in order to take advantage of the cheap land there. And suppose that high-value industries, like biotech and robotics and software, simultaneously decided to put their research labs in Boston rather than Gary because that’s where the best workers were headed.

In this case, you’d see Boston grow more than Gary, for reasons that had nothing to do with birth-rate-driven labor supply. Other research — for example, by Enrico Moretti — has shown that the sorting of talent and knowledge industries was strongly correlated with income divergences between American regions after 1970. Now, Acemoglu et al. do control for initial local education levels, but if sorting really began after 1970 (as Moretti has shown), that doesn’t really help. They also use “composition-adjusted” wages that try to model what local wages would be if education levels were held constant. But even if that adjustment is valid,⁸ it’s likely that a lot of skills aren’t captured by simply measuring who has a college degree.⁹

So in Acemoglu et al.’s telling, a substantial part of the reason the San Francisco Bay Area became Silicon Valley is not because the tech industry naturally tends to cluster in certain locations and draw in talented engineers and entrepreneurs, but because people in the Bay Area in 1940 didn’t have many kids, which forced Bay Area businesses to embrace automation instead. I simply don’t buy that story. I might eventually be persuaded to buy that story, but I don’t think this paper has sufficient evidence to persuade me yet.

Anyway, I am not claiming that Acemoglu et al. (2026) is a crappy paper. It’s clearly an important addition to the literature, and it deals with a very hard area of research where definitive results are very scarce. The basic idea is worth taking seriously. Maybe in a world where AI is growing by leaps and bounds, a scarcity of human workers should be the last thing on our minds!

But we shouldn’t regard this paper as definitive. And it contradicts a bunch of other research:

  • Kremer (1993) finds evidence that regions with faster population growth had faster technological progress.

  • The endogenous growth literature argues that because ideas are nonrival, larger populations are able to sustain faster technological progress — this is a basic assumption in Romer (1990), Jones (2022), and many other models.

  • Maestas, Mullen, and Powell (2023) find that aging was negatively correlated with productivity growth among U.S. states from 1980 to 2010;¹⁰ Ozimek, DeAntonio, and Zandi (2018) find something similar.

  • Aksoy et al. (2019) do a panel time-series regression across OECD countries from 1970 to 2014, and find that low fertility and low population growth are correlated with slower economic growth.

And even if Acemoglu et al. (2026) is right about the past, that doesn’t mean we can extrapolate it to the future. Jesús Fernández-Villaverde points out that you can’t necessarily do a linear extrapolation of effects at above-replacement fertility to effects at below-replacement fertility:

The fertility collapse now underway has no historical precedent. The seven decades of data the [Acemoglu et al. (2026)] paper analyzes, however carefully, contain nothing remotely comparable to the ultra-low fertility rates we observe today…

[T]he birth and fertility rates of 1950 provide little information about the consequences of the ultra-low birth and fertility rates we are experiencing today. Observations from a very different range of values are unlikely to capture the nonlinear cumulative effects of ultra-low birth and fertility rates…[E]ven in 1980, birth and fertility rates were not as low as they are today…A TFR of 1.56 means each generation is 76% the size of the last: the population declines about 0.9% per year, so after 100 years you retain roughly 40% of the initial population. A TFR of 0.75 means each generation is 37% of the last: about a 3.35% decline per year, leaving roughly 3.5% after a century. Hence, we are dealing with a factor of about 11. A TFR of 1.56 and a TFR of 0.75 both count as “low fertility” in a regression, but they are qualitatively different regimes. The 1980 variation the paper identifies lives in the gentle-decline world; nothing in their data resembles the second…

[W]e should not fool ourselves: we are sailing into demographic terra incognita, and in these waters, the pretense of knowledge is the most dangerous temptation.

In fact, Hayashi (2025) documents just such a nonlinear relationship between aging and growth, where countries with above-replacement fertility seem to benefit from lower birth rates, but countries with below-replacement fertility seem to do worse when their birth rates fall even further.¹¹

External validity and nonlinearity are big problems in much of growth economics, development economics, economic history, and so on (and often in other fields too). But it means that there’s a danger, when the world’s top economist writes a paper making big bold claims, that we end up deferring to that individual’s intellectual authority instead of recognizing the true uncertainty of the unprecedented changes our world is facing. I’m still very worried about the shrinkage of the human race, and I think you should probably still be worried too.

See also Acemoglu (2009), which theorizes that labor scarcity discourages the creation of technology that complements human labor:

The main result of the paper shows that labor scarcity will encourage technological advances if technology is strongly labor saving. In contrast, labor scarcity will discourage technological advances if technology is strongly labor complementary.

2

Acemoglu and Restrepo (2017) find that robots depress wages, whereas the entire mechanism in Acemoglu et al. (2026) relies on automation raising wages. Of course, Acemoglu might claim that robots are special, and not representative of automation technologies in general. But that would make the 2017 result a lot less important and generalizable than it was sold as being, back in 2017!

3

Also note that Acemoglu et al. (2026) can be read as an anti-immigration result. If young population growth stifles automation, doesn’t that mean we should restrict immigration in order to raise wages? That doesn’t mean the result is wrong, and it will certainly make MAGA types happy, but it does mean that it stands in conflict with the existing empirical literature on immigration and wages.

4

The “stacked differences” model does retain statistical significance after the inclusion of controls, but just barely. I wouldn’t put much faith in a borderline result like that.

5

The word “institutional” does appear once, but not as an explanatory variable for past patterns of growth:

At the same time, the demographic changes currently underway are accompanied by increased life expectancy (Scott, 2021, 2024), which may spur institutional changes, policies, and additional human capital investments that complement longer lifespans. These forces may counteract any negative effects of aging[.]

6

Actually, this is a bit beside the point, but I wish economists would stop using GDP per working-age adult as a measure of anything. Working-age adults are not some magical resource that creates GDP just by eating and breathing; they must actually work. Data on output per hour of work is readily available, and if it’s not available, output per employed person is usually a good proxy. I don’t see any good reason to use output per working-age adult. And you should NEVER mislabel output per working-age adult “output per worker”, as Acemoglu et al. (2026) do throughout their paper. Bad!!

7

Except in one section later in the paper, about WW2.

Post-1970 clustering effects could change the relationship between education and wages, in which case the adjustment wouldn’t hold.

In fact, the authors note the greater accumulation of college degrees in the coastal metros with low 1940 birth rates after 1970, but they attribute this — without justification, as far as I can tell — to deliberate local choices and policies rather than geographic sorting.

Everyone hates the “elites,” but who are they?

According to voters, it’s basically just rich people.

Matthew Yglesias
Aug 20
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Everyone likes to talk about “elites,” but what does that mean? Or what do people even think it means?

This week, Jerusalem and I discuss interesting polling from The Argument that asked Americans who they think the elites are. The answer is primarily the very rich, followed by celebrities and to a lesser extent business executives and elected officials.

The mass public largely rejects the conservative concept of an intellectual elite composed of professors, journalists, and people with advanced degrees and seems more aligned with the left-populist concept of anti-elitism as basically just hostility to rich people.

One point I raise is that the “celebrity” category may resolve some of the disjuncture here. After all, a famous and successful journalist or professor can shade into the celebrity category and therefore become elite. Certainly if what you’re interested in is social and political influence, then a famous journalist seems more elite than a similarly famous actor, athlete, or musician — while stipulating of course that the most famous actors, athletes, and musicians are much more famous than the most famous journalists.

My strongest disagreement with the voting public, though, is about its emphasis on the elite status of billionaires relative to business executives.

Of course, many billionaires are business executives and many business executives are billionaires. But to the extent that these categories become disjointed, I think someone like Walmart C.E.O. John Furner is a very important actor in American society even if his net worth is “only” in the low nine figures. To me, the whole point of a concept like “elite” is precisely to distinguish the idea of prestige and influence from mere wealth. Walmart founder Sam Walton’s grandson Lukas is a lot richer than the company’s present-day C.E.O. I’m happy to call him part of the elite just on the basis of his wealth, but, in practical terms, fewer people care what he thinks than pay attention to the views of Furner and other hired-gun C.E.O.s of major companies. Similarly, I would say that senators and four-star generals and admirals are absolutely part of the American elite despite receiving relatively modest compensation. What is the point of the term if not specifically to draw this distinction?

We also delve into some interesting findings about what most Americans believe the elite believes. Jerusalem notes that voters seem to perceive elites as disagreeing with them about basically everything. So most people believe in a government guarantee of health insurance and believe that elites do not support this. But most people oppose government ownership of most businesses, with a larger share saying that elites support the policy. Similarly, Americans believe that elites are against free trade and hold more traditional views about gender roles.

Jerusalem and I discuss all this and more, including the important question of whether we are elites.

Paid subscribers can watch the ad-free embedded video at the top of this post and read the full transcript below.

WATCH THE EPISODE ON YOUTUBE HERE

New episodes post every Thursday.

Jerusalem Demsas: Hi, I’m Jerusalem Demsas.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m Matthew Yglesias.

Jerusalem Demsas: And welcome to The Argument. This week is a little different. We had really interesting new poll results come out. The Argument does original polling every month. This month we decided to look into this question of elite perception. And that is, you know, there’s lots of discourse about what the elites think, what they’re doing, anti-elites, why are they messing up this country?

Matthew Yglesias: And we hate them, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: We hate them. We definitely…

Matthew Yglesias: Everyone is always against the elites.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes. The elites are bad, including — other elites think that elites are bad — and that’s very confusing for everyone. But it sort of got a lot of us internally thinking about this, about A), who are the elite? What do regular people think that the elite think?

Do they think elites are these highfalutin college professors who have their crazy left-wing views about gender and race? Do they think that elites are Bernie Sanders’ kind of version of just billionaires and these rich tech billionaires that Elizabeth Warren is raging against? Who are the elites?

This is obviously one poll. We have a really fun process where we’ve recruited polling experts across the ideological spectrum to review our poll language in advance to help us make sure that we’re being rigorous, etc. But I do want to caveat, this is one poll, and this is not something that has been extensively tested before. I hope we can test more of this in the future, but I think it surfaced so many interesting results. So we’re just going to talk about it today.

But Matt, I’m going to put myself in the position of the pollster.

Matthew Yglesias: OK. I’m going to answer the poll.

Jerusalem Demsas: You have gotten a ring ring from The Argument pollster, even though we do not do phone polls.

Matthew Yglesias: I’m hoping you’re doing text surveys.

Jerusalem Demsas: Exactly. But we’re pretending, and for this, for the purpose of the survey. So which of the following groups do you consider to be part of the elite? Business executives.

Matthew Yglesias: Definitely.

Jerusalem Demsas: Government employees.

Matthew Yglesias: Can I say, like, slightly? No.

Jerusalem Demsas: No. No, you can’t.

Matthew Yglesias: OK. I’m thumbs-downing government employees.

Jerusalem Demsas: College professors?

Matthew Yglesias: Well, I’m gonna give it a no.

Jerusalem Demsas: Billionaires?

Matthew Yglesias: Sure.

Jerusalem Demsas: Elected officials?

Matthew Yglesias: I say yes.

Jerusalem Demsas: Journalists?

Matthew Yglesias: No.

Jerusalem Demsas: Celebrities?

Matthew Yglesias: So I’m gonna say yes to this, but I think that this is important because to me, a celebrity is almost by definition elite. Like, the way you would know that somebody is a celebrity, in part, is that they are elite. And that when it comes to the college professors and the journalists —

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Like, I think that there are individual people whose primary occupation is that they work at a university or they work for a media institution, but who, if you asked me, like, “Is Larry Summers part of the American elite?” I would say yes, right?

And he’s not a billionaire, and he’s not a business executive. He’s not really a journalist, but he publishes columns all the time. He’s not a government employee, though he has been in the past. He’s a college professor, but it’s like, he’s famous.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Ezra Klein is part of the elite. You and I, we’re getting there, you know?

Jerusalem Demsas: One day, one day we’ll join the ranks of the elite.

Matthew Yglesias: No, but it’s like, as journalists, our eliteness is a function of how well-known we are.

Jerusalem Demsas: I guess, I mean, I want to get into some of the results here, but I mean, I think that, like, actually this question of what this word means is difficult for people because, you know, someone’s influence to me matters almost a lot more than their celebrity necessarily. Like, there are people who are in government who have, like, incredibly influential roles over the lives of, like, millions, if not billions of people who I would consider part of the elite, but, no, they’re not household names.

Matthew Yglesias: I agree. Listen, I mean, I’m trying to answer your poll, right? And it’s like, no, no, no, no, no, ’cause it’s different. If you assign me, like, “Matt, like, write an essay explaining, like, what does it mean to be part of the American elite?”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right, and I would say eliteness is an effort to capture an idea of influence. And so the reason business executives are the ones that I am least conflicted about is that, by definition, if you were the executive at a business, you are exerting…

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: …like leadership, decision-making authority over an institution that impacts people’s lives. University administrators, like, aren’t in your poll and aren’t business executives, but they are elite for some of the same reason, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Then, you have to say though, well, within university administrators, obviously administering a big university is more influential than a small one, all else being equal. But I think we also understand that Princeton is like a bigger deal than other universities that might be slightly larger, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: How do we gloss that? It’s a little hard to say, but the greater famousness of Princeton is part of that, right?

Jerusalem Demsas: Sure.

Matthew Yglesias: And so, celebrities in the elite, and it’s like, you know, you can get into sort of borderline cases, right? Like, who is a celebrity? You know, I don’t actually — when you get right down to it, Anya Taylor-Joy probably does not actually exert a lot of influence over American society, even though she’s fairly famous.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But movie stars who are, like, more famous than her maybe do.

Jerusalem Demsas: So yeah, it leads a spectrum. But let’s get to some results, ’cause Matt, I mean, to be fair to our audience, Matt has already seen the results of this poll.

Matthew Yglesias: Wait, wait, wait. I just wanted to loop back to the journalists and the college professors, though, right? Would you…

Jerusalem Demsas: No, I just want to tell people the answers though.

Matthew Yglesias: OK. No, no, no. But this is why I’m hung up on the celebrity thing.

Jerusalem Demsas: All right.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? Which is that if you have Anya Taylor-Joy level of fame, and it’s not because you’re in movies…

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: …it’s because you work for The New York Times.

Jerusalem Demsas: Or you’re an influencer or —

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, but a person like that would be very influential in America.

Jerusalem Demsas: But I don’t even know if that’s — I mean, this is what I find, like, kind of confusing. Like, there are these people who are super famous on TikTok and whatever, and they’re influencers in that people will watch them do get-ready videos and talk about their lives or whatever, and maybe they’ll buy some of the products that they’re hawking or whatever.

But if this person told me to vote for someone: irrelevant. If this told me to like — person told me to, like, you know, this is how I should think of, you know, dating or whatever, I’d be like, “I don’t care about your opinion. You have, like, quite literally zero influence over…” Like, “you’re an attractive person that I will watch do a video,” seems like, what influence do you really have?

Matthew Yglesias: So I think — but that’s wrong, right? I mean, I think an attractive, you know, a celebrity being like, “You know what, Jerusalem, JD Vance has a lot of really smart ideas,” that’s not gonna impact you at all.

Jerusalem Demsas: Certainly not.

Matthew Yglesias: But on specific issues, right? Like, I think, like, Ms. Rachel’s decision to be engaged in the Israel-Palestine conflict…

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: …is meaningful to people, that Taylor Swift’s advocacy on behalf of LGBT issues was — you know, it’s not super meaningful now, both because she kind of shot her shot on it and also because those issues kind of settled into a fixed pattern.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But shifting the conventional wisdom around what kinds of views it’s, like, acceptable for a person in what kind of demographic and cultural spaces to hold is very, very important.

And, like, you can see, like, how upset conservatives are about aspects of The Odyssey, that there is a big, and I think accurate, sense that what Christopher Nolan and Matt Damon and other, like, big influential people in Hollywood think, like, matters for setting the baseline of American culture.

Jerusalem Demsas: But I mean, yeah, I mean, I was surprised. I mean, to me, if you’d asked me in this poll, I mean, it’s hard obviously ’cause I’ve seen the results of it. So, you know, you have to take it with a grain of salt, whatever.

But celebrities as elites is obviously true. It’s almost like even, like, a, it’s like a, common phrase, like The Hollywood Rlite. It’s like just such a common thing to hear about people. And, like, you know, setting aside this whole spectrum thing about if you, like, have a show on BET, is that the same thing as being, like, a movie star for a Christopher Nolan film? Like, whatever.

But then, like, I actually think in some ways, like, the influence of celebrities is overrated here, in politics. Like, what did it matter that Taylor Swift endorsed Kamala Harris? What did it matter that there were rumors that Beyoncé was going to be at the DNC? Like, was anyone, like —

I mean, again, like, I don’t want to get too focused on partisan politics here, but those sorts of things, like, were almost cases where you could, like, check, like, did people, like, would that affect someone’s opinion about how and who to vote for? I think probably not because it’s almost like baked in that Hollywood elite are like liberals.

But yes, do filmmakers of popular movies affect the culture? Like, when Barbie came out, does that change or just reflect, like, where society is. I’m, like, increasingly more in the reflect bucket in our current media atmosphere. I think maybe things were different, like, you know, a couple decades ago.

But right now, like, Barbie to me, as someone who’s, like, maybe, like, too into the feminism, like, kind of debates of the day, well, it felt, like, dated. Like, even, like, the really popular feminist monologue that, like, you know, America Ferrera delivers in that film, like, it felt like I was watching something that had been written and was of the zeitgeist, like, six or seven years back.

And my point there is just that influence and elitism, I think, are actually not totally, like, overlapping concepts, both to people in our poll, and, I think, just in how commonly that word is used. But we should take a break. But when we get back, we’re gonna give you guys actually the results of what people thought.

OK, now that we’re back.

Matthew Yglesias: OK, let me just run down the results. OK, so in your sample, 77% say billionaires are elites.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Sixty percent say celebrities, 48% say business executives, 43% say elected officials, 25% say people making over $200,000 a year.

And then it gets lower, 12% government employees, 12% college professors, 9% people with graduate or professional degrees, 9% journalists.

Jerusalem Demsas: If you’re listening, this is a good episode to watch because we’ll put this on the screen for folks. But basically the only majorities the country is in agreement on is billionaires and celebrities. Nothing else clears 50%.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah. So here, I’m just going to have an old person moment here.

Jerusalem Demsas: Go for it.

Matthew Yglesias: In the write-up that Lakshya did for you guys, he sort of counterposes two theories of the elite. One is like the Bernie Sanders view that the elite is rich people.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And the other is a view that he attributes to Chris Rufo, which is that the elite is university professors and college graduates. My recollection — and so this poll was like an overwhelming victory for the left-populist interpretation of the elite.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: My recollection of an earlier era of discourse is that the right wing, as you were saying, would put a lot of stock in the Hollywood elite.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right. And that they would counterpose the elite as not as down and dirty in this, like, “We’re going to micromanage federal grant programs.” But this idea of celebrities in which — this is why I was leaning so hard on the idea of famous journalists and famous professors. Because I think the right-wing counterview that has the most traction with the public is that there’s this kind of murky stew of famous people.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Who, you know, are in a little bit of a self-congratulatory circuit of award shows, right? And sometimes it’s the Oscars and it’s just Hollywood people, but documentary filmmakers also get up at the Oscars.

And sometimes, like, it’s the Pulitzer Prize, you know, and it’s like more obscure writers and celebrities, but that there’s this circuit of fame and that it’s very left-leaning and that it’s specifically left-leaning on cultural issues.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: You know, and that it hops on these bandwagons, whether it’s Black Lives Mattering or, you know, whatever else, and that this cultural elite is important in America. And it is true that Chris Rufo has tried to programmatize this and literalize it in a way that I think people have not really bought. But it is also true that celebrities as elites outpoll business executives.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah. But, I mean, I find this a little bit hard because business executives, you could imagine this being — I mean, it could be like, you know, Tim Cook, but it also could be like the owner of a small company in your town. It’s like, I think it’s like not — I could imagine that those things would be mixed for people. And when you look at business executives at, you know, we look at the crosstabs, right? College-educated people, 57% of them say that business executives are elite and just 43% of non-college.

So, that indicates to me maybe, like, the types of business executives that were evoked by this question would’ve driven this answer a bit here. Also, I’ll say that with this, the other big gap is between Trump and Harris voters. Fifty-seven percent of Harris voters said that business executives were elite and just 40% of Trump voters did. That’s a 17-point gap.

Matthew Yglesias: Right.

Jerusalem Demsas: And Trump voters and nonvoters seem similar. So again, what kinds of business elite are you — business executives are you thinking about? I would imagine that maybe nonvoters, non-college-educated voters are imagining a more mainstream version of a business executive than the high-powered CEOs that maybe were evoked for you.

Matthew Yglesias: Well, I mean, I think there’s two questions about this that would be fascinating to see in further polling. I mean, one thing that has been occurring to me is my totally uninformed guess is that most people, particularly most left-wing people, overstate the correlation between being the executive of an important company and being a billionaire.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Because it happens to be the case at this specific point in time that Elon Musk is both the richest person in America and also is the CEO of companies that Elon Musk founded.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But Jeff Bezos is very, very rich and is no longer the CEO of Amazon.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Now, he still, because he owns so much Amazon stock, has a kind of embedded ability to control what Amazon does, but he’s like a retired playboy, you know, who sort of happens to be famous.

Bill Gates has not been operationally involved with Microsoft for a very long time. He’s not as rich as he used to be because he has transferred so much money to his foundation, but he, like, exerts a lot of influence and stuff through that.

A lot of billionaires, like the rich — we live in the D.C. area, and the richest people in Greater Washington are just heirs to the Mars candy fortune. And I don’t want to say they’re not elite, like, these are multi-billionaires, but they are not the business decision-makers whose, like, thoughts and feelings and ideas shape the economy of Greater Washington. And also, if you’re, like, envisioning, you know, the workers banding together, to fight for better pay or whatever. Like, they’re not — this is not who they’re — that’s not where the practical conflict lies.

You know, something I think we all know about public opinion is that if you ask people about stuff that they haven’t thought a lot about, they’ll give you answers that don’t necessarily make a ton of sense.

Jerusalem Demsas: Well…

Matthew Yglesias: And I think, like, most people have not spent a lot of time, like, scrutinizing the Forbes, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index and the Fortune 500 list and seeing how well these things line up.

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, I think one thing that we were concerned about that with our poll, because again, this is nothing that’s been polled a lot, the consistency across categories. I shouted out a couple of areas of divergence across college, non-college, etc.

But, in general, across categories, you don’t see a lot of divergence. Everyone is basically in agreement that billionaires and celebrities are elites.

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: But, I mean, I think that that kind of consistency should give you some level of confidence in this.

But I want to underscore two things here. Like, one, you kind of glanced at this, but there is this big effort amongst the right to categorize, like, almost like a Cultural Revolution-style version of elite to be people with graduate degrees, people who work in government. I mean, that was kind of a lot of the ethos behind DOGE. People who are college professors, journalists, the media. And it’s just, like, not flying.

At least, again, in this poll, only 9% of people would even say that people with graduate professional degrees are elites. They don’t think journalists are, they don’t think college professors are, they don’t think government employees are. None of that is true.

And you might think, “OK, well, did people think ‘elite’ was necessarily negative?” The other big part of our poll was asking people about their perceptions of elite views. So, like, what do you think elites think about?

Matthew Yglesias: Yeah.

Jerusalem Demsas: A variety of things. And, time and again, the big pattern you see in our poll is that people have view X. We ask them what they think a majority of Americans think, and they think, “The majority of Americans agree with me.” And then you ask them, “What do you think elites think?” And they think elites think whatever the opposite is. They think something fucking insane and horrible.

Their picture of elites is not super consistent. They will assign both very left-wing and very right-wing views to elites. But what is pretty consistent across the poll is that they will assign the opposite view that they hold.

And so, what that tells me is that people have a negative view of what it means to be an elite. They’re not like, “Oh wow, billionaires and celebrities, love them, so elite.” They’re like, “Billionaires and celebrities, these people are elites and they have views that are diametrically opposed to both me and the majority of Americans.”

And I find that, I don’t know, I find that super interesting.

Matthew Yglesias: OK, but it’s actually really funny because I think here’s the place where I think these poll results most go against the conventional wisdom, right? Which is that I think there’s a view among left-of-center politics gabbers that there’s a kind of a populist construct in America that is left-wing on economics, potentially very left-wing, and right-wing on culture, like, possibly very right-wing.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But, in the poll, 71% of respondents say that they support free trade agreements.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: But their perception is that elites are much more skeptical of free trade agreements. They say that it’s overwhelming opposition to government ownership of most businesses, but a perception that a large minority of the elite favors this.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yes.

Matthew Yglesias: Then, conversely, like, people attribute to elites a sexist view about men and women’s suitability for leadership.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? So people say that they think most people think men and women are equally suited to leadership, but that most elites disagree with that.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: Which, again, if you look at the characterization of elites as sort of rich business decision makers and celebrities, and it’s like, well, you know, like, most of the people in those positions are men.

Jerusalem Demsas: Mm-hmm.

Matthew Yglesias: Right? And, clearly, if America’s Fortune 500 board chairs, like, wanted women to be CEOs of companies, there would be more women CEOs of companies.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: And so, you know, this is one where, in some ways, I think people are being more clear-sighted than the discourse, right? Like, whatever is happening in corporate America, like, clearly the people in charge, like, in their — they would never say it. I don’t think you could find a CEO, maybe Elon Musk in public would say, “I think on average women are less suited to leadership positions.”

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: But that’s what they are doing, right? With their decision-making authority. Now, they could give you some stories about why it came out that way, but we can see what’s happening there. So, that I think is fascinating. Then, the one issue where the public is like populist on an economic question is that 66% of people say there should be government-provided insurance for all Americans. And they say that elites don’t agree with that.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: So that particular question, like, perfectly fits like a Bernie Sanders narrative. Like, we can come together across party lines to create government-provided health insurance for all Americans, which is what most people want, but it is opposed by the elite. On that question, yes. But the mass public wants to undercut your wages with NAFTA and they think elites are stopping that from happening. So…

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean, I am, like, to draw up the feminism stuff a bit here.

Matthew Yglesias: Welfare state liberalism.

Jerusalem Demsas: I mean —

Matthew Yglesias: It’s so hot.

Jerusalem Demsas: This poll confirms every single one of my priors, and isn’t that amazing? I mean, one thing I think that’s really interesting is there’s so much negativity around the term “feminism.” There’s countless, you know, articles and think pieces and whatever about how, you know, young people aren’t feminist anymore and feminism’s a dirty word and everyone’s returning to tradition, etc. Our poll finds — we ask people and we really — I, you know, what I try to do is, like, really give people outs so that we’re not artificially constraining them to views that I would find comfortable.

We asked “Which of the following, if any, do you believe describes feminism in practice? Please select all that apply.” So, they were able to select multiple of these answers.
