Stop making up reasons to be mad at your adversaries

A harmless old A.E.S. tweet, a paranoid anti-A.E.S. conspiracy theory, and the case for a mind of winter

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 3
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Abdul El-Sayed is in hot water in certain corners of the internet over a tweet from five years ago in which he said that on 9/11 itself he would mourn the victims of the terrorist attack but that the next day he would mourn the tragic ways in which the American response went awry.

Eyal Yakoby
@EYakoby
Abdul El-Seyed deleted this post. It would be a shame if it went viral.
8:45 PM · Aug 31, 2026 · 439K Views
201 Replies · 5.08K Reposts · 12.7K Likes

My sincere advice to anyone considering a run for elected office at any point in their life would be to never, under any circumstances, try to say anything thoughtful or provocative around a national day of mourning.

That said, as someone in the line of work where you are supposed to be thoughtful and provocative, this statement seems completely reasonable.

The view that the American military response to 9/11 ended up being unproductive is very widely held. Many innocent people died as a result of the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. An enormous amount of money was spent, money which could’ve been used in many other, better ways. Lots of American soldiers died or were injured. I used to be on the same workout schedule as a guy who lost his left foot to an I.E.D. in Iraq. I respect his service and the service of others I know who fought in those wars, but unlike my grandfather who fought the Nazis, I can’t really say that their sacrifices were worth it.

It’s a pretty fucked up situation, and El-Sayed is right about that.

Unless, of course, he’s actually a hardcore anti-American Islamo-leftist who hates this country and is leaping at the opportunity to besmirch its name on a sacred day of mourning.

But is he?

There’s certainly no evidence within the text of that tweet that he is. It’s true that if you want to look at the most outré things Hasan Piker has ever said and then assert both that those things reflect Piker’s true feelings about the world and that El-Sayed’s association with Piker during the Michigan Senate primary campaign reflects his uncritical endorsement of that version of Piker’s worldview, you can read the tweet that way. But that’s a fully circular argument. If El-Sayed had never tweeted about 9/11, you could still be mad about the other stuff. Being mad about the tweet doesn’t add anything.

And he has specifically disavowed Piker’s remarks about 9/11. What’s more, El-Sayed supports Western aid to Ukraine — he is not part of the campist anti-American left, while Piker seems to be.

Not to do a whole take about 9/11, and I don’t want to get started on Piker, but this is an illustration of a problematic internet trend where you decide first that someone is your enemy, then read everything he says through the presumption that he’s a bad guy, and then treat this purely circular reasoning as if it’s new evidence of new wrongdoing.

I thought both El-Sayed and Haley Stevens had kind of bad takes on Israel and that all things considered, El-Sayed was a riskier electability choice who creates unnecessary complications for Democrats’ effort to take the Senate. But he is, in fact, the Democratic nominee, and there’s no need to make that into something bigger than it is.

A mind of winter

My favorite poem is Wallace Stevens’s “The Snow Man” from 1921.

Stevens is obsessed with the relationships between sense and perception. In another of his poems, the longer and less snappy “The Man With the Blue Guitar,” the titular man is challenged by an unknown audience who complain “You have a blue guitar / You do not play things as they are.” The guitarist retorts that “Things as they are / Are changed upon the blue guitar.”

“The Snow Man” is about the blue guitar of our minds.

It’s tempting to look upon the bleak emptiness of a snowy New England field in January and read it as a kind of metaphor. And it’s true that a writer setting a story against the backdrop of a bleak New England winter who took the time to dwell on this imagery would be making some kind of metaphorical or thematic point. The ice storm in the 1997 Ang Lee movie is a point about the weather, but it’s also symbolism.

Like the characters in the movie, Stevens is a guy who lived in Connecticut. And if you live in Connecticut, you sometimes get bleak January weather. That’s just a thing that happens; it’s genuinely what the weather is like. It doesn’t actually mean anything. The short daylight in the New England winter can make you feel sad. The decline in the pace of social activity can make you feel sad. But it’s not the case that God has chosen the weather to symbolize something or make you feel a certain way.

Stevens calls on us to reject the fog of metaphor and to “have a mind of winter,” which will allow us to see “nothing that is not there and the nothing that is.”

This is, of course, a terrible engagement strategy. If you want to gain clout and clicks on social media, you have to imbue everything and everyone your audience already dislikes with secret meaning and nefarious portent.

People who don’t like El-Sayed frequently do this, and it’s a big vibe in general on Islamophobic Twitter. But when you see a headline like “Hochul wears hijab at N.Y.C. Islamic center ahead of 9/11 anniversary, sparking backlash,” you have to ask yourself what kind of sense this makes. It’s totally normal to dress in line with religious norms when you’re visiting a place that’s not of your faith, and why shouldn’t she go there two weeks before the 9/11 commemoration?

The negative responses are clearly people who don’t like Kathy Hochul looking for stuff to get mad at. And stuff like this is totally endemic to contemporary internet culture.

Hypothetical anger

You see this on all sides, of course.

Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory doesn’t change the fact that pro-Israel Democrats disagree with him about Israel, some of them quite strongly. This is categorically different from leftists who might be disappointed about being asked to support Mary Peltola, even though she’s moderate. Moderate as she may be, Peltola is still more progressive than Dan Sullivan. Pro-Israel Democrats in Michigan, on the other hand, are being asked to vote for El-Sayed, even if they’re closer to Mike Rogers’ views on the issue. It’s a real ask.

Still, Chuck Schumer and Gretchen Whitmer — who both pulled out all the stops for Haley Stevens — have endorsed El-Sayed. So did Elissa Slotkin. So did Stevens herself. That’s normal politics! But it’s become dogma on the left to seize on every bit of friction as evidence not of policy disagreements but of a secret plan to sabotage his election.

Cenk Uygur
@cenkuygur
I've never seen anything like this Michigan race. The Democratic Party is attacking its own candidate! In an absolutely pivotal race! I've seen more Democrats on TV attacking @AbdulElSayed than I've seen Democrats taking on GOP. Dems are attacking him more than Republicans are!
1:18 AM · Sep 1, 2026 · 311K Views
1.75K Replies · 2.01K Reposts · 15.4K Likes

There is just zero evidence of this. In fact, while Schumer has endorsed El-Sayed, El-Sayed says he doesn’t support Schumer for majority leader. Under the circumstances, they are getting along pretty well!

David Sirota is making stuff up here, though.

Or, rather, based on his longstanding dislike of the bogeyman “corporate Democrats” he has decided that it’s clearly the case that in a purely hypothetical situation in which those Democrats could be assured of a Senate majority while El-Sayed loses, they would sabotage him. From that he infers that in the actual, non-hypothetical situation these unnamed corporate Dems are “willing to risk losing Congress to try to get what they want.”

I would say that in the completely non-hypothetical context of the Michigan primary, left-wing Democrats were willing to risk losing Congress by backing the weaker electability choice to try to get what they want. But they did get what they want, and while I think El-Sayed will almost certainly underperform the fundamentals, he’ll probably win. And everyone is endorsing him.

It’s not helpful for the pro-Israel faction to make up things about him beyond the scope of that disagreement, and it’s equally unhelpful for his fans to invent conspiracies.

Choosing to be angry

I think one of the real tells of this rhetorical style is its obsession with hypothetical scenarios. Earlier this week, a woman carrying knives stabbed multiple people in Times Square before being killed by police officers. Because crime is a lot lower in New York City than it used to be and because events in Times Square are inherently noteworthy, this was the subject of a high-profile press conference featuring the mayor and the police commissioner, during which the mayor commended the officers for their swift action in saving lives.

A number of people got upset not at what Zohran Mamdani said or did but at the idea that had this same set of facts played out at an earlier time in Mamdani’s career, he would have had a different reaction.

Lee Kuan Yimby
@LeeKuanYimby
Zohran literally would have started a protest in this woman's name 3 years ago and called to abolish the NYPD.
Fox News @FoxNews
BREAKING: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani addresses the deadly Times Square stabbing, saying a woman carrying multiple knives stabbed two people before responding NYPD officers deployed a Taser and opened fire. "I want to thank the NYPD officers who stepped in and prevented a
3:49 AM · Sep 1, 2026 · 133K Views
17 Replies · 47 Reposts · 1.15K Likes

As a fan of counterfactual histories, I find this speculation plausible but … so what?

I’m glad that Mamdani has come closer to my views on these issues, and I’m glad that many of his supporters acknowledge the wisdom of his new approach, and I hope it brings us all toward a more sensible view of crime and law enforcement.

Now, again, if you just know deep in your heart that Mamdani is secretly burning with rage at the N.Y.P.D. and itching at the chance to go totally soft on crime, I guess you can find random splotches of data to “confirm” that.

But everything he’s actually saying and doing suggests that he understands the political imperative of low crime and that he broadly believes deference to the expert judgment of the existing set of police officials is a good way to secure that. And crime is, in fact, continuing to fall under this policy mix. Take the win!

Some of this is, obviously, opportunism:

  • If you don’t agree with Mamdani’s overall approach to being mayor, it’s objectively inconvenient for you that he’s done a good job of handling crime issues. So it might be better to just pretend he hasn’t.

  • If you want El-Sayed to lose, and you know his views on Israel are probably something the voters are reasonably comfortable with, it’s convenient to attribute to him a much farther-reaching anti-American view of foreign policy that he hasn’t actually articulated.

  • If you’re worried that El-Sayed running much weaker than Michigan gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson debunks your larger thesis about the electorate’s hunger for leftist candidates, it’s convenient to explain this away with a conspiracy theory.

But I also think a lot of people are just addicted to a kind of internet rage.

Hyper-negative coverage of the Mamdani administration clearly sells copies of the New York Post. If your whole brand is selling people an anti-establishment insurgency, you can’t really say “the primary is over, we didn’t get all our guys but we got some of them and now it’s time to shift into cooperative mode.” Negativity does well on the internet, in general.

It would be boring for people who disagree with El-Sayed’s actual positions to just say that again every day; it’s more engaging to make stuff up and pretend this old 9/11 tweet said something it didn’t say. But beyond the immorality of the opportunism, there’s something soul-deadening and misery-inducing about behaving this way. Do you really want yourself and your audience to be sad and angry all the time? It’s a lot better to try to keep a calm head and not read maximum nefariousness into everything you see.

title: Ingots We No Longer Trust

Ingots We No Longer Trust

America’s word is as good as gold — that is, unreliable

Paul Krugman
Sep 4
 
READ IN APP
 

In the Yap islands of Micronesia, rai stones carved out of crystalline limestone, with a hole in the center, are considered objects of great value, sometimes described as a form of money. However, they are often large — sometimes as big as 12 feet in diameter — and they rarely literally change hands, given how difficult they are to move. So they stay wherever they are. Their ownership is established by oral history, with changes in ownership established by appending transfers to that shared oral history. This is, by the way, a sort of preliterate version of the blockchain!

For the most part, monetary gold — gold held as reserves by national central banks — is a lot like the stones of Yap. Central banks own trillions of dollars’ worth of gold, which they sometimes sell to each other to settle international payments. But these transfers rarely involve physically moving gold across borders. A large fraction of the world’s gold reserves actually sits in a vault underneath the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, although the New York Fed does move ingots between compartments when transfers take place.

And why not? The sanctity of nations’ ownership of gold stored in New York is guaranteed by the word of the U.S. government — a government that is utterly reliable, because it honors the role of law.

Or anyway, that’s the country we used to be.

“Rule of law” is not a phrase often applied to the Trump administration. And the administration has special contempt for international law. Many of Trump’s tariffs have been ruled illegal under U.S. law, but more or less all of those tariffs were and are in clear violation of past agreements solemnly signed by previous U.S. presidents, including Trump himself.

So the idea that the U.S. government might devise some excuse to seize gold held in the Fed’s vault is no longer far-fetched. And nations are taking precautions. Earlier this week the Dutch central bank announced that it was shifting about $12 billion in gold from the vault in New York to the Bank of England’s vault in London. This follows a move by the French central bank to shift an even larger sum from New York to Paris. Other countries are considering similar moves.

The direct economic or financial impact of these actions will be minimal. There won’t even be large trans-Atlantic gold shipments: foreign central banks will sell their New York gold to private buyers in America and replenish it with purchases from private sellers in Europe.

But the symbolism is chilling. America is no longer trusted. Foreign governments can no longer count on us to obey the most basic rules, like the commandment that thou shalt not steal other people’s gold.

And even when Trump is gone, it will take many years of honest, responsible U.S. government to restore that lost trust.

Still extremely busy. So that’s all for today.

You can’t blame housing shortages for literally everything

Plus alternate Reconstructions, saving D.C. real estate, and the truth about Tupac

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 4
∙

READ IN APP
 

Join us on Wednesday for a Slow Boring D.C. happy hour! We’ll be downtown on September 9 at 6 p.m. Details available for paid subscribers at the end of this post.

Subscribed

Before diving into this week’s Mailbag, let’s talk television. Against my better judgment, I’ve become a fan of the new HBO Max show “Lanterns,” and it’s reminding me why I kind of hate TV. Is the show good? It seems good to me. At least, the three episodes that have aired are good. At least, they seem good. But are they actually good? The truth is that I have no idea. When you read a novel or watch a movie and you decide that it’s good, part of the goodness of the scenes or chapters that come at the beginning is how they relate to the overall story. And more to the point, if someone else tells you that “Moby Dick” is great, then when you come across something in the beginning that seems intriguing, you have reason to believe that the intriguing vibe isn’t just a vibe.

Other people who have actually read the end of the book say that it’s good.

But it’s not just that I haven’t seen the end of “Lanterns” and you haven’t seen it and none of the critics or podcasters talking about it have seen it — there literally is no end for anyone to see. An ending hasn’t been filmed. It hasn’t been written. It doesn’t exist. All this intrigue and vibes and setup and flashback could mean nothing. I was really happy to sit out watching “The Americans” while a lot of people I knew were singing its praises, then fire up the first episode after the final one aired and people were still saying it was great. And it is indeed great! I can tell you that because I know how it ends and it really all hangs together.

Michael Tolhurst: I am sort of curious. Have you investigated the housing stock and regulatory framework for housing in the Austro Hungarian Empire? Could the challenges of the Empire been solved by more market rate housing in growing industrial urban zones for national minorities to improve their economic standing and have more commitment to a joint polity? (Or, another way to put it, does the housing theory of everything really generalize *to everything*?) Is there an exciting alternate history genre waiting to be launched based on counterfactual housing policy?

I am only slightly knowledgeable about this, but I have looked into it a little because there is an obsession throughout the worldwide left with the successful public housing program that was inaugurated in the “Red Vienna” days of the 1920s and continues today in Austria. I think there are a lot of problems with the way this is usually invoked, and part of that involves dropping the historical context.

Obviously Vienna in 1910 was the capital of a large empire while by 1920 it was the capital of a rather small country that was ravaged by war and whose whole economy was in tatters. This is not really a situation that has much in common with any contemporary city, and it meant there were a lot of weird dynamics in place.

If you flip back to the prewar years, though, Vienna was growing very rapidly. I don’t know exactly what their land use policies were, but this is similar to what we see in the industrializing boomtowns of the American Midwest. It’s a reminder that zoning-induced housing scarcity is, broadly speaking, a postwar phenomenon. All across the Western world we used to know how to let housing supply grow with demand.

In 1850, the municipal boundaries of Vienna were expanded to include suburban districts beyond what’s today known as the “inner city” that was bounded by the old city walls. Soon after, the walls and adjacent fortifications were torn down to make space for new buildings and the construction of what today is the Ringstrasse. By the 1890s, the precursor to what today is the Vienna S-Bahn was in operation. So, contrary to the presumption of this question, I don’t think we can attribute anything in particular to housing issues when we’re looking at the problems of the late-phase Habsburg Empire. They seemed to have a pretty reasonable housing situation.

Beyond Vienna, as far as I know other Habsburg cities were also growing. The 1910 census, for example, apparently showed that 43 percent of the residents of Trieste were born outside the municipality. Of those about a quarter were immigrants from Italy (Trieste was a majority Italian-speaking city), and the rest were from elsewhere in the empire.

Share

Several years ago, when I made the case that the collapse of the Habsburg Empire was far from inevitable and the polyglot polity could have survived indefinitely if not for defeat in World War I, this internal migration was key to my argument. Austria was a relatively late industrializer compared with the leading countries of Western Europe, but by the 1910s the Industrial Revolution was beginning to take off. There were, however, marked regional differences inside the empire with the western parts considerably more advanced and prosperous than the eastern parts. In practice, this meant there was a lot of concrete economic value in the way that membership in the empire meant that people who spoke Romanian or Ruthenian or Slovene or Croatian or Polish had the ability to migrate to richer cities like Vienna and Prague. For much of the 19th century, lots of people were moving from Central Europe to the United States of America. But right around when World War I broke out, America was moving in the direction of restricting immigration, so the right to internal migration would have become more valuable.

Conversely, the aforementioned Trieste went into a spiral of decline when it switched from being the main port of the Austro-Hungarian Empire to one of dozens of mid-sized Italian coastal cities.

There would have been, in other words, pretty strong countervailing reasons for members of minority national groups to not want the empire to break up. But that internal migration would have, of course, also created tensions of its own. Big influxes of non-Germans into Vienna would have generated NIMBYism and what you can’t quite call “anti-immigration” sentiment but something politically similar. Again, though, this simply points to the need for the imperial government to act as an honest broker rather than as an instrument of German oppression, helping to manage a multi-lingual entity in a way that would facilitate peace and prosperity for everyone — just as today’s European Union has a lot of problems and controversies but is also broadly recognized as offering a lot of concrete advantages.

Matthew: Alternate history question of the week! Two American Civil War scenarios to consider:

1) The First Battle of Bull Run ends in a decisive Confederate defeat, destroying the Confederate army in northern Virginia and opening the road to Richmond. Is there an outcome where the American Civil War ends up being a few months of political violence followed by some kind of negotiated settlement for the Confederate states to return to the Union (with slavery likely intact)?

2) Rather than surrender and go home, Confederate forces in 1865 disperse into the hills and maintain a guerrilla war against Union forces. What does a prolonged campaign of insurgency/counterinsurgency in the South look like for post-war American politics? Would a violent Confederate insurgency result in a better outcome for the African-American population in the South, with U.S. Government forces reliant on them as valuable local allies (rather than as a victimized group that needed protecting and could ultimately be politically bargained away, as in actual Reconstruction)?

On (2), in terms of the perennial debates about what the war was really about, the fact that guerrilla fighting didn’t happen is very telling. Letting the Union take the cities and the railroad lines and fighting an endless insurgency from the countryside would, after all, be the normal way for a war of national liberation to proceed. But if you head to the hills to fight as a guerrilla, you can’t hang on to your estates and your slaves. And the goal of the war was to hang on to the estates and the slaves. Once it became impossible to win, the Southern elite surrendered on terms that would let them keep their estates even if they had to give up the slaves.

So I think the big difference in an insurgent war scenario is really that you would have ended up with land reform: rebel estates seized and allocated to freedmen (the fabled “40 acres and a mule”) or white collaborators.

For roughly the same reasons that the Democrats eventually won power and abandoned Reconstruction, I think northern whites would have lost patience with an endless guerrilla war in the South and backed down eventually. But as you suggest, it would have probably led to the creation of a more entrenched class of armed African American small farmers who would have been harder to displace than in the historical Redemption process where Southern whites regained political control of their states and disenfranchised African American voters. This is kind of wild speculation, but it’s possible that the ultimate political settlement of this longer-running and more violent version of the conflict would have been population transfers and a kind of de facto partition of the South.

In the 1880 census, considered a lot more reliable than the 1870 one, three Southern states — South Carolina, Mississippi, and Louisiana — had a Black majority and Georgia and Alabama were both at 47 percent. What if four or five of the 11 Confederate states had been Reconstructed permanently and the other six or seven Redeemed with population migrations between the two blocs? One could try to spin this out.

Separately, the Bull Run question is interesting. It seems like, yeah, the Confederacy might have collapsed fast. Then it would have turned out that when Southern senators resumed their seats in Washington, the Republicans would only have 31 seats out of 68. So it’s not just that moderate Republicans like Abraham Lincoln would have promised not to end slavery in the existing states; it’s not clear how the Republicans would have actually been able to enact any of their ideas about halting the spread of slavery into the territories. The whole secession concept was a panicky overreach that actually brought about the Radical Republican legislative hegemony that Southern whites were afraid of.

Share

lwdlyndale: Do you have a Tupac take?

If I told the world what I know, I’m afraid they’d kill me to keep me quiet.

Eric H: Do you lean more towards buying books or getting them from the library? Reading physical books, or reading on an e-reader, or listening to audio books? Does any of this vary based on genre, topic, or reason for reading?

I’m a Kindle guy — I love the portability and convenience. That’s not to say that print is bad, since I’ve read many books in print and where I have space I do like to have a shelf full of books that I admire. But on a practical level, I prefer to read on my Kindle.

Dan Diamond: Do you see a realistic path to revitalizing downtown DC and local real estate markets to the city’s pre-covid, pre-DOGE days?

One thing is that I sincerely think that while every other place on earth zigs against data centers we in D.C. ought to zag. The District of Columbia is unusual in not offering a sales and use tax exemption for people buying computer equipment to put in a data center, and we ought to consider changing course on that and clarifying our industrial zoning to facilitate data center construction. Our property tax base is seriously ailing at the moment, and it seems like an opportune time to grab some investment that will create jobs short term during a localized recession in construction and that will support the tax base over the longer term.

Beyond that, what we have right now is a central business district where the office space is like 20 percent empty and as a result the ground-floor-retail ecology in the central business district is also ailing.

The medium-term solution for this is for the office district to shrink geographically. Right now, there are non-trivial numbers of office buildings in the West End, Navy Yard, and NoMa, and those buildings should mostly close and be replaced by apartments and condos. Then the current office tenants in those neighborhoods could relocate to downtown proper, at which point the vacancy rate would normalize and the ground-floor-retail situation downtown would normalize as well.

A big problem that the city is having at the moment is that not only is the general DOGE shock to the local economy hurting demand for residential real estate, but the D.C. Council and the court system have also done a bunch of stuff to make us less attractive as a place to build and invest. The new mayor is committed to zoning reform and secured the support of most of the city’s local YIMBY activists. Allowing accessory dwelling units and rowhouses in the most exclusionary neighborhoods should do something to juice construction, but unfortunately with current demand conditions and capital competition I don’t think zoning changes are really going to get new multifamily builds. Smaller projects might be financially viable because they are subject to lower regulatory burdens, but if the mayor wants to make her YIMBY dreams come true, she needs to look at the broader regulatory system. Some of that is eviction rules and some of it is inclusionary zoning (which, remember, is a tax on housing), but some of it honestly is just rhetoric and openness.

Investors have gotten spooked over the past several years by the political direction of the city and that’s shut investment down. Electing a democratic socialist mayor doesn’t help.

On the other hand, to some extent it just means the thing investors feared would happen did happen. If the worst-case-scenario mayor showed up before taking office with some business-friendly regulatory reforms and then started taking meetings and speaking publicly about how she understands the need to attract private capital, that could really turn sentiment around.

The point of all of this is that despite the currently sagging market, the absolute price of housing in D.C. remains high. With a sensible, pro-growth regulatory structure, new multifamily housing should make sense financially. In fact, new multifamily housing is getting built in Virginia as we speak, despite it being exposed to the same regional economy. If there is demand for new multifamily housing, then the office district could shrink but become more vibrant and there would be plenty of demand for the city’s stores and restaurants. But if investors remain spooked, things will just sit partially empty instead of being repurposed.

America is still beating China in the AI race

The U.S. is staying ahead, though the costs of that lead are still unknown.

Noah Smith
Sep 5
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Most of the debate around AI, at least in the U.S., is not about the international aspect. The local political debate is all about data center construction; the national economic debate is mostly about fear of job loss, with a side discussion about a potential bubble; and the technological discussion, at least in public, is mostly about AI safety and risk. U.S.-China competition gets mentioned in certain circles, but it’s probably safe to say that it’s not Americans’ chief topic of concern.

But it still matters! For one thing, there’s the military aspect to think about. Cyberwarfare so far hasn’t been decisive in military conflicts, but AI’s incredible cybersecurity prowess could change that. If AI ends up strengthening defense more than offense — say, by finding all of the available exploits and patching them before an attacker can get to them — then cyberwarfare will become less important. But if those who possess the best AI models are able to successfully hack anyone using a less capable model to defend, it could lead to a decisive shift in the balance of power.

AI hacking doesn’t have mutually assured destruction, like nuclear warfare does. Imagine if China were to gain a big lead in AI models that gave it the power to easily hack into American banks and brokerage accounts and erase people’s wealth. It would cause absolute chaos in American society, but how could the U.S. retaliate? Launch nukes? Nor could the U.S. hack China in return, since China’s more capable AI would also be used to defend.

If either country opens up a large, sustained lead in AI capabilities, it might upend the balance of power between the two.

Not all AI issues are zero-sum, of course. If the U.S. and China both continue pushing forward with AI research at maximum speed, it may quickly cause safety issues. The recent AI agent swarm attack on Hugging Face shows that AI has reached the level where it can pose a significant hazard to human companies and organizations — and perhaps soon to human society itself. Bioterror risk is certainly the most terrifying, but there are plenty of other ways that highly capable AI could cause chaos.

The U.S. and China have a shared incentive to implement strict safeguards against these catastrophic risks, and perhaps even to regulate the pace of AI development. But given the Chinese Communist Party’s power-seeking nature, it seems much more likely that China would agree to cooperate on AI safety if U.S. capabilities were comfortably ahead. So even if the goal is cooperation, the U.S. should be thinking about how to keep its technological edge.

Fortunately, the U.S. is still beating China in the AI race. Our companies have better models, more compute, and far more revenue. But there are ways that the Trump administration, despite claiming to be the AI industry’s best friend, could squander America’s lead — especially by pushing Chinese AI talent out of the country.

U.S. models are still better than Chinese models

There have been several moments when it seemed as if China’s frontier models were catching up to America’s in capabilities. The most dramatic was the “DeepSeek Moment” in early 2025, which put Chinese AI on the map. More recently, the release of Moonshot’s Kimi K3 this July and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 a few weeks ago seemed to indicate that Chinese models were nipping at the Americans’ heels.¹ Z.ai especially made waves when it beat Anthropic’s famous Mythos model on one measure of cyber-hacking capabilities:

Chinese AI ​startup Z.ai said on Friday its open-source GLM-5.3 model had neared Anthropic’s restricted Mythos 5 in identifying software vulnerabilities…Z.ai said GLM-5.3 scored 84.5% on CyberGym, a test of whether a model can review code, identify security flaws and confirm that they are real. That was slightly higher than the 83.8% it reported for Mythos 5. The results have not been independently verified.

Note that this is just one measure of cybersecurity prowess, and that Mythos was still comfortably ahead on other measures:

GLM-5.3 lagged behind Mythos 5 in converting discovered flaws into working attacks — a standard part of defensive security research. Z.ai ​said its model scored 54.4% on the ExploitBench test of this capability, versus 78.0% for Mythos 5…In a separate timed test, Z.ai said GLM-5.3 completed 105 ​attack-development tasks in two hours and 130 in six hours. Mythos 5 completed 181 and 247 tasks, respectively.

But still, if Chinese AI could get within striking distance of America’s best, it was a big deal.

What this discourse rarely mentioned, though, is that Mythos is not America’s best. It was simply the best that’s been released. Mythos Preview came out in April, four months before GLM-5.3. And the original Mythos actually finished training three months earlier, in January, and was released internally in February.² Anthropic delayed its release due to cybersecurity concerns. Z.ai, being a fast follower, probably had far fewer such concerns. In fact, Anthropic has stated that it has internal models that are better than Mythos.

Meanwhile, OpenAI just released their new Astra model, also known as GPT-6 (the model that made the cartoon at the top of this post). Astra scored 100% on ExploitBench — the measure of whether a model could use a cybersecurity vulnerability to actually execute an attack — compared to GLM-5.3’s 54% and Mythos 5’s 78%.

In fact, Astra’s capabilities as a whole represent a big leap over anything that has gone before:

The company claims that Astra still falls short of full “recursive self-improvement”, but we may be starting to see a speedup in AI development from AI assisting human researchers.

Astra’s leap is so big that it has widened America’s lead over Chinese models to levels not seen for years. Here’s a chart by Erich Grunewald of the difference in the best model scores between the two countries:

On top of that, there’s some evidence that Chinese frontier models stay within striking distance of their American competitors partially through a technique called “distillation”, meaning that the Chinese model learns by talking to the American model. Anthropic got very mad about this back in February:

We have identified industrial-scale campaigns by three AI laboratories—DeepSeek, Moonshot, and MiniMax—to illicitly extract Claude’s capabilities to improve their own models…These labs used a technique called “distillation,” which involves training a less capable model on the outputs of a stronger one…[C]ompetitors can use it to acquire powerful capabilities from other labs in a fraction of the time, and at a fraction of the cost, that it would take to develop them independently.

But whether or not you think distillation should be cracked down on, it means that the gap between Chinese models and American ones may be more structural than it appears. If Chinese labs are forced to get some of their performance gains by copying American labs, it means they can stay close but can never quite catch up. That’s still a competitive threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s profits, of course, but somewhat less of a security threat to the U.S.

The U.S. still has much more compute, and export controls are working

For AI, the capabilities of the model aren’t the only thing that matters. You need a lot of compute to do the inference — i.e., to make the models “think”. The more compute you use, the better an answer you can generally get. You can bet that the tests on which Chinese models got their eye-catching scores were run with as much compute as the Chinese companies were able to apply.

But those models won’t always have that amount of compute, because China is severely compute-limited. For all its general manufacturing prowess, China is significantly behind in terms of semiconductor manufacturing; most of the AI compute in the world is still made by Taiwan, South Korea, etc. And export controls on AI chips prevent China from buying many of the most powerful cutting-edge devices.

The total amount of compute that China officially owns is therefore pretty small — around half as much as Meta or Amazon:

In actuality, China probably has access to more than twice this much. Some gets smuggled in, and then China accesses a lot more remotely, in countries like Malaysia. ChinaTalk had a good post about this back in April, in which they tried to estimate how much compute China can actually use, and they came up with a number of about 2.8 million H100 equivalents (compared to the 1.16 million that China officially owns):

But this is still not that much compared to the U.S. — it’s less than Microsoft owns, and just over half of what Google owns. All in all, the U.S. has about five times the compute that China does. And much of China’s compute is remote-access — this causes latency issues, and there’s uncertainty as to whether it might get cut off in the future.

This puts China’s AI at a distinct disadvantage. The top Chinese models will probably be limited in how much work they can do at peak intelligence at any given time. In an adversarial situation — say, if China and the U.S. are trying to hack each other — this could make a huge difference.

China’s compute disadvantage points to the success of the U.S.’ export control regime, put in place under Biden. Trump has loosened export controls on Nvidia chips, but enough are still in place that China has a fraction of the compute that America has.

And the most effective export controls — the prohibitions on sales of ASML’s advanced nanolithography machines, which have hobbled China’s domestic chip-manufacturing industry — are so far untouched. Despite rumors that China had managed to produce an Extreme Ultraviolet nanolithography machine, independent estimates suggest this goal is still far off:

China is unlikely to advance its semiconductor manufacturing capabilities fast enough to develop a viable alternative to ASML Holding NV’s cutting-edge extreme ultraviolet technology within the next decade, UBS Group AG analysts predict.

“They seem to be at a similar stage to ASML in 2004,” UBS analysts led by Francois-Xavier Bouvignies wrote in a note…UBS analysts cited patent activity, particularly around light source and laser subsystems, as showing maturity comparable to ASML 15 years before it began mass producing its EUV tools.

China will eventually obtain EUV capabilities — perhaps in the late 2030s. But by then, the cutting edge will have moved on to something better.

Inferior chipmaking tools and chip purchase restrictions mean that China will be at a hardware disadvantage in the AI race for a while to come.³

U.S. companies are still growing their revenues like crazy

Even if Chinese AI doesn’t surpass American AI in the short term, in the long term its companies could pose a threat to U.S. leadership. In order for Anthropic and OpenAI to sustain their leads over the Chinese models, they need to continually do huge amounts of research. That costs money, which has to be paid out of either investment dollars or revenues. If competition from Chinese companies prevents Anthropic and OpenAI from ever becoming profitable, it could starve them of both the investor cash and the profits to be able to continue their research efforts. American companies might then stagnate and fall behind their Chinese rivals.

There are worrying signs that this may already be happening. Companies are spending more on open-weight models (which are mostly Chinese):

The reason here is just cost. Companies are spending an enormous amount on AI, and they’re trying to economize; this is evident in the fact that usage of Anthropic’s most expensive public model, Fable 5, has been anemic compared to adoption of its cheaper models. That suggests that companies will increasingly turn to cheaper Chinese models for at least some tasks, and that Anthropic and OpenAI may be forced to cut prices in order to stay competitive.

So far, though, this isn’t happening. Companies are using Chinese models more, but they’re using Claude and GPT a lot more. Both companies now have annualized revenues in the tens of billions of dollars, and are increasing these at an exponential rate:

In case the chart is confusing, the y-axis is a log scale, so a straight line on this chart actually means exponential growth. Anthropic’s insane revenue acceleration in early 2026 — due to the introduction of the blockbuster Claude Code product and the rise of agentic coding — now looks to be winding down, but exponential growth from a base of more than $70 billion is still unprecedented and incredible. (And compare this to the revenue of Chinese AI companies, which is two orders of magnitude lower.)

In other words, if Chinese AI is eating into Anthropic or OpenAI’s bottom lines, it isn’t really causing much pain yet. Anthropic, which has managed to control its costs more effectively than OpenAI while raising revenues faster, may now be turning an operating profit.

And there’s reason to think that if the U.S. labs can stay ahead of the competition, users will always be willing to pay a premium for their product. For many uses, a model that’s 95% of the way to the frontier works perfectly well. But for adversarial applications — cybersecurity, financial trading, etc. — having a slightly better model could make all the difference. So companies and countries may always be willing to pay a huge premium to Anthropic and OpenAI, even if Chinese models have more total users.

That wouldn’t be an unprecedented outcome, either. Android has a global smartphone operating system market share of around 75%, as compared to only 20% for iOS. But iPhone users pay a huge premium, so Apple ends up capturing around 75-85% of the total profit in the smartphone market. Anthropic and OpenAI could end up being the Apple to China’s Android.

What would let China catch up?

So as of right now, the U.S. is still dominating China in the AI race. But this could change, of course, as it has changed for many industries where China came from behind and eventually displaced the market leaders. What could knock the U.S. companies off their perch and allow China to overtake them?

The obvious answer — but one I think is wrong — is data center bans. U.S. state and local governments are rushing to pause or cancel data center construction, amid an unprecedented bipartisan populist backlash. When the few forlorn defenders of data centers speak up against the bans, they often cite competition with China as a reason.

But I think this is vastly overblown. Even if most states block data centers in perpetuity, a few states will still allow them, and that will be just fine for the AI industry. Eric Levitz explains:

Although the number of places with severe restrictions (or outright bans) on server farms is rapidly rising, more than 90 percent of US counties had no significant constraints on data center development at July’s end.

What’s more, many of the most eye-catching recent policy changes are less significant than they appear. For example, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s pause does not actually halt data center construction in the Lone Star State. Rather, it essentially establishes a more thorough screening process, when server farms apply for electricity from the state’s grid. Projects that supply all of their own power through on-site natural gas — as a rising share of new data centers do — are exempt…

To be sure, cancellations have risen sharply since March…[A]t least 13 gigawatts of capacity have been nixed so far this year. But the capacity of permitted projects has also grown since April 1. And the ratio between blocked and active developments has not radically changed[.]

Even if the anti-data-center movement in the U.S. eventually wins, companies like Google and Microsoft can just put data centers in other countries that will be happy to have the business — Africa, the Middle East, or wherever.

That may cause some latency issues, as when Chinese companies access compute remotely. But ultimately it shouldn’t be that big of a deal. American companies will still design and own the chips, and sell the compute to the labs. Yes, this will require paying to import the services of data centers, which will expand the U.S. trade deficit. But we’re already expanding imports of AI-related products at an absolutely stupendous rate, so the demand for imported data would probably be there:

A bigger risk I see is macroeconomic. Despite soaring revenue, investment spending has been absolutely enormous, and the possibility of an AI bust can’t be ruled out. A lot of commentators still expect some sort of a crash in the next couple of years.

That crash wouldn’t stop the rise of AI, but it might shift its locus. Anthropic and OpenAI probably wouldn’t die in a crash — Amazon and Microsoft didn’t die in the dotcom crash of 2000 — but they would almost certainly be forced to make deep cuts in their research budgets for at least a year or two. Amazon and (to a lesser extent) Microsoft certainly were, back in their day — Amazon’s capex went from $287 million in 1999 to just $46 million in 2003.

Chinese companies, on the other hand, would doubtless be state-subsidized to maintain capex through any AI bust. There would be no equivalent bailout in America — the chances that American taxpayers would subsidize the fortunes of companies where even the regular engineers are centimillionaires, after that industry caused a general economic crash, and especially after AI companies spent years proclaiming that they would render most human beings economically obsolete, just out of geostrategic concerns, are probably nil.

So while the AI boom has so far favored America’s free-market system, China’s state-subsidized system will probably perform strongly in a bust.

But the biggest danger I see to continued U.S. AI dominance is the loss of Chinese talent. The U.S. AI industry depends heavily on Chinese researchers. A plurality of top AI researchers in the world come from China, but the vast majority of them — 72% — end up working in America. China historically has a horrible retention rate on its AI researchers; just 11% stay in China. This enormous brain drain is a big reason the U.S. AI industry has managed to stay ahead of China.

But that could be changing, fast. More Chinese AI researchers are returning to their homeland instead of staying in America. They’re undoubtedly being pulled by the money in the Chinese AI industry, and by government recruitment incentives. But some are also being driven away by Donald Trump’s restrictions on skilled immigration:

The number of people from China living in the U.S. on visas for purposes such as education and work, including H-1Bs, has fallen each year from fiscal year 2022 to 2024…In part, that is because H-1B visas, the main pathway for highly skilled foreign professionals to work in the U.S., have become a political flashpoint in the U.S., especially within the MAGA movement, with critics saying the program allows tech companies to hire foreign workers for cheap instead of Americans. The Trump administration has added a $100,000 fee for H-1B visas and is proposing higher wage requirements.

Chinese researchers would generally rather stay and work in America, where the best companies are. But if Trump keeps pushing them to leave, while China keeps welcoming them back with open arms, how long will America retain its talent advantage? Not long. And despite progress in automating AI research, talent is still the most crucial factor.

So if the Trump administration really wants to stay ahead in the AI race, they should absolutely roll out the red carpet for every good AI researcher in China. Of course, that would conflict with their top priority, which is expelling any and all immigrants. But that will leave America disadvantaged in what’s shaping up to be one of the most important technological competitions in human history.

Weaponized Interdependence

Who has the power in a trading world?

Paul Krugman
Sep 6
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

On Friday Donald Trump threatened to cut off all trade with nations with which the United States runs a trade deficit. His demand, oddly, was directed at the Federal Reserve: He would impose trade embargoes unless the Fed cuts interest rates. I won’t even try to untangle his logic, if there is any, because today’s primer isn’t about Trump. It is, instead, about how to think about a world in which governments — even the government of the United States, which created the rules-based trading system that prevailed until recently — increasingly use threats to cut off international trade as a tool of coercion.

“Geoeconomics” — the study of the ways governments can use national economic strength in pursuit of geopolitical objectives — is a hot topic right now, both among scholars and at international institutions. The International Monetary Fund made geoeconomics the theme of the June issue of its F&D magazine. Geoeconomics is the theme of the European Central Bank’s annual research conference, taking place next week, at which I’m giving a talk on “economic size and economic power.” Back in August I posted a primer on relevant measures of economic size. Today, continuing my homework for the talk, I’m writing about economic power.

Specifically, I want to talk about “weaponized interdependence,” a term coined in 2019 by the political scientists Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman. Farrell and Newman focused mainly on national governments’ efforts to exploit their control of international networks, such as America’s use of the dollar’s central role in the international monetary system to impose sanctions on nations it considers hostile. At this point, however, weaponized interdependence is everywhere: Iran attempting to force the United States to call off its war by closing the Strait of Hormuz, China threatening the West with a cutoff of rare earths, the Trump administration using the threat of tariffs to pressure Canada to remove cultural protections for French — or become the 51st state?

But how should we think about weaponized interdependence? There is a rapidly burgeoning theoretical and empirical research literature on geoeconomics, surveyed for example by Mohr and Trebesch (2025.) I am not a contributor to this literature, just a consumer! But this rapidly growing field isn’t yet part of the standard way we teach international economics, let alone the way people influential in policy discuss the world. So what I thought I could do today is lay out in a very simple, maybe simplistic way what I believe to be some of the main insights from thinking about international trade as a potential tool of coercion — and what it says about the current global situation.

Beyond the paywall I will address the following:

1. What is weaponized interdependence, and how does it differ from “trade war”?

2. The sources of trade-related power

3. The special case of depression economics

4. Who has economic power in today’s world?

5. Trade in a weaponized world...

AI keeps stubbornly refusing to take our jobs

Happy Labor Day!! Your labor is still valuable.

Noah Smith
Sep 7
 
READ IN APP
 

It’s Labor Day, so here’s a post about how human labor is alive and well in the age of AI.

I live in San Francisco and hang out with a lot of tech people, both in the AI industry and outside of it. And one thing that almost everyone I know here believes is that AI’s main economic effect is to displace humans from their jobs. Most people don’t have concrete arguments for why this should be true; it’s just an article of faith. The conventional wisdom is pretty well summed up by the first line of this tweet:

Tim Urban
@waitbutwhy
I really wish the rise of LLMs didn't come along with catastrophic job loss, massive privacy invasions, and maybe also the apocalypse. Because when you put those side effects aside, it is the COOLEST MOST WILD TECHNOLOGY EVER.
7:46 PM · Aug 24, 2026 · 254K Views
260 Replies · 228 Reposts · 4.71K Likes

In fact, AI companies themselves have spent years talking about how their inventions are going to render large swathes of humanity economically obsolete — an odd marketing pitch, perhaps, but one that seemed to reflect their honest expectations.

AI has the worst sales pitch I've ever seen

Noah Smith
·
Mar 26
Read full story

A lot of times, San Francisco tech people are out of step with the general public. This time, though, the public seems to agree. A recent Ipsos poll found that most Americans expect AI to compete with human workers more than it complements them. And Pew finds that this belief has even strengthened in recent years:

So basically, most people think AI is a job-killer. And yet somehow, this job-killer keeps stubbornly refusing to kill jobs. In the aggregate, the labor market is about as healthy as it’s ever been. The prime-age employment rate — the single best indicator of how many Americans have jobs — continues to hover near all-time highs:

Of course, there are lots of other things going on in the labor market right now besides AI. But most of those things — tariffs, the Iran war, etc. — are bad for employment. It’s not easy to identify some sort of positive shock that is canceling out the job-killing effects of AI.

Or maybe it is, if the shock is AI itself. Theoretically speaking, automation can create jobs just as easily as it can destroy them. Here are Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019), explaining the various ways that technology can affect the demand for labor:

Automation [can be bad] for labor because of a displacement effect—as capital takes over tasks previously performed by labor…

[A]utomation technology also increases productivity, and via this channel, which we call the productivity effect, it contributes to the demand for labor in non-automated tasks…

[T]he displacement effect of automation has [historically] been counterbalanced by technologies that create new tasks in which labor has a comparative advantage. Such new tasks generate not only a positive productivity effect, but also a reinstatement effect—they reinstate labor into a broader range of tasks and thus change the task content of production in favor of labor. The reinstatement effect is the polar opposite of the displacement effect and directly increases the labor share as well as labor demand. [emphasis mine]

In other words, automation can do three basic things. Yes, it can replace people and take their jobs. It can also make them more productive, which can both create jobs and destroy them.¹ And, crucially, automation can create new jobs for people to do. Power looms replaced master weavers, but they created jobs for technicians and engineers to make the power looms work. The internet automated much of the work of travel agents, but created jobs for web designers. And so on.

People who think of AI as a job-killer might not have thought of the second and third of these. Or they may have thought of them, but simply assumed they’re not a big deal. Anecdotally, a lot of tech people think that AI will keep substituting for more and more tasks until A) productivity increases just increase the demand for AI, and B) there are no new tasks left for humans to do. AI detractors, meanwhile — like Daron Acemoglu himself — often simply assume that new tasks created by AI will be “bad tasks” like misinformation and cybercrime that hurt the economy instead of helping it.

But these assumptions simply might not be correct. AI might be creating lots of new tasks for humans to do. For example, software engineers are writing less and less code themselves. Instead, they’re spending more and more time telling AI to write code — that represents a productivity improvement. But they’re also trying to figure out what code to tell AI to write, making sure AI is writing the kind of code they want, integrating that code into products, and so on. Those are all new tasks. There are also a lot of software engineers working on improving AI itself, and on discovering new applications for AI. Those are new tasks as well.

This helps explain why in the age of Codex and Claude Code, software developer jobs have been increasing as a percentage of total employment:

Guy Berger
@EconBerger
The doom of the software developer job has been greatly exaggerated... As a share of the US labor force, it's near the highest it's ever been and on a steep uptrend.
8:06 PM · Aug 14, 2026 · 184K Views
31 Replies · 120 Reposts · 720 Likes

Anecdotally, organizations that thought they could replace lots of their software engineers with AI ended up having to hire many of them back — sometimes at a premium.

In fact, this is a story we see throughout the economy. Alex Tabarrok recently reported on a Census Bureau survey about AI that’s been running since 2023. The Census Bureau calls companies up and asks them A) how AI affected their total employment, and B) how AI affects the tasks that workers do.

Most companies reported no change in overall employment, which could just be due to inertia. But of companies that did report a change, more reported an increase than a decrease!

And here’s the breakdown by sector:

The story was similar for tasks. Tabarrok writes:

Among firms using AI, 44% say it supplemented or enhanced work an employee already does. Ten percent say it performed a task an employee used to do. Eleven percent say it introduced a task no one had been doing.

Here’s the chart:

Rigorous research, meanwhile, sometimes finds negative effects of AI on labor demand at the industry level, and sometimes not. But at the company level, the evidence is clearer — Kharazian, Simon, and Stevens (2026) find that when companies adopt more AI, they tend to hire humans rather than replacing them. Here’s a blog writeup of their findings:

Ramp Economics Lab
We can finally say AI isn’t killing jobs
Dear Colleagues: The most important economic question of this decade asks how AI will affect jobs. Everyone wants to write that paper. Until now, no one has had the right dataset, so existing research has relied on a combination of guesses, surveys, AI exposure scores, and self-interested punditry. In fact, a recent paper from Stanford said the ideal da…
Read more
2 months ago · 63 likes · 14 comments · Ara Kharazian

And here’s a chart:

Interestingly, they find the same for entry-level jobs — the jobs that people usually identify as being most under threat from AI.

So despite Acemoglu’s skepticism, it looks like for now, the new tasks being created by AI are probably matching or even slightly exceeding the tasks replaced by AI. Of course this measure is “number of companies” rather than “number of jobs”, but the pattern is pretty clear.

The Economist, meanwhile, has a report on how AI is creating jobs, both through the “new tasks” channel and by boosting demand in areas that AI can’t yet touch — physical jobs like construction and HVAC installation. Here’s what they write about the productivity/demand effect:

The Economist estimates that AI has so far created around 1m new jobs in America. That easily exceeds the roughly 200,000 lay-offs attributed to AI since mid-2023, and appears more than enough to offset weaker hiring in many back-office roles. America’s AI infrastructure splurge has created many of them…The Economist tracked five industries at the heart of the data-centre build-out, from electrical contracting to equipment manufacturing. Since 2023 employment in them has risen by roughly 320,000 more than broader…trends would suggest…LinkedIn, a social network for strivers, estimates that nearly half a million data-centre jobs were created between 2023 and 2025 in America, with data-centre technicians and engineers among the most common recent hires…

The scramble for workers is showing up in pay cheques, too. Indeed finds that installation and maintenance jobs at data centres advertise wages about 40% higher than comparable work elsewhere…In the year to June, average hourly earnings rose more than 13% in electrical-equipment manufacturing and nearly 8% among electrical contractors. [emphasis mine]

And here’s what they write about new tasks:

AI is also creating a new class of white-collar jobs. Engineers build the models, data annotators label their inputs and judge their answers, “forward-deployed” engineers adapt them for customers, and newly minted “heads of AI” decide what companies should do with the technology. Some of these roles barely existed until recently. Many are quickly growing in number. Postings for heads of AI, AI engineers and directors of AI have roughly doubled since 2023-24, according to LinkedIn…

Preliminary research by Gad Levanon, chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute…reckons roughly 1% of professional jobs are now “AI jobs”…[P]rofessional occupations closest to the AI boom—engineers, software developers, mathematicians and data scientists…have added roughly 730,000 jobs above trend in recent years[.] [emphasis mine]

What about specific occupations? Technology has certainly destroyed many specific types of jobs over the centuries — there are (basically) no more elevator operators, human telephone operators, or people who do manual typesetting for printing.

And yet in recent decades, we haven’t seen as much of this sort of occupational destruction. For example, a lot of people thought the internet would kill travel agents. And while the industry was hit hard, there are still plenty of travel agents left:

The reason is probably that the job of “travel agent” is much more flexible and “messy” than older types of jobs like elevator operator; travel agents do a whole lot of different tasks, so they’re harder to replace than people who just stand there and press a button. That makes modern jobs harder to replace entirely.

It’s a good bet that AI will eventually make some occupations obsolete. But so far, despite awe-inspiring progress in model capabilities, it’s extremely hard to find occupations that have seen significant replacement by AI. Top AI researchers who famously predicted the end of human radiologists saw their predictions get confounded. Truckers, too, are doing just fine.

The most impressive example might be translators. It seems pretty obvious how AI could replace human translators, and yet it hasn’t done so yet:

Abi Olvera
@Abi0lvera
I was wrong: I thought AI had destroyed translator jobs. US employment of human translators is “more or less stable, and is projected to remain stable over the next decade.” @random_walker points out “there's really no ceiling to the amount of things you can translate and the…
10:17 PM · Aug 30, 2026 · 122K Views
12 Replies · 36 Reposts · 227 Likes

Here’s a chart:

If you could go back to 2022, and tell people that in four years, AI would be solving frontier math problems, but we’d still have the same number of people working as translators, how many would have believed you?

It turns out that it’s very natural for people to overestimate the degree to which AI will take their jobs. Hartley et al. (2026) have a really excellent paper called “Job Loss Fears in the First Years of Generative Artificial Intelligence”. Here’s a thread explaining the paper’s findings.

Basically, the authors find that fear of AI job replacement is extremely common:

And they find that the more people’s jobs are exposed to AI, the more they think their jobs are about to be replaced:

In fact, the more of their day people spend using AI at work, the more they’re afraid of being replaced!

And yet when the authors looked for a correlation between AI exposure and actual job loss, they found…absolutely nothing. People’s fears simply haven’t come true yet.

What’s going on? The authors hypothesize that people who use AI more start to understand its ability to replace the tasks they do at work. But as we keep finding, replacing tasks isn’t the same as replacing jobs. People keep finding new things to do in their roles at work — sometimes things AI can’t do yet, but often things that couldn’t even be done until AI made them possible!

It seems like we’re uncovering a consistent human blind spot here: People don’t actually know how they produce value at their jobs. Modern jobs are much more than a simple collection of tasks — they are pieces of a complex machine that produces value in ways that an individual worker often doesn’t even see.² So when AI comes along and starts replacing people at various tasks, it just ends up making them more valuable as pieces of their corporate machines.

How long that situation will persist, of course, is an open question. AI leaders are starting to realize that it might take a very long time for the full effect of their inventions to be felt:

Fireside Alpha
@firesidealpha
Sam Altman admits he was wrong on AI's timeline and says society and the economy will adapt more slowly "I thought when we got to GPT-4, which was back in 2023, that very quickly after that there was going to be much more disruption, software businesses up for grabs right away,…
Fireside Alpha @firesidealpha
Sam Altman reveals building Codex was a "crazy kamikaze mission" to beat Claude Code and that most of the best coders he knows now use Codex. "We were way behind Claude Code, and it seemed like a kind of crazy kamikaze mission to try to beat them with a coding app." "The https://t.co/XRf7g5dVa2
12:44 PM · Aug 23, 2026 · 6.38M Views
386 Replies · 291 Reposts · 3.24K Likes

This is why the AI companies’ recent messaging pivot — many now say that AI will create jobs rather than destroying them — may be honest, rather than a cynical marketing ploy to calm public outrage.

But then there’s the question: Can this situation persist indefinitely? No one knows, of course. But my bet is that while many occupations will eventually be mostly replaced by AI, humans will still have plenty to do. I’ve argued that in order for AI to start replacing human jobs wholesale, it’ll have to get much more agentic — which will make it inherently more unreliable from a human point of view. So I predict that humans will always have jobs keeping AI agents on track.

Even if I’m wrong, though — even if the AI job apocalypse does eventually come — it doesn’t seem like it’s coming soon, and it certainly isn’t here right now. Everyone keeps thinking that AI is a job killer, and AI keeps on refusing to be what everyone expects.

Happy Labor Day!

Subscribed

Share

1

Higher task-level productivity can destroy jobs by letting employers do more with less. It can create jobs by creating economic growth, which boosts labor demand. But I think Acemoglu et al. might overlook another source of productivity-driven job creation, which is variety. When carmakers became more productive, they became capable of pumping out more different makes and models of cars. This probably made consumers want cars more, because people enjoy variety — GM famously overtook Ford by offering more models, more frequent model updates, and more colors.

2

This is why jobs may feel like “bullshit” to the people doing them, even as they command high wages in the market.

Neo-Nazis and the Impotence of Trumponomics

Crude economics doesn’t explain what just happened

Paul Krugman
Sep 7
 
READ IN APP
 

Neo-Nazis — no point in euphemisms — just won big in the rough equivalent of a state-level election in Germany. America’s leading neo-Nazi — again, no point in euphemisms — congratulated the AfD (in German) on the result, and in return received “thanks for your support” from the AfD’s lead candidate.

In the days and weeks ahead there will be many analyses of the results and its implications from people who, unlike me, know something about German politics. For now, let me do something more parochial, and write about what the Sachsen-Anhalt election might teach us about U.S. political economy.

So, about America: Make America Great Again meant different things to different people — racism, of course, being a key component. But in Donald Trump’s mind it also clearly meant trying to bring back “manly” jobs. He would do this by imposing tariffs to eliminate trade deficits, which, in his garbled version of economics, would end huge U.S. “giveaways” to surplus nations. And this would, in turn, lead to a huge revival of U.S. manufacturing employment.

Why is Germany relevant to this story? Because in terms of both trade balances and manufacturing Germany is, in effect, the anti-America. Where we do indeed run large trade deficits, Germany runs huge surpluses. And while Germany, like every other advanced economy, has seen the manufacturing share of employment decline over time, it remains a more industrial nation than the U.S. has been since the 1980s.

Indeed, relative to the size of its economy, Germany runs trade surpluses and retains large-scale manufacturing employment to an extent that lies far beyond the wildest dreams of Trumponomics.

And none of this appears to make a bit of difference to the resentment that underlies right-wing extremism on both sides of the Atlantic.

Start with trade. Here are balances in trade in goods and services for the two nations, expressed as a percent of GDP:

The U.S., as Trump constantly emphasizes, consistently buys more stuff from other nations than they buy from us. In his mind this means that we are being ripped off (as opposed to attracting large inflows of foreign investment, which as a matter of sheer accounting necessarily implies that we run trade deficits.) In any case, however, the Germans should be feeling pleased with themselves for running big trade surpluses, and hence taking advantage of the rest of the world, right?

Somehow, they aren’t.

America’s large trade deficit in manufactured goods does mean that we have fewer manufacturing jobs than we would if that trade were balanced. Robert Lawrence of the Peterson Institute for International Economics estimates that eliminating the deficit would raise the manufacturing share of employment from 7.9 to 9.7 percent, similar to my own back-of-the-envelope calculations. Correspondingly, Germany, with its large manufacturing surpluses, has relatively higher manufacturing employment as a share of total employment. Here are trends in industrial employment — a bigger category than manufacturing alone, but the trends are similar:

Even Germany has gradually become “deindustrialized,” but even now it is more of an industrial nation, as measured by where the jobs are, than the United States has been for at least 35 years. Has this insulated Germany from the bitterness and political extremism that many U.S. observers attribute to deindustrialization? Apparently not.

So here’s one way to think about the political economy here. The economic component of MAGA might be described as a plan, or maybe a concept of a plan, to make the U.S. economy more like what it was in the 1950s, when we didn’t run trade deficits and had a lot more men working in industry. But this might also be described as a concept of a plan to make America more like Germany. And what the results in Sachsen-Anhalt show is that even if such a plan were to deliver the promised results (which it wouldn’t), it would do little if anything to reduce politically radicalizing resentment.

I should mention one more lesson from the AfD’s victory, one that has me reconsidering some of my own beliefs.

Many U.S. observers, me included, have laid considerable stress on the problem of “left-behind” regions — rural and small-town areas bypassed by the rise of a knowledge economy, which tended to favor large, highly-educated metropolitan areas. These economically stranded regions have been plagued in particular by declining employment among men of prime working age, a decline that in turn is associated both with social problems and with strong support for Trump and hard-right politicians in general.

For many years it has been common to think of the former East Germany, which includes Sachsen-Anhalt, as one of the many European analogues to what Austin, Glaeser and Summers called the Eastern Heartland. Indeed, East Germany, which had near-full-employment among working-age men, went through an extended period of men-not-working after German reunification.

But that story is now long out of date:

Residents of the former DDR still consider themselves economically disadvantaged, and their incomes are somewhat lower than the national average — although not, as far as I can tell, as low in relative terms as poorer U.S. states. But in any case the tale of East Germany as a deeply depressed region no longer fits the facts.

What, then, is the moral of this analysis? Mostly it’s negative: Crude economic factors don’t explain the fascist shift in Germany. And Trumponomics, even if it worked (which it doesn’t) wouldn’t end the resentment feeding our own authoritarian movement.
