Destroying women’s sports in order to save it

Dems are quietly becoming more reasonable, and Republicans are revealing their true colors.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 16
 
READ IN APP
 

There are people on Bluesky who believe I am “obsessed” with the issue of trans women participating in women’s sports, which is not the case. I am, rather, frustrated by Democrats’ tendency to take a No Compromise With the Electorate Approach to a question that while nuanced, doesn’t require a doctorate to understand and that also involves low stakes compared with other questions related to trans rights.

So I’ve been heartened to see Rob Sand, James Talarico, Amy Acton, and Josh Turek take a more pragmatic approach to this issue. And it’s especially heartening to see that while there is of course some blowback against these candidates, it’s mostly not being led by anyone with real clout or power.

In particular, we’re not seeing safe seat Democrats blast these politicians for their more moderate stances.

That is, in a lot of ways, the most important aspect of the politics. Democrats — including Democrats in safe blue seats who hew to activist orthodoxy on this question — are making it clear that the tent includes a diversity of opinion and that holding the same views as a large majority of the public does not make you a proto-fascist.

This will hopefully allow for some refocusing of attention on the question of who actually is supporting women’s sports and why.

For example, note that even Sophie Cunningham, who has spoken out against the participation of trans women in women’s sports, does not appreciate Enes Kanter Freedom’s efforts to troll his way onto a W.N.B.A. squad. It’s the difference between a woman who is a professional athlete giving her view about a policy question that is, currently, totally hypothetical and a person trying to gin up controversy and draw attention to himself.

An even more egregious example comes from Washington state, where conservative activists have put a trans sports initiative on the ballot that would require affirmative sex verification in order to participate in girls’ school sports. This is not the standard practice even in the many red states who’ve adopted rules on this topic, and by creating new barriers to participation, the new rule would likely generate fewer opportunities for girls to play sports.

It’s not entirely clear to me why the Washington initiative is written this way. In Rachel Cohen Booth’s reporting, the proponents just deny that it says that, but it appears that they are wrong. Advocates for the initiative did not provide Booth with any legal experts who would back up their account, and when I asked Grok (seeking a “based” analysis of the controversy), anti-woke artificial intelligence agreed with her.

It’s basically impossible to know what they were thinking when they drafted this, but it’s clear that they weren’t thinking about the best interests of girls’ sports or female athletes.

Which in a lot of ways is the natural order of things. Promoting women’s sports is and always has been a progressive cause. Lately, this topic has been a political godsend for the right, but conservatives were never actually going to center women’s sports as a cause worth fighting for.

Destroying the village in order to save it

In most of these political arguments, progressives’ point that there are actually very few trans athletes is pretty unpersuasive. You still need a rule about who can play on which teams, and people are entitled to care about what the rule says.

But when it comes to an implementation and verification regime, the underlying rareness really is a relevant consideration.

To justify doing something that will inconvenience, embarrass, or possibly deter a huge number of girls from participating in sports, you need to be addressing a quantitatively significant issue. And this just isn’t one. Under the Washington Interscholastic Activities Association’s current policy of gender self-identification, there are 10 trans athletes out of 200,000+ kids playing middle school and high school sports in the state.

What’s more, by an overwhelming margin, these trans athletes are not people who’ve snuck surreptitiously onto sports teams. They came out as trans and that identity is known to parents and school officials.

If Washington state and its voters want to change current policy, that’s fine (my wishy-washy take is that stringently enforced sex segregation for middle school is probably unnecessary but that for high school it typically is). You can, though, just make a new declarative policy without subjecting everyone to a verification regime. In 99.9 percent of cases, there’s going to be zero controversy. If somebody wants to make a big deal about a specific athlete’s status, it’s not that hard to do an SRY gene test with a cheek swab, which is used as a proxy for biological sex. But in the real world, this is almost never going to come up.

I did a double take when I saw this story because I know Democrats have been in the habit of raising the prospect of universal genital inspections as a reason to oppose a chromosomal definition of sex for the purposes of sports. But obviously there’s no actual need to do that! And yet, here the authors of the Washington initiative seem to have done it.

Republicans don’t care about women’s sports

In what I think is a related development, earlier this year the Heritage Foundation put out a report blasting the whole idea of Title IX parity for male and female athletes in American schools.

I was glad they did it. Not because I agree, but because this is the actual conservative position on gender and sports!

I’m old now, so I remember back in 2003 when the Bush administration considered gutting Title IX parity but backed off under pressure. But then in 2005, with Bush’s re-election secured, they grew bolder and wrote new guidance to make it far easier for schools to say there just wasn’t interest from female students in playing sports. In 2010, the Obama administration reversed the Bush rule. This is politics! Democrats pushing an ambitious vision of social change and equality; Republicans pushing for traditionalism.

Subscribed

And unlike the trans issue, the implications of basic Title IX rules are far reaching. There’s a reason the U.S. women’s ice hockey team does better in international competitions than their male counterparts and the women’s soccer team does much better than the men — America has made unusually large investments in athletic opportunities for girls and it pays off. American men do very well overall at the Olympic Games, for example, but American women do even better because most of the world is behind us in women’s sports.

Like anything else in life, it’s perfectly fair to debate this. But my point is that this is a fairly big-picture, fairly long-running debate. It has intersected recently with L.G.B.T. policy in a way that landed Democrats on the wrong side of common sense and public opinion. But it’s pretty clear who stands where in the broader debate.

The endgame

This larger dynamic also helps explain why Sophie Cunningham was getting booed at games after speaking out in favor of the principle that only cisgender women should play in the W.N.B.A. The actual fanbase for most women’s sports in the United States in general, and certainly for the W.N.B.A., is quite left wing and disproportionately queer. They understand Cunningham to be doing right-wing politics, and they don’t like it.

By the same token, the family and I were at the Washington Spirit women’s soccer game last weekend and there was quite a bit of advocacy material in the section for the die-hard Spirit supporters. The video that introduces the team at the start of the game starts with a paean to the diversity of the district and depicts everyone getting to the game on the metro. It’s a very progressive fan base!

Notably, though, there are no trans women playing in the National Women’s Soccer League or the W.N.B.A. In both cases, the written rules could be construed as either barring them or not. And I think that status quo serves the business interests of these enterprises, as an explicit ban would probably antagonize a bunch of fans but an influx of players with XY chromosomes would mess up the competition. This is why Kanter Freedom’s intervention reads as obnoxious to fans of the league — he’s trying to embarrass people and make it hard for the W.N.B.A. to please all its stakeholders, not addressing an actual problem.

The thing I would urge progressives who are not sports fans to understand about high-level sports is that these are literally zero-sum competitions to which generic progressive interest in inclusivity does not apply. If there had been a trans woman in the U.S. Open draw, that would have almost certainly mechanically squeezed out a cisgender woman.

Conversely, I think it would be constructive for non-opportunistic conservatives to admit that they’ve won the argument about this.

Subscribed

The Women’s Tennis Association tour does not admit trans women. The W.N.B.A., regardless of its ambiguously worded policy, is in fact not full of people self-IDing into the league. The International Olympic Committee has adopted a rule using SRY testing. The N.C.A.A. has a simple declarative policy with no specific verification process. Democrats are not objecting to any of this or promising to reverse it. People don’t like to admit they made mistakes, so don’t expect Democrats to explicitly acknowledge that it was the Obama Department of Education that put on the table the idea that there needs to be a uniform national policy here. But they really have retreated from that view and seem content to let all kinds of sports bodies adopt rules on their own accord, and the trajectory of those rules is pretty clear.

When conservatives move toward something like mandatory sex verification for middle schoolers, though, that puts the debate back in more traditionally progressive terrain.

That’s a rule that’s only going to reduce girls’ participation and burden female athletes and their families for the sake of, I guess, rooting out the occasional extremely rare case of someone with an undiagnosed difference of sex development. And the broader Title IX fight is a classic left/right political battle, where conservatives just want to shrink opportunities and funding for girls’ sports.

How to stop Hitler

Read Hayek, but don’t listen to him about the specifics of the rise of fascism.

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 17
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Hey guys! For a while now I’ve been hosting a podcast, called “The Argument,” with Jerusalem Demsas, the editor in chief of The Argument magazine. We realized that rather than sending everyone a separate podcast email each week, it would make more sense to incorporate the Thursday podcast releases into the morning’s article.

The podcast itself has a few different episode formats, but once a month or so we do a “book club” episode where we read a classic book. This week’s was Friedrich von Hayek’s 1944 book “The Road to Serfdom.” In our conversation, Jerusalem and I really dug into Hayek’s ideas. But as someone who’s interested in history, I also wanted to write in greater depth on the specific historical argument of the book.

For an 80-year-old book written by an Austrian guy in a language he didn’t speak natively, Friedrich von Hayek’s 1944 book “The Road to Serfdom” is incredibly engaging and accessible. It’s also crackling with insights on nearly every page — I kept furiously highlighting passages that reminded me of contemporary controversies and phenomena so I’ll have quotes and points for future articles on everything from antitrust policy to Waymo to health care.

What’s remarkable is that even though the book is really good and I strongly recommend it to anyone interested in the future of liberalism in these fraught times, its ostensible core thesis also seems totally wrong.

Hayek wrote it in the middle of World War II, when lots of people in America and especially Britain were looking at the semi-planned wartime economy and seeing it as a model for peacetime. He thinks this is a bad idea (this part holds up) that if implemented will lead to a totalitarian regime (this part does not) and also that German retention of planning concepts from World War I during the interwar period is causally responsible for the rise of Adolf Hitler, which I think is so clearly wrong that I can’t help but quote from the introduction, where Hayek writes that “few are ready to recognize that the rise of fascism and Naziism was not a reaction against the socialist trends of the preceding period but a necessary outcome of those tendencies.”

I want to emphasize that the book is not at all a detailed survey of German politics in the 1920s and 1930s; it’s a book about economics and political theory.

And that’s why it’s a good book and why on the podcast we mostly talked about the insights we think hold up. But I think this impulse to gild the lily and attribute the rise of Hitler to deep intellectual trends is an example of a pretty common fallacy of assuming that an incredibly important world event must have incredibly important roots.

One point I tried to make last week about 9/11 is that while Osama bin Laden was swimming in some big currents of violent Islamist political thought that have deep roots and semi-broad sociological appeal, the specific theory whereby blowing up office buildings in New York City would advance that cause was quite weird. It’s easy to imagine a world where the same basic ideological currents are in the mix but nobody ever says that and all of world history is different.

By the same token, Hitler was a fairly marginal figure on the eve of the Great Depression. It was poor short-term economic management plus the questionable short-term political calculations of the non-SPD German parties that brought the Nazis to power. It was a very big deal for world history, but not an inevitable consequence of the whole structure of German intellectual life.

The real story of Hitler’s rise is mostly a history of contingency — bad choices by specific influential politicians first wrecked the German economy and then handed power to Hitler.

Paying subscribers can find the rest of the article beneath the paywall, along with the transcript for this week’s episode of “The Argument” podcast. The embedded video below is also ad free for paid subscribers. The public version of the episode is available on YouTube here.

The Nazis were a minor party in 1928

You often hear from Germans that the hyperinflation of the early 1920s broke the back of the Weimar Republic and laid the groundwork for Hitler.

John Maynard Keynes’s 1919 book, “The Economic Consequences of the Peace,” is also quite popular and influential. In it, Keynes argues that the reparations imposed on Germany would be economically destabilizing and lay the seeds for future conflict rather than preventing it. Hearing about these things sometimes creates the impression that the whole Weimar era was a doomed series of disasters. But in fact, the hyperinflation ended in 1923 and a new stable currency was introduced. Keynes’s book is famous because his insights were accepted by American leaders who implemented the Dawes Plan to make reparations manageable and set things aright. Dawes won the Nobel Peace Prize and the German economy recovered.

In the 1928 German federal election, the Nazi Party got 2.63 percent of the vote, putting them in ninth place.

Prussia, by far the largest state in Germany with over 60 percent of the country’s population, also had an election in 1928. There, the Nazis got 1.8 percent and also finished ninth. In Bavaria, the second largest state and home of Hitler’s original base, they got 6 percent and finished fifth. Saxony, the third largest state, didn’t have elections in 1928, but in their 1929 Landtag election the Nazis got 4.96 percent — good for seventh place. In the fourth biggest state, Württemberg, there was a 1928 election where the Nazis were tenth with 1.8 percent of the vote.

I don’t need to bore you by going further down the list. But if you actually want to analyze the political events in Germany in the years leading up to Hitler’s rise, you do have to engage with these details.

Over the past decade, tons of bad takes have attributed the rise of populist-right political parties to economic hardship when it’s pretty clear that actually a large minority of voters agree with their anti-immigration tough-on-crime message. But one reason these takes are popular may be a kind of historical memory in Europe of the interwar period when there were basically no political debates about immigration. There is plenty of evidence that lots of German people held antisemitic attitudes and were angry about World War I. But very few people had any interest in voting for a violent, demagogically antisemitic, pro-war political movement until the Great Depression.

The Weimar Republic really did have a number of structural weaknesses, starting with the really goofy federalism of a system with one state that had a majority of the population and then tiny states like Lippe with 164,000 people (the Nazis finished ninth in Lippe’s 1929 election, by the way, behind the Reich Party for Civil Rights and Deflation). They also had a persistent block of 10 percent or so of people voting for the Communists even during the good economic times. Catholic and Protestant right-wingers had trouble working together. German liberalism was relatively weak and yet divided between two different political parties. The Social Democrats were stuck between rhetorical radicalism and the practical realities of governance.

But there’s no reason to think things couldn’t have trundled along with the various party leaders getting more sophisticated at the art of representative government over time. The problem was the economy went to shit.

Germany tumbled into economic and political disaster

In the 1925 German presidential election, Paul von Hindenburg, backed by a coalition of right-wing parties, defeated Wilhelm Marx from the Catholic Centre Party, who was mostly counting on Social Democrats for votes. Hindenburg won with only 48 percent of the vote because the Communists insisted on running a spoiler candidate who got 6 percent. That’s an annoying turn of events, but also just normal politics in a democracy. Everyone is dealing with the basic issues of coalition management, and it superficially appears that the ability of the Communists to retain a core base of loyalists no matter how ridiculous they act is the primary problem for the German center-left.

But shortly after those 1928 elections in which the Nazis did so poorly, the Great Depression hit.

Unemployment increased massively, which eroded the popularity of almost all the mainstream political parties. It also created a large bloc of idle young men with time on their hands to join either Nazi or Communist paramilitary organizations to achieve some sense of purpose and meaning in life.

By the time new elections were held in the fall of 1930, industrial production had fallen by over 25 percent, and it’s not a huge surprise that both the Nazis and the Communists saw their vote share rise. This new parliament made the political situation extremely difficult, but even so there was hope. As Barry Eichengreen has famously shown, most countries began to recover rapidly from the Great Depression once they ditched the gold standard and allowed their economy to reflate.

The exception is Germany, where, uniquely, an end to gold led not to reflation but to a massive wave of bank failures that further pummeled the economy.

What happened here? Well, Thomas Ferguson and Peter Temin argue persuasively in their 2001 paper on the crisis that the key problem was Hindenburg’s determination to pursue an aggressively nationalist foreign policy, which screwed up the opportunity to get the long-term loan from France that Germany needed to stabilize its budget.

Cut off from international capital markets, Germany ended up going off gold in a way that panicked foreign depositors and exacerbated the economic crisis. The Nazis had made huge gains in the 1930 elections, and when Germans went to the polls in 1932 the economy was worse than ever. Though Hitler was still well short of a majority, he did lead the largest bloc in parliament. And at that point, Hindenburg and the rest of the German right decided to throw in with Hitler rather than work with the socialists.

Practical management matters a lot

This is a lot of words to say that while I think Hayek’s book provides an incredibly powerful critique of central planning, I really don’t see how you can avoid the conclusion that powerful elements in German society — in the military, in the old aristocratic class, and in the business community — did do what he says they didn’t do and turned to the Nazis as an alternative to the socialists.

But the reason anyone was even in a position to make a choice like that was the extremely bad macroeconomic management in Germany. This was in part just mistaken ideas about economic policy from the people in charge and in part Hindenburg’s perverse decision to prioritize things like a customs union with Austria and heavy cruiser construction over maintaining a pragmatic economic relationship with France.

All of Germany’s problems were also in part downstream of the parallel economic collapse in the United States, which was also likely mostly avoidable if Herbert Hoover and the Federal Reserve had made smarter choices. The American Depression, of course, also generated massive political change — we just had a much more benign opposition. It’s also one of the unfortunate twists of history that the Nazis just genuinely had pretty good judgment about macroeconomic policy in the mid-1930s and ended up gaining a halo of prestige and public support from driving an effective economic recovery.

Where I think Hayek is persuasive is that having seized power, attempting to do a (“national”) form of socialism turns out to work a lot better if you’re also willing to implement a brutal dictatorship.

Something that really resonated for me in the book across the generations is his point that a kind of nice-guy liberal socialism has a lot of superficial appeal to intellectuals but doesn’t really make sense. The more you want to organize the economic system around telling everyone what to do, the more you need an overwhelming consensus about values that can’t really be secured through liberal means in a liberal society.

And to this day, I see people like Matt Stoller tossing off ideas like “China, by contrast, where the superrich are not in control, and which has a coherent governance model, the same kind of existential fears about A.I. simply do not exist,” as if the presence of a totalitarian regime is incidental and a Chinese regulatory model could be easily replicated in a Western democracy. What I think we learned from post-WWII history, though, is that rather than efforts to introduce state ownership and comprehensive price regulation in Britain leading to authoritarianism, it simply didn’t work well.

The United Kingdom actually did a bunch of the stuff Hayek warned them against in the late 1940s, and he was right that it wasn’t sustainable or workable. But the upshot was it mostly got dismantled because it was done by wishful thinking liberal socialists, not by the hard men of a fascist movement. Authoritarianism didn’t come into Germany via a slippery slope; it came quite suddenly because a non-authoritarian government catastrophically mismanaged a massive economic crisis. The route to the Bolshevik takeover of Russia was totally different but similarly involved catastrophic mismanagement of an urgent crisis that allowed a group of people to rapidly leap to power from the margins of society.

There’s something unsatisfying about “don’t lose a huge war” or “if your country tumbles into recession, make things better rather than worse” being the big takeaways from epic political disasters. After all, everyone agrees you shouldn’t do those things, and it would be more interesting and emotionally satisfying if these cataclysms related more to deep intellectual arguments. But the shallow stuff matters a lot.

It’s making a lot of good points, but as an account of mid-century totalitarianism, like, I don’t know. I don’t buy it, but he’s a really smart guy. You learn a lot. He has not convinced everyone. I guess that’s the difference with Friedan. She really has just won the argument.

Jerusalem Demsas: Yeah.

Matthew Yglesias: I mean, people disagree about that. We still have value pluralism, but I would say her ideas are dominant today, whereas Hayek’s ideas are falling into some abeyance in a way that we could benefit from elevating.

Jerusalem Demsas: All right. Well, thank you all for listening to this episode of The Argument. If you have book suggestions for our next book, please let us know. We have taken those in the past. You can do that in the comments of The Argument, of Slow Boring, tweet us, share this podcast with your friends on social media, and we’ll see you next week.

Matthew Yglesias: Bye.

Roundup #88: Is it time to panic yet?

AI risk; AI and growth; AI and Saas; Rich people; Christians vs. Nazis; Japanese culture; State capacity; City size

Noah Smith
Sep 18
 
READ IN APP
 

This week’s roundup has a lot of AI in it. Fortunately or unfortunately, it seems like a lot of the news is going to revolve around AI for the rest of our lives. That was true of industrial technology in 1870-1970; people basically got used to the idea that railroads and factories and oil and industrialized warfare and such matters were central to the way the world was run and to the collective future of humanity. AI is going to be like that going forward, and we’re just going to have to get used to that. So let’s make it as fun and interesting as we can!

1. Americans are getting scared about AI risk

AI risk has exploded onto the national scene. AI companies and AI researchers generally believe that the technology they’re building has the capacity to do great harm — perhaps even to end the human race — if it’s not developed more slowly and deliberately. There are five main groups of people opposing the slowdown:

  1. The Trump administration, which is worried that an AI slowdown might also slow down economic growth

  2. Investors who think a slowdown might hurt their bottom line

  3. Libertarians and techno-optimists who think regulating technological progress is bad on principle

  4. China hawks who worry that a slowdown would let China take the lead in the AI race

  5. Progressives who spent the last few years telling themselves that AI doesn’t work, that AI is a huge economic bubble, and so on, and who now can’t bring themselves to admit that yes, the techbros actually built something that works.

This is a strange alliance indeed. The last of these — the progressives who simply couldn’t admit that billionaire-funded private industry could build something powerful enough to endanger humanity — were the strangest of all, since their refusal to acknowledge the effectiveness of AI basically put them in an alliance with libertarians, hawks, and Trump. In fact, in recent days there has been a tremendous civil war within the progressive movement between the “AI is dangerous” and “AI is fake” camps, with Bernie Sanders supporting the former and his former comms director David Sirota supporting the latter.

But although it has the support of the president (for now), the anti-slowdown coalition is losing in the court of public opinion. Nate Silver has a post rounding up the evidence:

Silver Bulletin
A supermajority wants to slow AI down
This has been one of those weeks when it feels like everything Silver Bulletin covers is happening at once. Democrats have continued to have a very good run of polling since Labor Day, with our Senat…
Read more
18 hours ago · 141 likes · 26 comments · Nate Silver

A bipartisan majority is now worried about existential risk from AI:

And a bipartisan majority thinks AI is moving too fast:

Barack Obama, probably the most successful American politician of this century so far, is telling Democrats to make AI safety one of their tentpole issues.

This is remarkable. I don’t think I’ve ever seen such bipartisan national unity on any issue in my adult lifetime. Trump is standing firm against the tide of public opinion here — as he has on the Iran War, tariffs, and other issues. But it’s not clear how long he’ll be able to hold out.

2. A very cool debate about AI and growth

Quite apart from the question of whether AI will kill us is the question of whether AI will deliver explosive economic growth. There’s a pretty epic public bet on this:

Ben Moll
@ben_moll
Some real diversity of opinion at Google DeepMind: @alexolegimas joins the bet while his colleague @SamuelAlbanie takes the other side increasing his existing stake! Total size of pot now $425,000! benjaminmoll.com/growth_bet/
Ben Moll @ben_moll
Thanks to @willmacaskill, @SamuelAlbanie, @tomcohen for taking the other side of this bet at 4:1 odds and to @andrewho03 for joining on my side. Here are the final terms we agreed on https://t.co/NSQZKbfBIy More (within) ~7 years from now 😃 https://t.co/8Ta8sjm9jB
6:39 AM · Sep 1, 2026 · 165K Views
20 Replies · 14 Reposts · 274 Likes

The people on the “fast growth” side are mostly AI researchers, while the people on the “slow growth” side are mostly (but not entirely) economists. This is an exaggerated version of a broader disconnect — AI researchers are generally more optimistic about AI’s impact on economic growth than economists are:

But the people publicly betting on fast growth are making an even more extreme forecast — they’re forecasting 15% growth, which is much higher than the 5.3% that AI experts forecasted as their most optimistic scenario. That’s an absolutely stupendous growth rate — China has hit it only in one year (1984) since it began its rapid growth, and that was when it was a very poor country. And yet, a number of people in the AI industry think it’s going to happen to us very soon.

Economists — even those who work on the economics of superintelligent AI, like Alex Imas — are skeptical. In a recent blog post, Imas and Ben Moll explain their thinking:

Ghosts of Electricity
Will AI soon lead to double-digit growth?
The following post represents the personal views of the author(s) and does not reflect or represent the positions of their employers…
Read more
9 days ago · 182 likes · 22 comments · Ben Moll and Alex Imas

Basically, they foresee a bunch of factors combining to limit AI’s contribution to economic progress in the short term:

  • Slow diffusion of AI technology throughout the economy,

  • The “J-curve” effect where productivity tends to fall right after a big innovation comes out (because companies need to spend resources adopting the new technology rather than on their existing businesses)

  • The difficulty of automating the physical world with robots

  • Political barriers to adoption

  • The difficulty of reorganizing production processes around AI

  • The persistence of activities that consumers want to keep having humans do (the “relational sector”)

  • Bottlenecked inputs to the AI industry (e.g. chips)

  • Baumol’s cost disease

  • AI disasters that slow adoption

That’s a lot of reasons! It makes sense that at least some of these will end up having an effect. Whether AI’s rapid improvement is enough to overcome all of these, and propel us to 15% growth, is something I guess we’ll have to see for ourselves. Personally, I lean toward the economists’ more measured expectation, but I’m prepared to be surprised on the upside.

3. AI keeps stubbornly refusing to kill SaaS

One of the most entertaining storylines about AI is how it keeps refusing to destroy all the things people say it’s about to destroy. On Labor Day, I noted that AI keeps stubbornly refusing to kill jobs. A month ago, I noted that AI keeps stubbornly refusing to kill Indian back-office outsourcing companies.

Now Ernie Tedeschi and the excellent folks over at Stripe Economics have a post about how AI is stubbornly refusing to kill the Software as a Service industry:

Stripe Economics
The SaaSpocalypse was more like a RenaiSaaS
In early 2026, markets staged a sudden and severe repricing of enterprise software. Nearly $1 trillion in valuation had been wiped out by early February, and perhaps as much as $2 trillion including the subsequent weeks. The entire episode came to be dubbed the …
Read more
8 days ago · 38 likes · 5 comments · Ernie Tedeschi

Earlier this year, when coding agents came out, there was a bloodbath in software stocks. Why would anyone pay Salesforce or other companies big bucks to make and maintain software for them when Claude Code could just do it all for a lot cheaper?

That logic made some intuitive sense, except things didn’t turn out that way — at least, not yet. In fact, SaaS companies started making more money in the age of AI! Tedeschi and the Stripe team tracked an index of publicly traded SaaS companies and found that their revenue has grown faster since coding agents came out:

And SaaS stocks have made up all of the ground they lost:

Ernie’s post has many more fun charts.

What’s going on here? Well, for whatever reason, companies are still willing to pay for software instead of trying to roll their own with Claude Code. And SaaS companies are probably improving their own productivity by using AI. As in so many other areas of the economy, AI is proving to be a complement when people thought it was going to be a substitute.

That could all change, of course, if and when AI gets good enough, or when new AI-centric business models disrupt older ones. But for now, the simple story of AI replacing everyone and everything just isn’t happening.

4. America’s quiet, boring rich people

Owen Zidar is one of my favorite economists. His meticulous empirical research with Eric Zwick on inequality in America has fundamentally changed how I think about the issue. Now that research has become a book, entitled The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There. I haven’t read it yet, but I’ve read some of the underlying papers, so I know it’s going to be good.

Anyway, Zidar and Zwick have an article out in The Atlantic explaining their findings. Here are some excerpts:

When Americans picture the ultrarich, they typically think of tech billionaires such as Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg, whose wealth lies predominantly in shares of publicly traded companies. They might also think of Wall Street financiers and celebrities such as Taylor Swift. But far more typical are…owners of successful privately held businesses…By our calculations, about 1.7 million Americans have each built a net worth of at least $10 million by owning a private business. For every CEO of a public company, there are more than 1,000 private-business owners with a net worth of more than $25 million…

What we found changed how we think about inequality…Today, when Senators Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders propose making the rich pay their fair share, they aim at Wall Street and Silicon Valley. But far more relevant to the story of inequality in America are the everywhere millionaires who quietly press their elected representatives for favorable treatment. The tax code bears their imprint far more than it does Musk’s…

A loophole that lets private-business owners avoid Medicare taxes has similarly been justified as a break for the little guy. Preserving the family farm has been a pretext for passing ever larger exemptions to the estate tax, to the point that a married couple can now pass on $30 million to heirs tax-free. Hiding behind small business, in short, has proved a devastatingly effective strategy for the rich…[T]he everywhere millionaires have one thing in common: They own what have become known as pass-through businesses…[L]awmakers have carved out multiple loopholes, so a dollar earned from owning a business is routinely taxed much less than a dollar earned in wages. [emphasis mine]

In fact, though I haven’t yet joined the ranks of Zidar and Zwick’s “everywhere millionaires”, I probably will do so — Noahpinion is a pass-through business (an S-corporation), and although I haven’t yet managed to get Congress to create tax loopholes for Substack writers, the generally favorable tax treatment these businesses receive has certainly lowered my tax bill.

So perhaps it’s not in my financial interest to promote Zidar and Zwick, but I will do so anyway. Expect to see more about their work on this blog in the months to come!

5. Christians vs. Nazis

Christians and Nazis should be natural enemies. The original Nazis in Germany persecuted the Catholic Church, and attempted to create a new state religion that co-opted some elements of Christianity while rejecting the Old Testament. Christianity is, at its core, a universalist faith, open to human beings of all races, while Nazis are…not that.

In the U.S., neo-Nazis have been weak enough where they haven’t tried to usurp leadership of the Right from conservative Christianity. But as Christianity wanes and online rightism rises, the two may now be coming more into direct conflict. Erick Erickson, a Christian conservative pundit, recently wrote a post exposing one network of neo-Nazi influence on the Right:

Erick Erickson's Show Notes
The Midwestern Führerbunker Driving the Right Off the Cliff
Editor’s Note: I’ve worked on this for weeks. Yes, it is long. I beg you to read it all. I’ve kept it as easy to understand as I can. Please read it. You guys always ask me to “name names.” Challenge accepted…
Read more
2 days ago · 422 likes · 148 comments · Erick-Woods Erickson

Some excerpts:

Charles Haywood made his fortune selling shampoo…[H]e has spent the years since writing out, at length and under his own name, what he would like to do with your country.Rod Dreher, who is no man of the left, read Haywood’s online ramblings and described Haywood as pouring out vile from “deep in his Midwestern Führerbunker”…

In a document he calls the Foundationalist Manifesto, Haywood explained that his preferred government “will not be democratic.” The state “will have unlimited means,” because “properly viewed, the state is not constrained externally.”…The state will seize the assets of “any citizen who views himself as a global citizen.”…Those are his words, from the manifesto that earned him a friendly sit-down with Tucker Carlson in September 2022…Elsewhere he has speculated about serving as a “warlord” at the head of an “armed patronage network,”…

Haywood’s personal foundation has given the Claremont Institute $390,500 since 2022…Haywood sits on the publication committee of Claremont’s American Mind, one of four men who do. Claremont let Haywood’s fraternal order get itself incorporated under Claremont’s own nonprofit status. That order is the Society for American Civic Renewal…[T]he president of Claremont, the chief executive of New Founding, and the chief marketing officer of the Blaze are all members…

Haywood himself…has argued that the Allies, not the Nazis, were the genuinely barbaric power in World War II, has insisted the war was not much motivated by the horrors of Nazi aggression, and gushed that Tucker Carlson and Darryl Cooper “boil down all my political plans.” Cooper argues that Churchill, not Hitler, was the villain of World War II…In a 2023 debate…Haywood raised the hypothetical of a real white nationalist with real political power, and answered that you should cooperate with that person in order to destroy the power of the left.

There’s a lot more in Erickson’s post, but you get the point. Erickson notes that the Haywood/Claremont nexus is separate from the “groyper” network organized around Nick Fuentes, which has received a lot more attention; the two parallel rightist networks share similar ideas, but the Haywood/Claremont group is an intellectual movement aimed at elite influence, while Fuentes is an entertainer in search of an audience of disaffected overly-online young men. Erickson also notes that both the Haywood/Claremont people and the groypers have ties to JD Vance, who has emerged as the paramount leader of the New Right.

Anyway, this should go without saying, but I’m rooting for Erickson, Dreher, and the Christians in this fight, and I think they deserve help exposing the neo-Nazi moneymen and elite influence channels. There’s a tendency among progressives — and especially among leftists — to view everyone on the Right as essentially part of one solid undifferentiated bloc, but this has never been true. I have many differences with conservative Christianity, but it was never Nazism, and it has never been ambiguous which one was worse.

6. Japan is not a “Confucian” society

One thing that has always annoyed me is when people call Japan a “Confucian” society. Confucianism certainly had a historical influence in Japan — it was an important school of political thought in Japan from around 1300 to the late 1800s, especially during the latter half of that period. It did have some influence on the development of Japan’s education system (though not nearly as much as in China and Korea). But it was never nearly as dominant as it was in China and Korea, and it never morphed into a quasi-religion the way it did in those other countries. Japanese people will regularly tell you about how Koreans are much more Confucianist than they are.

Anyway, I’m not the only one who gets annoyed by the “Confucian” label. Here’s Richard Hanania:

Richard Hanania
@RichardHanania
Is "Confucian" culture an actual trait East Asian countries share? This Confucian category is gerrymandered in a way that would make a Congressman blush. richardhanania.com/p/the-east-asi…
12:52 PM · Sep 12, 2026 · 55K Views
15 Replies · 7 Reposts · 98 Likes

Hanania’s entire post about differences between Japan and other East Asian nations is worth reading, but his invocation of the Inglehart-Welzel World Cultural Map is especially powerful. The World Values Survey, which goes around asking people from various countries about their values, puts out this map periodically. Here’s the more recent version:

You can see a little movement from Hanania’s earlier version — Hong Kong and South Korea have become a bit more secular — but Japan is still the clear outlier in the “Confucian” category. Its values are far more in the direction of “self-expression” — very close to the U.S., in fact (though North Europe and the Anglosphere still reign supreme in this regard).

To anyone who has lived in Japan, this is hardly a surprise. The country is highly individualistic, creative, and socially nonconformist, despite a penchant for following rules and procedures. Japanese parenting is also far more laissez-faire and far less education-obsessed than Chinese parenting. If you want to read more, I recommend the book New Japan: Debunking Seven Cultural Stereotypes, by David Matsumoto; it’s two decades old at this point, but still perfectly relevant.

In other words, “Confucian” is lazily applied to Japan as a racial category, rather than any kind of a useful description of the culture and society.

7. State capacity: It works.

One unpopular position I’ve stuck to over the years is that a strong bureaucracy is good. I don’t mean “bureaucracy” as in red tape and regulation; I mean a competent, empowered civil service that can perform crucial government functions efficiently and well using in-house expertise. This is also called state capacity. Over the past half century, conservatives and progressives made a devil’s bargain to slash state capacity — conservatives got to cut the size of government, while progressives got to outsource core government functions to progressive nonprofits.

The problem was that this often ended up costing the government much more money to do things like build trains and roads, because the government ended up getting ripped off by expensive consultants, ineffective and sometimes corrupt nonprofits, opportunistic unions, etc. — as well as suffering constant delays that increased costs even more and sometimes prevented anything from being completed at all. A decade ago, the New York Times published a story called “The Most Expensive Mile of Subway Track on Earth”, detailing how lack of state capacity had made NYC’s famous train system increasingly dysfunctional and unaffordable.

So I was very happy to see a story (by Tahra Hoops) about how NYC’s Metropolitan Transportation Authority has actually invested in state capacity, and how this investment is yielding results:

The Rebuild
How the MTA Learned to Build Again
Last week, the MTA announced something that American transit agencies almost never get to announce: it finished a major infrastructure project 60 months ahead of schedule and $195 million under budget…
Read more
a month ago · 18 likes · 1 comment · Tahra Hoops

Some excerpts:

Last week, the MTA…finished a major infrastructure project 60 months ahead of schedule and $195 million under budget…Since October 2023, crews replaced 196 bridge structures and more than 12,600 feet of railroad along the Park Avenue Viaduct…And to top it all off, they did it over 28 weekends without delaying a single train…

The project was done effectively through prefabrication, sequencing, and a project team empowered to actually manage the work…Phase 1 wrapped 21 months ahead of schedule in October 2025. Phase 2 finished the weekend of July 25, five full years early, with the final cost coming in $195 million under the initial $960 million budget…

Before 2019, capital projects at the MTA were run separately by each operating agency…In 2019, the MTA consolidated all of it into a single delivery organization, MTA Construction & Development, bringing nearly 2,000 employees from those scattered capital divisions under one roof. One agency, one accountable executive, one set of lessons learned that actually compound from project to project…In 2023, C&D awarded more than $8 billion in new contracts at prices 6.2 percent below the engineer’s estimate, saving nearly $300 million, and in 2025 it reported another $1.2 billion in savings while completing 41 elevator replacements, double its previous single-year record, each finished about two months faster on average…

C&D shifted to design-build contracts, which put design and construction under one contract so the builder owns the gap between the drawings and the dirt, and bundled similar projects into single procurements rather than bidding out ten station upgrades ten separate times. It also started pulling work back in-house instead of defaulting to consultants[.]

This is great progress, and shows the value of the state capacity approach to infrastructure. Whether other states and cities will pay attention is another question. Hoops notes that L.A.’s D Line extension is mired in the typical endless series of delays and cost overruns. Five decades of going in the wrong direction is hard to reverse overnight.

Still, the MTA’s success shows that in most cases, all you really need in order to get infrastructure built cheaply is the political will to do so.

8. Will self-driving cars make cities more dense or less dense?

A lot of people just assume that self-driving cars will make cities less dense. After all, simple logic dictates that if a car trip is less burdensome — if you’re able to get work done or watch TV or scroll social media during your commute instead of being forced to keep your eyes on the road — then people will be willing to live farther away from their places of work. That suggests that like the car itself, self-driving cars will lead to urban sprawl — which is why many urbanists don’t like the notion of self-driving cars, despite the obvious safety benefits.

But in fact, the economics of self-driving cars and city size are a lot more complex and subtle. Ed Glaeser, one of the greatest living urban economists, has a new paper exploring the topic. After explaining the relevant economic theory, he argues that Waymos and other autonomous vehicles will make people want to live in dense urban areas more, rather than less.

Glaeser notes that people who live in dense cities actually spend more time commuting than people who live in the suburbs (something I wrote a post about a couple of months ago). That means urbanites stand to benefit more from self-driving car trips than suburbanites, who generally already have shorter (and probably less stressful) commutes. Thus, he argues, self-driving cars will complement urban life more than suburban life, and make people want to live in denser cities. He expects the effect to be modest, but it’s still in the exact opposite direction from what people’s intuitions suggest.

Fundamentally, this is because people typically misunderstand the nature of American suburbia. They imagine bedroom communities where people commute to and from a central business district. Some suburbs definitely do behave like that, but most are like little cities themselves, with office parks where people work and strip-malls where people shop. Suburbanites trade the variety and financial opportunity of the big city for the convenience and safety of the suburbs. But self-driving cars make big cities more convenient.

Urbanists who throw a lot of hate at self-driving cars should stop to consider that perhaps their anger is misplaced.

Fear Strikes Out

But the hatred remains

Paul Krugman
Sep 18
 
READ IN APP
 

On Wednesday Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, gave a speech affirming the EU’s willingness to move toward making Canada an “associate member.” Nobody quite knows what that would mean, and it might be mostly symbolic. But it would be a kind of declaration, by both Europe and Canada, of reduced dependence on the United States. And the next day Mark Carney, Canada’s Prime Minster, strongly endorsed the idea.

Donald Trump predictably, reacted with rage, calling it a “hostile act,” threatening to cut off all trade with Europe.

And nobody cared.

Last year the EU responded to Trump’s clearly illegal tariffs not by retaliating, but by making a humiliating deal. But at this point Europe has apparently decided to stop fearing Trump.

Canada’s defiance is even more remarkable. Canada’s economy is extremely dependent on the United States both as an export market and as a supplier, while the EU has historically been a vastly less important trading partner:

So Canada has a lot to lose from trade conflict with the U.S.

Furthermore, geography does not favor a Canadian pivot toward Europe. Distance still matters a lot for world trade, especially for complex value chains like the one that links the U.S. and Canadian auto sectors. And to take some representative distances, Toronto is only 435 miles from Chicago, but 3,935 miles from Frankfurt. So one might think that Carney would be cautious about offending the man who is still president of his giant neighbor.

But foreign leaders have more or less given up trying to placate Trump.

When I try to think about the current state of Trumpism, I find myself revisiting Machiavelli’s The Prince, which is, after all, sort of a user’s manual for autocrats. Machiavelli is often cited as having said that it is better to be feared than loved, but what he actually said was somewhat more complex:

Upon this a question arises: whether it be better to be loved than feared or feared than loved? It may be answered that one should wish to be both, but, because it is difficult to unite them in one person, it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with … Nevertheless a prince ought to inspire fear in such a way that, if he does not win love, he avoids hatred.

Obviously Trump isn’t doing well on the “avoiding hatred” front. Pew’s survey of international views of the United Statesshows a stunning collapse in confidence that the U.S. president will do the right thing:

Domestic polls, of course, show very low approval for Trump. What’s truly striking, however, is that those who disapprove of Trump mostly disapprove “strongly.” The Navigator poll, for example, shows 48 percent of Americans strongly disapproving of Trump, much larger than the total number approving and 2 ½ times the number who strongly approve.

So many people both at home and around the world hate Trump. That has, however, been true since quite early in the Trump II administration. What has really changed is the dissipation of fear.

Globally, the most obvious reason nations have stopped fearing Trump is the debacle in Iran. At the start of the Iran war most people imagined that, whatever else one might say about Trump’s America, it had by far the world’s most powerful military. But what we’ve actually seen is one failure after another, as the U.S. military has failed to subdue the Iranian regime, been forced to abandon some of its own bases in the region, and depleted its supplies of munitions. Now America has refused to help Saudi Arabia against the Houthis — perhaps because we no longer have the necessary capabilities.

What about economic power? Trump clearly could do a lot of economic damage to Canada. But the U.S. economy would also suffer from all-out trade war. And while the damage from trade war would be much smaller as a percentage of U.S. GDP than Canadian GDP, Canadians appear to be solidly behind Carney, while Americans, to the extent they even know what is happening, appear by a small plurality to support Canada’s position:

And yes, foreign leaders are looking at the likely results of the U.S. midterm elections. From fiftyplusone:

So they look at the prospect of a president who will have less ability than ever to punish his perceived enemies, at home or abroad.

Globally, then, Trump is in exactly the opposite position of where Machiavelli said a prince should be: hated but not feared.

The situation in the U.S. is somewhat less blatant. Businesses — even businesses like the auto industry, which have a lot to lose from trade wars — remain quiet, presumably because the Trump administration retains considerable power to punish them via contracts, regulations and so on. (In many ways Trump has been acting as if he wants to destroy the U.S. auto industry, or at least leave it hopelessly uncompetitive as the world electrifies.) Even in America, however, fear of Trump is palpably fading.

Now, even a massive blue wave in November won’t end Trump’s ability to do immense damage to the nation and world — damage that he may well do out of sheer spite. He is, after all, exactly the kind of person who will feel, not that he failed America, but that America failed him.

More about that in future posts. For now, let’s cautiously celebrate a clear decline in the fear Trump inspires, abroad and at home.

Trying to convince people you’re right is underrated

Plus prepper takes and the end of history

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 18
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Before getting to the Mailbag, I want to say something about the increasingly salient A.I. debates happening online. Trying to think about policy involves forming views about a lot of contested questions, many of which don’t have immediately obvious answers. That means you necessarily find yourself deferring to an extent to the judgment of other people. Which means that something very important to do in life is decide how to assess which people are reliable sources of information.

The way that I think a lot of people go about doing this is kind of basic friend/enemy politics. They emotionally or intellectually anchor around some particular point and then just try to align with the people who are aligned with them on that.

And I think that’s a mistake. The fact is that for basically any widely held political view, a huge share of the people who hold the view are going to be ignorant, intellectually sloppy, or otherwise badly flawed in their reasoning. That’s just what people are like.

What you ought to do instead is try to see which people casually toss off false statements about things that are easily verifiable. One salient example this week is that I’ve seen a lot of conservative-minded people who decided to align with the White House’s regulatory skepticism on A.I. safety saying that the people who are pushing concerns about the risks of A.I. are the exact same people as “climate doomers” and anti-nuclear activists.

Erick Erickson
@EWErickson
The nuclear power doomers became the climate doomers and now they’re the AI doomers. The only commonality is they want the United States to recede.
10:49 PM · Sep 14, 2026 · 103K Views
131 Replies · 252 Reposts · 1.52K Likes

Anyone who is saying this either doesn’t know what they are talking about or (worse) does know what they are talking about and is choosing to lie to you.

That’s not a good person to listen to on this subject. For better or worse, the relationship between the climate movement and the effective altruist community has been very antagonistic over the years precisely because the latter group did not accept the totalizing and apocalyptic narratives the climate people were invested in.

To be maximally generous to Erickson, he was just popping off without looking into it. That’s not ideal epistemic behavior, but I think we’ve all done it (certainly I have) and it can be useful as a learning experience. But if you pop off, get told you’re wrong by better-informed people, and then plow ahead unashamedly, that’s bad. Don’t do that. Don’t listen to people who do that.

The Digital Entomologist: Will Stancil and Parker Molloy got into it on Bluesky. Molloy’s theory seems to be that Talarico showed he’s transphobic, and it acceptable to work to reduce his support which could result in Paxton winning — possibly leaving a 50/50 Senate which remains in the thrall to the Trump personality cult. Her argument seems to be that the election is the best time to try to influence a politician. It is better to defeat the one who is closer to you, than to keep the pressure on for the next 6 years. How does post election influence work? How can one convince trans activists that they are better off talking to Talarico for the next 6 years than being ignored by Paxton?

I certainly agree that vote blue no matter who reduces the influence of those whose votes can be taken for granted during the election, but I also think that those voters still have a lot of influence during the term if they in part of the coalition. Or is that incorrect?

I think the big thing that has gone weirdly missing from a lot of progressive thinking about the political system is the concept of “persuade people that you are correct.”

Bluesky users frequently accuse me of being the one who ignores the possibility that public opinion can change, but that’s just not the case at all. The way the political campaign for marriage equality worked was that the vast majority of politically active gays and lesbians in the United States loyally supported John Kerry and Barack Obama and downballot congressional Democrats in 2004, 2006, 2008, and 2010 because Democrats were on their side on politically feasible gay-rights causes like an employment non-discrimination law. The other thing that L.G.B.T.Q. activists did during this period was persuade the American public that they were correct about marriage. They didn’t browbeat Democrats in red states for refusing to take the unpopular side of the issue. They didn’t even browbeat Democrats in blue states for refusing to take the unpopular side of the issue. They understood that it was their job to convince people and they did.

That was a case of unusually rapid opinion change and it was also unusually clear-cut that the direction of change was from mass opinion to elected officials.

Elite persuasion also matters, though. The housing abundance movement’s big success over the past 20 years has been taking what used to be an obscure academic analysis from Ed Glaeser and turning it into something that is broadly acknowledged as true by the relatively small minority of Americans who bother to care about the details of housing policy debates. The successful elite persuasion around this has been the basis of bipartisan state laws from Florida to Maine to California. It’s why Elizabeth Warren and Tim Scott worked together to enact a small-but-meaningful federal housing-supply law. And it’s why we increasingly have journalists on a housing beat and a growing academic literature exploring the nuances of how the political economy of housing supply really works.

By the same token, I would say the failures of YIMBYism are largely failures of persuasion. Notably, the Republicans of the Northeast don’t seem to agree that the overregulation of housing supply is a major economic problem for Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, and Massachusetts. Republicans don’t govern any of these states, but what they think and do matters because voting for bipartisan bills is inherently less risky for everyone, so the lack of YIMBY Republicans makes it harder for YIMBY Democrats to get anything done. If New York Republicans thought about housing the way Phil Scott and Kelly Ayotte think about housing, then Kathy Hochul’s moves toward housing abundance would be much more politically efficacious and the situation would be transformed.

There’s a lot I could say about the sociology of why New Hampshire and Massachusetts Republicans have different views of this, but I don’t think the kind of pressure campaigns that activists like to talk about have anything to do with it. The Massachusetts Republicans just haven’t been convinced!

Share

Closer to the meat of the question, I don’t really like the rhetoric of “vote blue no matter who.” If you compare Ken Paxton with James Talarico on trans issues, it’s just night and day. If the only thing you care about is trans rights, then Talarico is more supportive than Paxton, so you should vote for Talarico because he is closer to your position even if he doesn’t entirely agree with it.

To again analogize to housing-supply stuff, I don’t think I’ve ever heard of a politician who is as much of an extreme YIMBY as I am. But I don’t run around doing takes like “Burhan Azeem threw YIMBYs under the bus by opposing unlimited building height in the city of Cambridge.” That would be insane. He spearheaded an effort to legalize six-story buildings throughout the city and ended up compromising on legalizing four-story buildings throughout the city (plus you can go to six if you meet some onerous inclusionary zoning standards). That’s a huge deal! He’s an amazing YIMBY champion. I would love for even more expansive upzoning to be politically viable but, you know, it isn’t.

Different activist communities, I find, just talk themselves into different levels of sourness about politicians. YIMBYs are, I think, all the way on one end of the spectrum and thrilled to praise everyone from Zohran Mamdani to Ron DeSantis for taking constructive action even though nobody is actually doing the full thing we think they should be doing. The people on Bluesky who are angry at Talarico even though him winning the election would obviously be good for their cause are over at the other end.

But what I really find striking about this is not the attitude toward Talarico per se but the extent to which the movement does not try to persuade people that they are correct. As a person who reads a lot of articles and has certainly read a lot of commentary on this topic, almost none of it is devoted to trying to persuade me that gender self-identification is the right way to assign people to sex-segregated sports teams. The people who believe that have been very successful at creating a situation where lots of left-of-center writers never express any doubts on the merits (think about the many prominent writers who’ve never addressed the topic), but they don’t try to set my doubts at ease. You are allowed, though, to try to convince people to change their minds.

More broadly, a topic that gets kicked around a lot — most recently by Nate Silver, Jerusalem Demsas, and me on a podcast — is the relationship between moderation or centrism as a political tactic and liberalism as a political philosophy. These are, obviously, not the same thing.

But more than Jerusalem I do think they are related things. And this question of persuasion versus coercion as an approach to electoral politics is part of the connective tissue. Part of the spirit of liberalism is to believe in persuasion on the merits as a core pillar of political change. Another part is to believe that political parties will and should alternate in power. If you believe those things, you are going to believe that in practice forging bipartisan consensus is the key to durable change and that electoral pragmatism is how party leaders should address most issues most of the time. So you end up converging on tactical centrism as a worthwhile way of life.

As I’ve said time and again, if you take it seriously, the YIMBY movement is incredibly radical and is a core example of how people who believe in free markets can position themselves as dissenting from the status quo. But it is also true that YIMBYs, in practice, have mostly achieved political success through bipartisan strategies, tactical moderation, and trying to have a cheerful attitude toward winning halves of loaves. I don’t think that’s a coincidence. It speaks to the fact that it’s a deeply liberal cause — it’s about an egalitarian vision of human freedom — in much the way that the gay-rights movement of the 1990s and 2000s was.

Doug Elmendorf: Matt, You explained last week that AI safetyists and super-optimists should make similar financial investments because both groups expect AI to be “incredibly transformative.” But what about other aspects of behavior? A super-optimist might buy more sunglasses because the future is so bright. But should a rational safetyist, recognizing that rogue AI might take down the power grid or allow biological attacks, buy a house on the coast in rural Maine, get a generator and a large storage tank filled with diesel fuel, stockpile clean water, ...?

I do personally own a house in rural Maine that has a generator and its own well, so make of that what you will.

The main thing I think about this is that entirely separate from anything to do with superintelligence, the risk of novel pandemics is structurally increasing largely due to population growth and increased travel. Something that is relatively easy to do to help prepare yourself and your family for the next pandemic is to have reusable elastomeric respirators on hand. They are small and not very expensive and the more people who stockpile this kind of thing in advance the less supply chain stress there will be when the shit hits the fan. I also have a far-UVC lamp that can hopefully incinerate viruses. My emergency supplies box also includes sort of generic stuff like firestarters, a multi-tool, duct tape, paracord, water filters and purification tablets, and so forth. I don’t know that I actually have any necessary skills to make it through a survival situation, but it doesn’t hurt to have basic stuff on hand in case.

Share

Vas: You mentioned in your 9/11 retrospective that Obama and Clinton were constrained in a way W wasn’t, and that gave W an opportunity to be a great president. I agree Obama had constraints W didn’t, but Clinton was in the same framework wasnt he?

Also, I think generally the greatest presidents (Washington, Lincoln, FDR) made their greatness by coming at a challenging time and leaving the country in a better, stronger state after them. To some extent, the constraints allow for greatness.

Looking at your greatest presidents, I agree that they came along at challenging times and left the country in a stronger state. But unlike in your framing, I would argue that all three also took advantage of relatively unconstrained authority.

For Washington that was in part his unique prestige and in part just the fact that as the first president, he had a set of much less settled institutions to deal with than any later president ever would. The fact that he chose to step aside voluntarily after eight years and pass authority to a successor, John Adams, who was broadly like-minded but not a family member or hand-picked crony, had tremendous significance simply because he really could have acted very differently.

For Lincoln and F.D.R. it was enormous congressional majorities plus wartime powers.

Clinton served during a time of very low constraint on the United States as an international actor but of intense domestic political constraints. He had these big ideas on health care and he just couldn’t get them done. He had ideas about welfare reform that were better than the ideas in the bill he eventually signed because he was dealing with an opposition Congress. He can claim credit for sound macroeconomic policy and he signed some good bipartisan bills. But that’s really just making the plays the defense gives you. I’m not a hater by any means — he was in some respects a real political genius, but it’s different from the Bush situation where it was really left to him to explain and narrativize what was happening and he chose to point the country toward Iraq when he easily could have not done that.

Person With Internet Access: How do you think Francis Fukuyama’s “The End of History and the Last Man” holds up 35 years later? What, if anything, from it explains the current Western liberalism struggles?

I wrote and deleted enough answers to this question that I think the right answer is “I need to re-read the book and answer the question properly.” All I’ll say for now is that my recollection of it from about 20 years ago is that it makes a lot of points that are actually very insightful about the current crises of Western liberalism and the thesis is way less triumphalist than it is often remembered.

My analytic doubt about his thesis is how well his treatment of Islamism holds up.

“In the contemporary world only Islam has offered a theocratic state as a political alternative to both liberalism and communism,” Fukuyama wrote in his original 1989 essay. “But the doctrine has little appeal for non-Muslims, and it is hard to believe that the movement will take on any universal significance.”

In Fukuyama’s recent appearance on “The Ezra Klein Show,” he mentions this glancingly but it doesn’t really get pursued. Instead he says that “radical Islamism is not an ideology that’s going to ever conquer the world … in the years since 9/11, it has kind of faded.”

That’s all true but also maybe a bit too flip. Thanks to events in Syria and Iraq, Islamist political parties have more power than they did 25 years ago. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict has taken on a less secular and more religious flavor. In places like Egypt, you see liberals (both Egyptian liberals and foreign policy elites in Western countries) betraying their commitment to democracy to combat a local Islamist movement that while dramatically less radical than al-Qaeda, is still fairly illiberal. You have Western writers like Shadi Hamid arguing that America should deprioritize liberalism in favor of democracy and also that Muslim immigrants shouldn’t face pressure to assimilate. You also have very illiberal forces rising on the right precisely because they believe Muslims can’t or won’t assimilate. I don’t have a fully worked out take on this or recall exactly how (or if) Fukuyama discusses Islamism in the book, but there’s plenty of meat on this bone to chew.
