Why I send my kid to low-income urban public schools

Not every school with unfavorable demographics is a dysfunctional mess — policy matters!

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 22
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

I disagree with Nikole Hannah-Jones about a lot of issues, but I thought her recent piece about her regrets over sending her daughter to her poor-performing local public school rather than acting like most parents and deploying her financial means to maximize school quality was extremely well-written, emotionally affecting, and honest.

I’m also a little sad to say that among acquaintances of mine, especially non-parents, the main takeaway from the story seems to be that the threads of idealism were completely misguided and every parent has an absolute obligation to do everything in their power to optimize for their own kid.

Reading the story, I had some uncomfortable moments because Kate and I have made structurally similar choices with our son’s education. From pre-K (which starts at age three in D.C.) through fifth grade, he went to our local public elementary school, a Title I school that is 47 percent Black, 20 percent Hispanic, and 22 percent English language learners; it was even less white when he started.

He now goes to our locally zoned middle school, which has similar demographics.

Since he’s only been at the middle school for a few weeks, I can’t speak to the experience in detail. But our experience being the affluent family at a mostly low-income majority-minority elementary school was fine — good, even. Not without difficulty or downside, of course, but even from a purely selfish viewpoint, I’d say the difficulties and downsides were minor compared with the price of private school tuition or the annoyance of moving to the suburbs.

What’s more, not only do I think it’s been a fine decision on a selfish family level, I think that it has accomplished some of our broader goals. The school primarily serves low-income families and many of the kids do have difficult home lives and discipline problems at school. But the school was still a well-run, happy place for our child, who learned to navigate a much broader range of social interactions than if we’d sent him to school only with other affluent children, and the presence of a critical mass of affluent, educated, engaged parents I think made a real difference in the lives of the teachers and the students.

I’m not here to quibble with Hannah-Jones’s take on her experience, and our situations are certainly not identical.

Instead, I’m writing to those who reacted to her piece with blanket skepticism about inner-city schools or with hostility to the idea of considering the needs of other children when deciding what to do for your own, because it would be a shame if every affluent urban parent of a toddler decides they need to flee to the suburbs.

Maybe you do and maybe you don’t. But the actual details of schools that serve high-need populations vary quite a lot, and it’s worth both engaging with the specifics of your local situation and thinking about the general policy questions.

D.C.P.S. has been on an upward trajectory

One key difference between our situation and Hannah-Jones’s is that while Washington, D.C. Public Schools (D.C.P.S.) was notoriously bad for a very long time, it’s been on a broadly positive overall trajectory.

Some of the gains at D.C.P.S. reflect the fact that more affluent parents have been enrolling their kids in public school, which has mechanically pushed the averages up. But we’re not looking at a pure compositional effect — D.C. has been showing stronger results across all the major demographic subgroups (I really recommend Josh Boots’s article for Capital Commonsense if you want a detailed rundown of all the good news).

Why have the schools in D.C. gotten better?

I think it’s broadly because under ex-Mayor Adrian Fenty a contentious new “reform” regime came into power under the stewardship of D.C.P.S. Chancellor Michelle Rhee, who became a national media celebrity thanks to her battles with the teachers’ union.

Fenty failed to secure re-election after one term, but his successor, Vincent Gray, replaced Rhee with her deputy, Kaya Henderson, who did not seek national media attention in the same way but essentially stayed the course.

This Fenty-to-Gray transition stabilized and consolidated the reforms, and then while current Mayor Muriel Bowser’s 11 years in office have been fairly uncreative on K-12 education, she hasn’t really done much to alter the positive trajectory.

One particularly effective component of these reforms is a well-designed performance pay system for D.C.P.S. teachers that ensures that the most effective teachers are very generously compensated by national standards. That has improved retention of the teachers you would want to retain and made D.C.P.S. a good place to teach if you’re the kind of ambitious educator who wants to take on big challenges and deliver results.

D.C.P.S. has also been a national leader, albeit not necessarily on the Mississippi scale, in implementing a rigorous phonics-based early-literacy program.

These changes have not miraculously solved every problem in every school. But they have improved things. And they’ve made D.C.P.S. an appealing place for families like ours who believe in public education but aren’t naive about it.

Our son’s former elementary school has been at the forefront of these changes. It’s not the top-testing school in the city (as in any city, the highest-testing schools all have very high shares of rich, highly educated parents), but it performs incredibly well on value-add and demographically adjusted measures. It’s led by an energetic principal who works hard to recruit strong teachers and it was written up in the New York Times as an exemplar of sound early-literacy instruction.

But these things aren’t automatic, and parents can play a big role in creating a virtuous cycle.

For several years, Kate and one of her friends ran the school’s Parent Teacher Organization. They raised a lot of money, primarily from the minority of affluent families at the school, and used that money to support the teachers and make their lives easier so the principal’s work of recruiting and retaining them would be easier.

But there’s more to it than just donating to the P.T.O. It’s also the parents with more resources who’ve been disproportionately involved in volunteering for the school’s fall and spring celebrations, which are widely attended by the entire school community. Kate organized and ran, with the help of a coach we hired, a soccer club for fourth-grade boys when there was no room for them on the school team. Another dad in the class taught a chess club when the school needed inexpensive after-school activities. Other parents chipped in and handled the administrative tasks of registration so that kids whose families couldn’t afford extracurricular activities weren’t left out. The presence of more affluent families doesn’t make schools better by magic; it’s being actually involved in things that helps lift other families up.

The background policy conditions are important too, though. They include the teacher pay stuff I mentioned earlier, but the school also ran a pretty tight ship on discipline. Our time there wasn’t without difficulty on this front (as Hannah-Jones mentioned in her piece, out-of-class times like lunch and recess can be particularly challenging), but the school made a strong effort to communicate rules clearly and enforce them consistently. And I think everyone who cares about equality and integration needs to understand that if rules aren’t enforced — whether that’s in public schools or public transit or whatever else — people are going to opt out. There’s a ton you can do to help your kid outside of school, but if the discipline piece doesn’t work, there’s no salvaging that. And at our school it worked pretty well.

Outside options

For all that I’m positive about the education offered at my child’s elementary school, there was no math tracking (everyone is lumped together in the same class regardless of ability); the main educational focus has been on improving outcomes at the low end. To the point of Boots’s Capital Commonsense article I mentioned earlier, D.C.P.S. has actually achieved improvements at the low end, which is important to me. A lot of insane stuff has been done in American school systems in the name of equity, and what D.C. did was actually get better results for the most struggling students. It’s one reason we feel so strongly about continuing to participate in and support D.C.P.S.

Subscribed

Still, that focus doesn’t necessarily create the best environment for the brightest kids.

Our solution has been outside math tutoring. We’re certainly not unique in this respect — lots of parents across America use programs like Kumon or Russian Math. We’ve opted for individual tutors rather than big national chains because that was more convenient, but this sort of supplemental work has been key to keeping our kid happy and engaged at his public school.

What I would say, though, is that lots of parents all across America end up using some kind of supplemental instruction. If you send your kid to a diverse urban public school, you probably will, but moving to the suburbs is no guarantee that you won’t. And while it costs money, it really is a lot cheaper than private school or moving to the fanciest school district.

Our middle school doesn’t have enough kids to do within-grade tracking (a “regular” sixth-grade math class and an “advanced” sixth-grade math class, for example), so they instead do a form of math tracking where if you place strongly at the beginning of sixth grade, they just send you over to the seventh-grade math class. When our son learned that option existed, he was eager to qualify, so he worked hard over this past summer to make sure he did well on his entrance test. He’s always liked math, but he was more motivated and excited about math at school than he’d been in years!

The English classes at his school aren’t tracked at all, but he’s always been an avid reader who spends plenty of time with books of his own accord. We were disappointed, though, by how unambitious the curriculum was in terms of assigning books. What we’d ideally like the school to do — and what I think a private school or a better public school would, in fact, do — is have recommendations on hand to push a precocious reader forward with material that will challenge him but not be so dense as to make him miserable. Instead, for our kid, it fell to Kate to come up with some more ambitious books for him to read this year.

We’ll see how it goes.

One distinction I want to draw here, though, is between a school that is genuinely bad or dysfunctional in the sense that the teachers and the staff can’t or won’t do their jobs properly and a school that simply isn’t really oriented to our child.

Our elementary school is genuinely a very well-run school, a safe and nurturing environment full of talented staff who work tirelessly to care for the students. But it’s also true that the staff’s main job is trying to get the bottom third of students up to an acceptable level of competence. And they’re really good at this! But at a diverse public school like this one, if you want a lot of enrichment for a kid who finds school pretty easy, you need to put in some effort and money to find supplemental options outside of the school.

If you end up way further out on the effort spectrum with homeschooling or on the money spectrum with private school, you can almost certainly get a more tailored experience.

On the other hand, as long as your kid is happy, I think there’s a fair amount of value in learning to get along with different kinds of people, to deal with a certain amount of being a little bored, and to not constantly be the center of attention.

Some common sense

I feel that I have pretty banal views about all of this, and I’m a little wary of the hotter takes I see flying around on social media:

  • Obviously don’t send your child to a totally dysfunctional school or one where they’re miserable. I don’t think K-12 schools have a huge impact on the objective life trajectory of the children of affluent professionals (I’m pretty sure Nikole Hannah-Jones’s daughter is going to be just fine), but your child’s quality of life in the moment still matters.

  • On the other hand, it’s valid and correct to give some consideration to the impact of your choices on other people’s children. A country full of people who care about their community is going to be a much better country than one where parents are all gassing each other up into amoral familism.

  • Most of all, don’t just assume that your local public school is dysfunctional if it serves a low-income population or has below-average test scores. Make an effort to actually look into demographically adjusted measurements of school performance. There are plenty of well-run schools with so-so or below-average results due to challenging demographics. A school that’s doing well with the students it has will probably also do well with your student.

One thing that’s frustrating to me in almost all conversations that I have with parents about our children’s collective schooling is how little interest there is in education policy.

People toss off casual remarks about school budgets that aren’t true. Or they have concerns about the disciplinary environment or level of academic rigor, but they don’t pay attention to the Obama-Trump-Biden-Trump ping pong on discipline (Trump is right) or the pernicious influence of the “grading for equity” movement. I’ve felt good about the management of D.C.P.S. during my son’s entire school career, but there’s a new mayor incoming who is allied with people who I think have unsound views about public education.

I have no particular desire to leave D.C.P.S., and neither does our son, but there are some downsides to sending your kid to even a well-run diverse public school (there are also upsides like “it’s free” and “I can live in a neighborhood I like”). But if it stops being well-run, that’s a totally different question.

Left-of-center professional circles tend to be unfortunately torn between people taking refuge in exclusionary suburbs and then hand-waving about underfunded inner-city schools or else asserting that desegregation efforts are like a magic wand that will make all dilemmas and tradeoffs go away. If you want public education to work (and I do), you need to insist on things like reasonable discipline policies, reasonable amounts of ability-grouping, and reasonable levels of academic standards. If you don’t, then the impulse to privatize access to schools either formally with vouchers or informally with zoning becomes hard to resist.

It’s “Underwear on the Outside” Time

Trump’s continuing downward spiral into sundowning

Paul Krugman
Sep 23
 
READ IN APP
 

Note: Heather Cox Richardson and I will do a Substack live today at noon ET. You can watch it here.

In the 1971 comedy film Bananas a third-world nation’s strongman announces his new policies:

From this day on, the official language of San Marcos will be Swedish. Silence! In addition to that, all citizens will be required to change their underwear every half-hour. Underwear will be worn on the outside so we can check.

Yesterday, addressing the General Assembly of the United Nations, the president of the United States declared, among other things,

The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much, now here and after officially called superintelligence, changing the name. The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake … From this point forward, all of United States documents and hopefully the world will be changed to use the much more accurate term super as opposed to artificial.

This came just two days after Trump announced that his planned gigantic Triumphal Arch overshadowing Washington DC will

house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.

Most reporting on Trump’s speech emphasized either his belligerence — his rejection of global cooperation — or the fact that almost everything he said was a lie. But isn’t the bigger story the fact that the leader of what used to be the world’s most powerful nation — I say “used to be” because America’s power is collapsing before our eyes — has clearly and undeniably lost his mind?

I’m by no means the only commentator to see parallels between Trump’s UN speech and the scene in Bananas. But comparing Trump to a fictional character is unfair — to the fictional character. After all, in Bananas the mad dictator is quickly removed from power. In America today, some Republicans are quietly distancing themselves from Trump. A few are even voicing subtle, elliptical criticisms. But will he be impeached, or face 25th Amendment proceedings? Not a chance.

Indeed, let’s be honest: the only reason these faint hints of Republican rebellion are newsworthy is that they come after years of slavish obedience and flattery — obedience and flattery that continued even though Trump’s deteriorating mental state has been obvious for a long time.

I wrote a post titled “It’s Sundowning in America,” inspired by Trump’s demented demands that he receive the Nobel Peace Prize, 8 months ago. The damage being done by Deranged Trump Syndrome was already obvious. And that was before Trump squandered America’s military credibility, as well as a dangerously large share of our munitions, on his catastrophic war-of-choice in Iran.

There’s a high probability that Trump’s power will be considerably reduced in the aftermath of the November midterms. Polls point to a blue wave that is highly likely to give Democrats control of the House and more likely than not to deliver the Senate. If that blue wave does indeed materialize, I expect that there will be an enormous sigh of relief across the country because it will be a major, if not fatal, setback for Trumpism.

However, we shouldn’t let the short-term relief of a November victory blind us to the long-term realities. Trumpism did not emerge out of thin air – that is, an unfortunate draw of the democracy cards. Instead Trump and Trumpism is the culmination of a decades-long threat to American democracy, to the moral, legal and social fiber of this country.

There is a straight line from Koch Brothers money, allied with segregationists and religious fundamentalists, that runs through the Federalist Society and the Roberts Supreme Court, through the MAGA-fied Republican Party, through the crypto-industry and the tech-broligarchy, that leads to Trump. And it will take a single-minded, fearless and incorruptible new generation of Democrats to defeat this many-headed hydra.

We should also recognize that Mad King Donald will still retain a great deal of power even with a Democratic Congress. He won’t feel that he has failed America, he will believe that America has failed him and try to punish the nation accordingly. Thus he will use his remaining power vindictively not just against the victorious Democrats, but also against the American people.

And if Democrats win the White House in 2028, they will inherit a badly damaged nation.

So while we may be justified in celebrating if the election goes as predicted in November, don’t take your battle-gear off yet. There is a long road ahead.

The Republican urge to start wars in the Middle East

And other ways Trump has failed in his second term

Matthew Yglesias
Sep 23
 
READ IN APP
 

Soon after the 2024 election, I published an article titled “How Donald Trump could succeed: Or, more likely, fail.”

I think that clearly, as of late September 2026, he is failing.

The once-vaunted “vibe shift” has evaporated and young voters have swung back to the left. We have a House incumbent in a Trump +15 district distancing herself from Trump’s immigration policy. The big question of the midterms is whether Democrats can win Senate races in Iowa, Texas, Alaska, and Kansas — states that should not be in play.

This doesn’t mean that MAGA is down for the count, by any means. The Republicans have a daunting cash advantage and the Senate math is objectively very difficult for Dems.

But Trump is undeniably unpopular. And in terms of the scale of his failure, it’s worth reflecting on the fact that Republicans’ best electoral news is just that while Democrats have good nominees in a number of well-chosen races, the national party leadership has not moved to the center since 2024 and a lot of blue state progressives are being replaced by even-further-left politicians.

That’s keeping Republicans in the game, to an extent. But it also underscores the reality that Trump is doing the opposite of crushing and discrediting the left — he’s rocket fuel for thermostatic counter-mobilization, just like he was back in the “Woke 1” days.

So if Trump has failed, how does my own diagnosis hold up?

I think the answer is that it’s pretty good, but not perfect.

My most successful, most fundamental forecast, one that I think a lot of tech industry people might have benefited from listening to, was that Trump was more likely to fail than succeed. Something about the Silicon Valley fast-follower mindset seems to make these guys struggle to understand the basic nature of the political pendulum, and a lot of folks like Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos who used to have more progressive personas bought high on MAGA right after Trump won, when they should have hedged their bets.

Presidents usually overreach, and Trump is certainly not a person of above-average discipline or judgment.

Bad luck or bad policy?

One thing I noted in the piece was that despite Trump’s anti-war rhetoric on the campaign trail, the national security team he announced shortly after the election was “an extremely hawkish group that screams ‘hot war with Iran.’”

In retrospect, I wish I’d made a bigger deal about this.

I noted at the time that it seemed like a team that would lead the country into war with Iran and then hedged with the observation that presidents sometimes surprise us. So far so good! What I didn’t do in the piece was dwell on the idea at any length, which is too bad because I was right about the team of super-hawks and this seems to have kind of wrecked Trump’s presidency.

I mentioned this back in April, but there’s a weird finding in the economics literature that Democratic Party presidents enjoy systematically better economic performance even though they don’t pursue systematically better economic policy.

Republican war-mongering is their worst economic policy

Matthew Yglesias
·
Apr 9

Mark Mills writes in City Journal that the economic chaos unleashed by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz should teach environmentalists that they are underestimating the indispensability of oil and gas to the world economy.

Read full story

The explanation, according to Alan Blinder and Mark Watson, is that “the Democratic edge stems mainly from more benign oil shocks, superior total-factor-productivity (T.F.P.) performance, a more favorable international environment, and perhaps more optimistic consumer expectations about the near-term future.”

They seem to primarily understand this as a question of good luck. But having watched both the George W. Bush and second Trump presidencies unfold, I think it’s because Republicans have systematically bad foreign policy that is inattentive to the downside risk of saber-rattling and hawkishness. Trump made a great show of breaking with the Bush-era “neocons” over their idealistic invocations of democracy-promotion. But the actual problem with Bush-era foreign policy wasn’t belief in democracy; it was excessive belief in the potential upside of coercive military force. Trump has retained the error while reconfiguring the goals.

Overreaching on immigration

In the piece, I also argued that “nothing did more to drive support for Trump than backlash to the multi-year span of chaos at the southern border due to widespread exploitation of asylum loopholes,” which gave Trump a huge opportunity to reap a political win by forcefully doing what voters wanted and shutting down the irregular inflow of unselected immigrants.

He did that, and I think it’s worked well for him.

I also said he’d be tempted to try to actually deliver on the promise of “mass deportation” from the interior and that this would probably generate backlash.

My view was that the most prudent course would be to return to the Obama administration’s first-term policy of rapid-fire jailhouse pickups of illegal immigrants arrested for non-immigration crimes in cooperative jurisdictions and to try and avoid picking other fights. Trump has done plenty of that style of immigration enforcement, but he’s also done a lot of more aggressive interior-enforcement actions of the sort that I thought would spark mass public backlash.

They kind of have, but my read of the evidence is that it’s much less backlash than I would have hoped and much less than a lot of progressives seem to believe has actually occurred — Trump’s immigration approval rating has drifted down, but it’s significantly higher than his overall approval rating or approval on any other major issue.

Or to put it another way, the really clear backlash has been to extreme forms of overreach — such as immigration officials literally killing American citizens without cause and the White House covering for them.

That’s incredibly bleak and it did generate, eventually, some pullback from the administration. But they’ve really gone quite far on immigration issues. Interior enforcement has been consistently aggressive, they are stripping as many people as possible of legal status, they’ve deported a considerable number of people erroneously, they’re messing up skilled legal immigration — and I think it’s hard to argue that they’re paying a big price.

This dynamic is bad for Trump in a handful of South Florida and South Texas districts that are heavily Latino but swung heavily to the right in the 2020 and 2024 cycles, so it’s not like there’s zero backlash.

But still, immigration is consistently one of Trump’s best-performing issues, so he’s kind of incentivized to do cruel, flashy things to drive attention to it and away from the core affordability questions that are crushing him.

Moving backward on affordability

I noted in the piece that the most obvious way Trump could fail would be by trying to actually implement his campaign promises on tariffs, since they directly contradicted the mass public’s urgent desire for cheaper stuff.

“Trump’s supporters in the business community say that he’s just lying and won’t do this,” I wrote, “that he’ll use the threat of tariffs to coerce certain policy concessions out of certain foreign countries.”

I thought threatening tariffs and then calling off trade wars in exchange for minor, superficial, or even totally fake concessions was a pretty good idea given how much Trump himself dominates the MAGA information space. The risk to his presidency was that he’d really do it.

Subscribed

Trump very early in his administration did the huge Liberation Day tariffs, faced massive market and political blowback, and backed down. But ever since backing down, he’s been trying to recreate Liberation Day in the aggregate while minimizing stock market blowback. In terms of the problem Trump is trying to solve, this has worked. Notably, the data center industry has gotten exemptions so that the construction boom is going on unabated.

But this does not help people with the cost of living.

In fact, the furious pace of A.I.-related investment is raising the price of consumer electronics that compete for the same stuff.

Meanwhile, the tariffs as such are not having that large an impact on the overall cost of living. But in political terms, they’re a salient and obvious example of a president who was elected on a promise of lower prices acting to make prices higher.

I said in the piece that it was “basically inconceivable” that Trump would avoid the kind of deficit-financed regressive tax cut that added inflationary pressure to the economy and pushed up interest rates and, indeed, that’s exactly what Trump did. So we have not only the war spiking energy prices but also Trump’s two most high-profile economic initiatives — the One Big Beautiful Bill and the tariffs — both pushing up the cost of living.

It’s honestly incredibly stupid to win an election on the basis of making an impossible promise of lower consumer prices and then to take deliberate policy actions that go in the other direction. But here we are.

A cautionary tale, not a model

I don’t want to claim oracular wisdom on any of this, but I do think the general tenor of my forecast — that Trump would probably overreach across a broad range of issues and spark significant backlash — was basically borne out and a lot closer to the mark than once-widespread speculations about a vibe shift or a realignment.

The immigration backlash point proved, I think, to be further away than I thought it was, which still didn’t stop Trump from going too far.

The immigration case is a particularly pointed illustration of why I find it disturbing that so many progressive policy entrepreneurs continue to cast Trump’s approach as a model to emulate rather than as a cautionary tale.

I do understand the appeal of heavily relying on legal creativity and aggressive assertions of executive power as the main mode of policymaking. The alternative is to focus on winning supermajorities, which requires a more moderate big-tent approach or else relying on bipartisan legislation as the main mode of policy change.

But even on immigration, where Trump had the public squarely on his side and he acted with maximum aggression and got away with more than I thought he would in terms of public opinion, he hasn’t actually enacted any permanent legislative change. I’ve seen conservatives on social media jumping up and down with delight about Trump enacting a new “public charge” regulation for visa issuance that reverses the Biden administration’s reversal of conservatives’ prior effort to enact this regulation in Trump’s first term.

This kind of see-sawing is inherently less impactful than a push to change actual immigration law would be. But to change the statutes governing who gets visas and the terms by which foreign-born people or residents of mixed-status families can access the social safety net would require Republicans to set priorities and to give Democrats some wins on topics that Republicans have decided are lower priority.

By insisting on purism, you find yourself limited to executive actions and you actually achieve less.

And it seems to me that as progressive schemers plot their agenda for 2029, they are basically aiming to recapitulate these mistakes. The reason Trump didn’t genuinely focus on reducing the macroeconomic drivers of high prices and high interest rates is that doing so would have required sidelining his pre-baked ideas around taxes. Democrats, similarly, will face a choice between doing internal coalition management by rebranding a progressive-interest-group agenda as “affordability” and actually focusing on affordability. And then on the broad suite of other agenda items, they will face the same tradeoff between purity-maxxing through executive action and the annoying — but ultimately more impactful — process of securing durable base hits through bipartisan legislation.

If you want to reshape the country in more profound ways than that, you need some combination of winning huge congressional majorities and/or being popular enough to survive midterm backlash cycles, either of which requires being way more prudent and disciplined than Trump was rather than plowing ahead like a bull in a china shop.

If you want to find a Republican model to emulate, I would forget Trump and look at New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte, who is cruising to re-election in a state Kamala Harris won despite a terrible national political climate.

Notably, she pulled this off without being a Phil Scott type who’s checked by a Democratic supermajority in the legislature. There’s a red trifecta in New Hampshire, and they have chosen to behave in a disciplined way — they refused to do a MAGA gerrymander of the House map, for example, to avoid nationalizing state politics — and have made incremental policy gains and built power.

I often hear that it’s impossible for political coalitions to be disciplined in the social media era, but while I agree that it’s hard, I think this is learned helplessness. They’re disciplined in New Hampshire. Trump and the Republicans have been very disciplined about abortion, while they’ve chosen to be reckless in other areas and are paying the price.

Democrats shouldn’t try to harness that same recklessness to progressive ends; they should learn to behave more prudently.

No, you are not on Indigenous land

A repost from 2024.

Noah Smith
Sep 24
 
READ IN APP
 

I’ve been dealing with more rabbit problems today, so here’s a repost to tide you over til tomorrow.

The Republican party has become an extremist party. ICE’s brutal campaign of terror in American communities, Trump’s attacks on press freedoms and election integrity, the coup attempt of 1/6/2021, Trump’s military threats toward Greenland, and friendliness toward Vladimir Putin are only a few of the more prominent examples of this extremism. And they’re probably going to be punished for it in November; polls show rapidly deteriorating support for both Donald Trump and the GOP that has fallen in behind him.

Good. Extremism ought to be punished. I’ll have lots more to say about the Republicans’ failures in the days to come.

But even though Democrats deserve to win, that doesn’t mean they’re free from the creeping extremism that has taken over essentially all of American politics and public discourse in the age of social media. Although Dems are not nearly as extremist as the GOP, they have become a much more ideologically extreme party than they were during the days of Obama. Dems’ extremist positions include dogged opposition to any form of effective immigration enforcement, tolerance of systematic (and systemic) racial discrimination, various trans issues, and…land acknowledgements.

Land acknowledgements? Really?? Isn’t that just a respectful way of acknowledging that the land we’re on used to belong to Indigenous people? Isn’t it just a way of saying “Hey Indigenous people, we haven’t forgotten you”?

Well…no. As I wrote in a post two years ago — still one of my most popular posts of all time — land acknowledgements don’t just recognize Indigenous people. They are a way of fundamentally delegitimizing the United States — of declaring that this is a country that has no right to exist. And beyond that, land acknowledgements implicitly advance a theory of collective racial ownership of territory that is morally indistinguishable from the worst blood-and-soil nationalism of the racist far Right.

Nor are land acknowledgements a fringe practice, limited to progressive cultural spaces. As Dave Weigel recently reported, they have become a sort of ritualistic utterance at Democratic Party events:

Democrats' decision to formalize land acknowledgments in their party meetings could haunt their candidates more than they realize…A tradition of naming historic Native tribes during regional events that started in Australia before spreading to Canada, arriving in the US via art exhibitions, is now part of every major party event…The 2016 Democratic convention did not contain a land acknowledgment. But the practice of beginning events with a nod to slaughtered tribes and "stolen" land spread during President Barack Obama's second term and Trump's first term, along with other progressive ideas about race and history…Democrats did not have campus conferences where they agreed to embrace language that conservatives see as anti-American…They just adopted the terminology when activists told them it was a good idea.

Land acknowledgements are not a big electoral issue. But in the long term, they represent — and contribute to — the creeping rise of anti-American and illiberal ideology on the broad American left. That will probably be an electoral liability at some point, but more fundamentally, it’s a departure from the liberal nationalist ideology that made the Democrats such an effective governing party in the 20th century.

So anyway, here’s my post from 2024.

The United States, like all nations, was created through territorial conquest. Most of its current territory was occupied or frequented by human beings before the U.S. came; the U.S. used force to either displace, subjugate, or kill all of those people. To the extent that land “ownership” existed under the previous inhabitants, the land of the U.S. is stolen land.

This was also true before the U.S. arrived. The forcible theft of the land upon which the U.S. now exists was not the first such theft; the people who lived there before conquered, displaced, or killed someone else in order to take the land. The land has been stolen and re-stolen again and again. If you somehow destroyed the United States, expelled its current inhabitants, and gave ownership of the land to the last recorded tribe that had occupied it before, you would not be returning it to its original occupants; you would simply be handing it to the next-most-recent conquerors.

If you go back far enough in time, of course, at some point this is no longer true. Humanity didn’t always exist; therefore for every piece of land, there was a first human to lay eyes on it, and a first human to say “This land is mine.” But by what right did this first human claim exclusive ownership of this land? Why does being the first person to see a natural object make you the rightful owner of that object? And why does being the first human to set foot on a piece of land give your blood descendants the right to dispose of that land as they see fit in perpetuity, and to exclude any and all others from that land? What about all the peoples of the world who were never lucky enough to be the first to lay eyes on any plot of dirt? Are they simply to be dispossessed forever?

I have never seen a satisfactory answer to these questions. Nor have I seen a satisfactory explanation of why ownership of land should be allocated collectively, in terms of racial or ethnic groups. In general, the first people who arrived on a piece of land did so in dribs and drabs, in small family units and tiny micro-tribes that met and married and fought and mixed and formed into larger identities and ethnicities and tribes over long periods of time. In most cases, the ethnic groups who now claim pieces of land as their own did not even exist when the first humans discovered or settled that land.

But even in those cases when it did exist, why should land ownership be assigned to a race at all? Why should my notional blood relation to the discoverers or the conquerors of a piece of land determine whether I can truly belong on that land? Why should a section of the map be the land of the Franks, or the Russkiy, or the Cherokee, or the Han, or the Ramaytush Ohlone, or the Britons? Of course you can assign land ownership this way — it’s called an “ethnostate”. But if you do this, it means that the descendants of immigrants can never truly be full and equal citizens of the land they were born in. If Britain is defined as the land of the Britons, then a Han person whose great-great-great-grandparents moved there from China will exist as a contingent citizen — a perpetual foreigner whose continued life in the land of their birth exists only upon the sufferance of a different race. This is the price of ethnonationalism.

The downsides of ethnonationalism have been exhaustively laid out in the decades since World War 2, and I’m not going to reiterate them all now. Suffice it to say that most nations of the world have moved away from ethnonationalism — there is an informal sense in which some people still think of France as the land of the Franks and so on, but almost all nations define citizenship and belonging through institutions rather than race. Israel, one of the few exceptions to this rule, receives a large amount of international criticism for defining itself as an ethnostate.

And yet these days I am subjected to a constant stream of ethnonationalist claims from progressives in the country of my birth. Here’s one from the ACLU of Nebraska:

ACLU of Nebraska
@ACLUofNE
This is your reminder that you’re on Indigenous land. Acknowledging that alone isn't enough. We all have a responsibility to support Indigenous communities in their work toward overcoming the lasting harms of colonization. Here are three ways to get started:
2:30 PM · Nov 28, 2024 · 1.32M Views
1.96K Replies · 20 Reposts · 152 Likes

And here’s an Instagram post from Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib:

This isn’t just something you see on social media around Thanksgiving. “Land acknowledgements” have become ubiquitous in progressive spaces and institutions — just the other day I saw one at my friend’s community dance recital.

These land acknowledgements are, legally speaking, incorrect — there is no legal sense in which the land on which they are being performed belongs to a Native American tribe. These are moral claims about rightful land ownership. But the moral principle to which they appeal is ethnonationalism — it’s the idea that plots of land are the rightful property of ethnic groups.

There is an obvious moral appeal to these land acknowledgments. They are a way of decrying the brutal, cruel, violent history of conquest and colonization. And they probably feel like a way of standing up for the weak, the marginalized, and the dispossessed.

Yet what should we think of the morality of following the principles behind land acknowledgements to their logical conclusion? “Decolonization” of the land of the U.S. would likely be an act of ethnic cleansing surpassing even the previous conquests — there are 330 million people here now, and almost none of them descend from Native Americans. An attempt to dispossess 330 million people would inevitably involve violence on a colossal scale. Here was Najma Sharif Alawi’s famous tweet right after the October 7th Hamas attacks on Israel:

Of course, “colonizers” could presumably avoid violent death or second-class citizenhood by voluntarily deporting themselves. But where would they go? Take me, for example. My ancestors were Lithuanian Jews. I could leave the country of my birth and go “back” to Lithuania — a land I don’t know, whose language I don’t speak. Yet my ancestors were not “indigenous” to Lithuania either; they moved there from somewhere else. What if the ethnic Lithuanians chose not to accept me? Where would I go then? Israel? But the folks who do land acknowledgements would consider me a “colonizer” there as well.¹

Would I then wander the Earth, desperately seeking some ethnostate that would allow me and my descendants to live there as a permanently precarious resident aliens?

Once the logic of land acknowledgements and “decolonization” is followed, it leads very quickly to some very dark futures. Assigning each person a homeland based on their ethnic ancestry, and then declaring that that homeland is the only place they or their descendants can ever truly belong, would not be an act of justice; it would be a global nightmare made real, surpassing even the horrors of previous centuries.

And in practice, any attempt to create such a world would inevitably lead to violent resistance by the groups in danger of being “decolonized”. The orderly world of nation-states would dissolve into a chaotic free-for-all of competing irredentist claims, backed by genocides and expulsions. Ten thousand October 7th-style attacks would be followed by ten thousand Gaza-style wars.

I do not want that, and you should not want it either. The American people certainly don’t want it, and the insistence of progressives on intoning land acknowledgements has probably tanked the movement’s cachet in wider society. I agree with “Wanye Burkett” when he says that land acknowledgements have probably hurt the Democratic party:

Americans do not want to see their country destroyed in the name of irredentist ethnonationalism. Nor do I blame them.

So does this mean we should paper over, ignore, or deliberately forget America’s history of violent conquest? Absolutely not. That history ought to be remembered, so that we don’t repeat it in the present day. The world’s evolution from one based on ethnic cleansing and territorial conquest to one based on fixed borders and institutions is something to celebrate — and something we must fight to preserve. We need to remember what the world used to be like, precisely so we can avoid backsliding. The most recent of conquests, expulsions, and genocides should be the last to ever happen.

And what of the Native Americans who still live in America today? Must they simply be regarded as the unlucky losers of history, and told to either assimilate into broader American society or shut up?

Absolutely not. For one thing, tribal organizations still exist — they may notionally represent ethnic groups, but they are institutions. And they are institutions with which the United States has many agreements and legal obligations that must be honored, which often give the tribes sovereignty over areas of land. Neil Gorsuch has been especially active in pushing the Supreme Court to uphold tribal rights, and I think this is a good thing.

But respect for Native American tribal organizations doesn’t have to stop at ancient obligations. There are ways to incorporate those tribes into the modern American nation that both respects them and their history and helps them prosper in the present.

Vancouver, Canada shows us an example of how this can be done. Part of Vancouver’s downtown urban area is officially under the governance of the Squamish Nation, rather than the city itself. The Squamish Nation, realizing they could do whatever they wanted with that land, decided to build a giant high-rise housing development:

Over the next few years, that skyline will get a very large new addition: Sen̓áḵw, an 11-tower development that will [put] 6,000 apartments onto just over 10 acres of land in the heart of the city. Once complete, this will be the densest neighbourhood in Canada, providing thousands of homes for Vancouverites who have long been squeezed between the country’s priciest real estate and some of its lowest vacancy rates.

Sen̓áḵw is big, ambitious and undeniably urban—and undeniably Indigenous. It’s being built on reserve land owned by the Squamish First Nation, and it’s spearheaded by the Squamish Nation itself, in partnership with the private real estate developer Westbank. Because the project is on First Nations land, not city land, it’s under Squamish authority, free of Vancouver’s zoning rules. And the Nation has chosen to build bigger, denser and taller than any development on city property would be allowed.

Here’s a picture of what it will look like:

An even bigger development called Jericho Lands is now being planned, by a consortium of tribal organizations, on land officially owned by Vancouver.

Hilariously, Vancouver’s NIMBYs are complaining, claiming that the developments are not in keeping with Indigenous tradition. But Canada’s First Nations seem to have little interest in hewing closely to other people’s view of what their traditions are. Modern people do not want to live like premodern farmers. They are not mystical Tolkien elves. They would like to have shiny new apartment buildings and walkable neighborhoods.

This, I believe, is the key to respecting and honoring Native Americans — not to focus on the tragedies of their past, but to give them the right to build a better future. Tribal lands should definitely have the autonomy to do whatever they want with their lands, including building housing or industry. In fact, we’re starting to see a pattern emerge where Native Americans embrace laissez-faire policies toward industry and manage to poach business from their over-regulated neighbors:

Tesla is ramping up efforts to open showrooms on tribal lands where it can sell directly to consumers, circumventing laws in states that bar vehicle manufacturers from also being retailers in favor of the dealership model…

Mohegan Sun, a casino and entertainment complex in Connecticut owned by the federally recognized Mohegan Tribe, announced this week that the California-based electric automaker will open a showroom with a sales and delivery center this fall on its sovereign property where the state’s law doesn’t apply…The news comes after another new Tesla showroom was announced in June, set to open in 2025 on lands of the Oneida Indian Nation in upstate New York.

This sort of thing could lead to a win-win for the U.S. and Native American tribes. American reindustrialization is being held back by a thicket of procedural requirements and local land-use regulations; if tribes were able to use their special legal status to circumvent those barriers, it could end up benefitting everyone.² The tribes would get both jobs and the ability to tax local industry; America would get to execute an end run around the NIMBYs that are holding it back.

In fact, it’s probably possible for various American cities to turn over parts of their land to tribal jurisdiction, with the assistance of the federal government. This would probably result in dense urban developments like the ones being planned in Vancouver. But even if it didn’t, it could have other commercial benefits — again, a win-win for the U.S. and for the tribes. That would certainly be a lot more substantive than a bunch of land acknowledgements. And it would likely satisfy many people’s desire for “giving land back” to Native Americans, without embracing dubious moral principles of ethnic land rights and irredentism.

In other words, you’re not living on Indigenous land right now, but you could be in the future — and it might be pretty great.

The general principle here is that instead of a dark world of ethnic cleansing in the name of “decolonization”, we should try to build a bright future where Native Americans and the United States of America exist in harmony and cooperation rather than in conflict. And that principle doesn’t just apply to America, but to the whole world. The history of land ownership is a violent and terrible one, but that doesn’t mean the future has to be more of the same.
